#6248. Don’t Scan This Abroad: The QR Code Travel Scam Tourists Miss

QR codes are everywhere when we travel now, on restaurant tables, parking meters, hotel signs, airports, train stations, and transit machines. This travel scam known as Quishing or QR code phishing is becoming the fastest growing travel scam warning out there. Most QR codes are legitimate, but scammers are using fake QR code stickers and fake payment pages to catch travellers when they are tired, rushed, or distracted.

QR code travel scam happens when a fake QR code sends travellers to a fraudulent website. The code may be placed over a real QR code on a parking meter, restaurant table, hotel notice, airport sign, or transit machine, or it may arrive by text or email pretending to be a fine, toll, ticket, or check-in request. The safest rule is simple: Pause. Check. Then pay.Read out post: 20 Common Travel Scams and How to Avoid Them

A scammer does not always need to hack a system or damage a payment machine. Sometimes they print a fake QR code sticker and place it directly over a legitimate code.

From a quick glance, the sign still looks official. The logo may look familiar. The instructions may seem normal. The page that opens may copy the colours, layout, and branding of the real company.

You think you are paying for parking, ordering food, checking into a hotel, or settling a toll. Instead, criminals may be collecting your credit card number, password, phone number, licence plate, email address, or other personal information.

The FTC has also warned about fake traffic violation texts that begin with a QR code and try to scare people into paying a fake unpaid balance.

The FTC has warned that scammers hide harmful links in QR codes to steal personal information, including by placing fake QR codes over real ones on parking meters.

Many restaurants now use QR codes for menus, ordering, or payment. Most are legitimate, but travellers should still be cautious. This is the easiest travel scam for QR code phishing as everyone uses it.

A menu QR code should usually show a menu. Be careful if it asks for information it does not need, such as your passport number, banking details, hotel room number, or a password.

Before scanning a QR code on a restaurant table, look at the surface. Does it look printed into the menu or table sign, or does it look like a sticker placed on top? If it looks raised, crooked, bubbled, or mismatched, ask staff for a printed menu or the restaurant’s official website.

Parking is one of the easiest places for this scam to work because travellers are often rushed and confused.

You may not know the local parking app. You may be dealing with another language. You may be worried about getting a ticket. That pressure makes a “scan to pay” sticker feel helpful.

Before paying through a parking QR code, inspect the sticker, read the URL preview, and check whether the payment page matches the city, parking authority, or official app named on the machine.

If anything feels off, do not use the QR code. Type the official website yourself, use the official parking app, pay at the machine, or ask local staff for help.

Airports and transit stations are full of QR codes: Wi-Fi, directions, tickets, luggage storage, forms, lounge access, and service information. Travel scams often happen when travelers are in a hurry. If you need wifi, a taxi, some food, QR codes are often the easiest way to catch you off guard.

That does not mean every code is unsafe. It means you should slow down when a public QR code asks for payment, passwords, ID documents, or personal information.

The FBI warns that malicious QR codes can send people to fake sites, steal victim data, embed malware, or redirect payments. The FBI warns that criminals can tamper with QR codes to redirect payments, steal login and financial information, or send people to malicious websites.

The easiest way to avoid this scam is to build one habit before you scan a public QR code.

Do not scan just because a sign looks official. Public signs, parking meters, table cards, and posters can be tampered with.

If the message says you must pay immediately, avoid a fine, settle a toll, confirm a booking, or prevent a penalty, slow down. Urgency is one of the biggest warning signs.

Before your phone opens anything, look at the QR code itself.

We call this the scratch test. You are not damaging the sign. You are simply checking whether the QR code feels or looks different from the rest of the surface.

Canadian readers can also check the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security’s QR code safety guidance and report fraud through the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre.

Most phones show a preview of the website before opening the page. Read it.

Look for misspellings, extra words, strange endings, random letters, shortened links, or a domain that does not match the company, hotel, restaurant, city, or attraction.

Do not rely only on the padlock symbol. A secure connection does not automatically mean the site is legitimate. The real question is whether you are on the correct website.

The FTC has also warned about fake traffic violation texts that include a QR code and pressure people to pay a fake unpaid balance.

For payments, passwords, account logins, or identity information, the safest option is often to bypass the QR code.

Open your browser and type the official website yourself. Use an app you already installed from the official app store. Ask an employee for the correct payment method. Contact your hotel, airline, rental car company, or bank through the phone number on your booking or card — not through the number on a suspicious page.

First, do not panic. Scanning a QR code does not automatically mean your information has been stolen. The bigger risk usually begins when you enter payment information, type a password, download a file, or provide personal details.

Close the page immediately if the link looks wrong, the message creates urgency, or the site asks for information you did not expect to provide.

Do not download an unfamiliar app or file from a QR code.

If you entered credit card information, contact your bank or card issuer using the official number on the back of your card or through the official banking app.

If you entered a password, change it through the official website or app. If you reused that password anywhere else, change it there too.

Watch for follow-up messages. A scammer who has some of your information may later pretend to be your bank, hotel, airline, rental car company, or payment provider.

Report the fake QR code to the business, parking authority, hotel, airport, or local authority so they can remove it.

A QR code may be suspicious if it looks like a sticker placed over another code, has peeling edges, opens a strange URL, uses a shortened link, creates urgency, asks for information that does not make sense, or directs you away from the official website or app.

At a restaurant, a QR menu should not need your passport or banking password. At a parking meter, the payment page should match the city or parking authority. At a hotel, a check-in code should not send you to a random payment page outside the official booking system.

The BBB has also warned consumers to double-check QR codes before paying for parking.

No. QR codes are part of modern travel, and many are perfectly safe.

The goal is not to panic every time you see one. The goal is to stop treating every QR code as automatically trustworthy.

A few seconds of inspection can protect you from a much longer financial or account-recovery problem later.

QR codes are convenient, but convenience is exactly what scammers are using against travellers.

Before scanning a public QR code at a restaurant, parking meter, hotel, airport, train station, attraction, or transit stop, remember the rule:

Inspect the code. Read the link. Go directly to the official website or app when money, passwords, or personal information are involved.

That tiny pause may be the thing that saves your trip.

Scanning a QR code is not automatically dangerous. The danger usually begins when you open a suspicious page, enter payment details, type a password, download a file, or provide personal information without checking whether the site is legitimate.

Inspect the physical code for stickers, raised edges, bubbles, peeling corners, or anything placed over another code. Then check the URL preview before opening the page. If the link looks strange or does not match the official company, city, hotel, or attraction, do not use it.

Before entering payment information, make sure the website belongs to the official business or authority. When in doubt, use the official app, type the website manually, pay directly at the machine, or ask staff for the correct payment method.

Contact your bank or card issuer immediately using the official number on the back of your card or your banking app. Watch for suspicious charges, replace the card if needed, and do not use any contact information from the suspicious website.

#6247. What Travelers Should Know About the Galápagos Floods—and the Ongoing Impact of El Niño

On October 30 and 31, 2026, torrential rainfall on the Galápagos's Santa Cruz island caused waterways to overflow, flooding neighborhoods, damaging homes, and disrupting essential infrastructure. The local government declared an emergency, with over 2,000 people affected by the damage. This places the Galápagos among several beloved tourism destinations that are already grappling with the effects of El Niño.

The news has also left many travelers wondering: Is it safe to travel to the Galápagos right now? And how should those with upcoming cruises and hotel stays proceed?

Rodrigo Jácome, who runs La K-leta Guest House and a small coffee farm on Santa Cruz, which is the archipelago's main inhabited island and a central hub for tourism, says the flooding has not damaged key tourism infrastructure—though it devastated other local livelihoods. “The flooding affected residential neighborhoods that are not particularly close to the main hotel areas,” says Jácome, who lost most of his coffee harvest in the rains. For those with upcoming travel, and locals who rely on travelers to make a living, however, “tourism operations resumed within days.”

Authorities have reopened most visitor sites in the Galápagos National Park, and transportation has resumed, though conditions remain subject to change. Below, we report on all of the impacted areas across the Galápagos, which tours may be rerouted, and how to stay up on the news as future weather develops, according to those on the ground. Plus, local tour operators share advice on planning accordingly for trips in the months ahead.

Santa Cruz is where you'll find many hotels, restaurants, tour operators, and transportation connections, and the area that experienced the most significant damage. Santa Cruz serves as a major base for day trips and cruises to other islands. Most visitors arriving by air fly in via neighboring Baltra, where the airport is located.

Puerto Ayora, the island's main town, and the highland parish of Bellavista, were among the affected areas. Floodwaters damaged homes and roads, disrupted water and electricity services, and forced families to evacuate. The flooding also affected transportation infrastructure connecting Santa Cruz to Baltra Airport, the main gateway for visitors arriving by air to Santa Cruz. The road reopened on November 5 and reconstruction work is being carried out in parallel, allowing travelers to continue arriving to the island as planned.

Although the emergency was concentrated in Santa Cruz, other islands also experienced heavy rainfall and localized flooding. Whitman Cox, a Galápagos National Park naturalist guide based in San Cristóbal, which is known for its sea lion colonies, volcanic landscapes, and popular snorkeling and diving sites, says there was no such damage in San Cristobal, but access to some of the beaches around the island has been restricted as weather conditions change.

Travelers should therefore check conditions for all destinations on their itinerary, across the archipelago, rather than assuming all islands have been affected equally. Constant communication with tour guides, your hotel, or cruise line is the best way to get up-to-date information.

While the Galápagos National Park has progressively reopened, the Los Humedales sector in Isabela (above) remains closed.

As of November 9, flights to Baltra and San Cristóbal were operating on their regular schedules, according to local reporting. Tourism activities have also continued, although some visitor sites remain temporarily closed.

The Galápagos National Park has progressively reopened areas following safety assessments: As of November 9, Playa El Garrapatero in Santa Cruz was accessible again, while popular visitor sites Las Grietas, El Chato, and El Puntudo remained restricted. In San Cristóbal, La Lobería and Punta Carola had reopened, while surfing spots Puerto Chino and Playa Baquerizo remained closed. The Los Humedales sector in Isabela also remained closed. From November 9-18, Tortuga Bay, a beach in Santa Cruz, will be closed as a preventative measure due to tide changes.

The UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office updated its Ecuador travel advisory on November 1 to include the flooding on Santa Cruz. It advises travelers to follow local authorities' instructions, avoid flooded areas, and confirm travel arrangements with airlines and tour operators.

Cox emphasizes that travelers shouldn't panic—El Niño is a natural weather cycle. “People can still come. We shouldn't frighten them," says Cox. His main guidance is to be patient. “They may encounter transportation difficulties between certain points, which could take additional time.” He adds that the park has done its best in the interest of safety by closing the above sites as a precautionary measure.

The flooding comes as Ecuador experiences an El Niño event, a climate phenomenon characterized by unusually warm ocean temperatures across the equatorial Pacific, which can alter atmospheric circulation and rainfall patterns. In Ecuador, El Niño is often associated with heavier rainfall, particularly along the coast and in the Galápagos. However, its effects vary by region and over time.

According to the National Institute of Meteorology and Hydrology (INAMHI), the El Niño event remained active and was strengthening for the upcoming months with weather reports suggesting that heavy rainfall may last until February 2027.

The potential implications for travelers include heavy rain, temporary road closures, changes to boat excursions, and restricted access to natural visitor sites. Weather conditions can also affect marine activities and inter-island transportation.

However, this is not the first time El Niño has impacted the islands, and tour guides understand how to prepare. “It is a cyclical part of nature that we have seen every 10-15 years,” says Charles Wittmer, president of the Association of Boat Operators in the Galápagos, ADATUR. “Nature is unpredictable and if anything, this is a chance to see the adaptations of animals to changing weather conditions,” he says. “Remember: this is a natural laboratory of evolution.” On the wildlife front, Wittmer mentions that Galápagos penguins and cormorants adapt to warming ocean waters. And there's a plus: These shifts in marine ecosystem activity may increase the variety of species spotted while snorkeling.

If you have an upcoming trip, local tourism specialists recommend staying informed and remaining flexible. It’s best to ask about excursion alternatives when booking a tour in the islands, should weather create the need to pivot.

Before departure, confirm your flights and accommodation directly with your airline and tour operator. Ask whether your planned excursions are operating as anticipated and whether alternative activities are available if certain visitor sites are closed. Ask your tour guide for updates daily.

It's also a good idea to purchase travel insurance that covers weather-related disruptions, medical emergencies, and unexpected accommodation or transportation expenses. Travelers can monitor official updates from INAMHI and the Galápagos National Park social media and from their website with forecasts, and plan smart by allowing extra flexibility in travel connections and excursions. Remember to also pack lightweight rain protection and waterproof bags for electronics and important documents.

Like Cox, Wittmer emphasizes that nature is out of our control. “People should bring clothing and be ready for heavier rainfall and be flexible in their expectations.”

Though travelers come to the Galápagos for the nature, local guides are the greatest resource in appreciating this place—and navigating it in uncertain times.

Whether staying in local communities, visiting for a few hours on cruise excursions, or simply passing through in transit, travelers contribute to the livelihoods of local businesses and workers, many of whom are also dealing with the consequences of the flooding, simply by visiting. As Jácome puts it, “Tourism is needed now more than ever to help rebuild the communities that lost everything.”

Consider booking locally owned accommodation, hiring licensed local guides, eating at independent restaurants, and purchasing goods from small businesses.

As always, travelers should also be mindful that affected neighborhoods are not tourist attractions. Avoid visiting damaged homes or taking photographs of residents dealing with the aftermath of the flooding without their permission.

If you are traveling to Galápagos right now, consider packing water purification tablets, basic first-aid supplies, and hygiene kits to done to affected families (your guide or hotel can assist with routing these to the right place). You can also check with local emergency centers or your tour operator upon arrival to donate pet food or clean clothes directly to the most impacted neighborhoods.

If you want to contribute to recovery efforts from afar, several organizations and initiatives have mobilized support:

Fundación Charles Darwin: The foundation is part of an emergency fundraising initiative, with proceeds directed to the Santa Cruz emergency response committee (COE) to support urgent community needs.

San Francisco de Quito University: The University has established a SOS Galapagos fund, collecting donations on their campus in Quito. They also have a donations link.

Fundación Torraja: This local organization is administering a Community Kitchen and providing meals and donations directly to families who lost their belongings in the floods.

#6246. 9 NYC Christmas Markets for Food, Fun, and Getting All Your Gift Shopping Done

New York City is electric any time of year, but few months on the calendar are as magical as the final two. In the run up to Christmas in New York, the Big Apple transforms into a holiday winter wonderland: think twinkling lights on street posts, elaborate department store window displays, and marquee theater events like New York City Ballet’s The Nutcracker or the Radio City Rockettes. It’s also probably the best time of the year to shop, thanks to a flurry of NYC Christmas markets that set up everywhere from Bryant Park to Grand Central Terminal.

But with so many to choose from, and locations all over the boroughs, how do you know which one is best for you to visit? That’s where we come in. Not only are we yearly visitors to all the annual markets, we’ve already done the research to scout the best newcomers to the field for 2026. Below, find our New Yorker-vetted NYC Christmas markets worth a holiday visit, from favorite and famed ones like Union Square’s, to newer events like Eater Under Wraps and Field + Supply.

Read our complete New York City travel guide here, which includes:

The rink at Bryant Park is tied only with Wollman in Central Park for the title of most famous in the city, and it's part of the Winter Village that runs here every year.

Location: Bryant Park, New York, NY 10018

Why we love it: There’s something for everyone at the massive Bank of America Winter Village at Bryant Park in the heart of Midtown. Gift givers will love The Holiday Shops by Urbanspace, a European-style market made up of “jewel box” kiosks filled with 180-plus vendors stocking everything from cozy winter hats to artisanal ornaments, while outdoor food stands at The Lodge provide plenty of fuel like s’mores and sausages for your shopping escapades. The Winter Village is also home to one of the city’s most famed ice rinks, which is free to use (though skate rental fees apply if you don’t bring your own).

The Grand Central Holiday Fair is celebrating its 21st year within the iconic terminal's shuttle passage.

Location: Vanderbilt Hall, Grand Central Terminal, 89 E. 42nd Street, New York, NY 10017

Why we love it: If you’re not exactly a fan of the cold weather, we have good news: New York City is also home to a handful of fantastic indoor holiday markets. The longest-running is the Grand Central Holiday Fair inside the city’s transportation crown jewel, Grand Central Terminal. The train station’s annual Holiday Fair inside Vanderbilt Hall features over thirty small businesses selling handmade gifts, plus an Uncommon Goods pop-up and an outpost of the Grand Central Gift Shop for all the train lovers on your list. And speaking of trains: after you’re done shopping, stick around the Terminal to watch the famed Holiday Train Show, featuring model trains trundling along decorated tracks that feature NYC landmarks and even the North Pole.

Union Square Holiday Market remains the gold standard classic for most New Yorkers, with 185 vendors spiraling out in a seemingly endless array of booths.

Location: Union Square, New York, NY 10003

Why we love it: If you say “holiday market” to a New Yorker, chances are they’ll direct you to the bustling Union Square Holiday Market. With nearly 200 vendors spread across concentric half-circles of booths, we’re not exaggerating when we say you can find the perfect present for everyone on your list at this sprawling pop-up. Some buzzy vendors to look out for this year? The MB Edit for vintage accessories and silk scarves, Hudson Valley Seed Company for organic bulbs and seeds, and make sure to save time to explore the many food purveyors for snacks, like Fan-Fan Donuts from James Beard Award nominee Fany Gerson. Pro tip: As the city’s most famous market, it can get quite crowded on nights and weekends, so try to opt for daytime weekday visits if possible.

Location: 100 W. 77th Street, New York, NY 10024

Dates: Every Sunday from November 29 until December 30

Why we love it: While many of New York’s most famed holiday markets have the polish so closely associated with the city, one of the reasons Grand Holiday Bazaar is beloved is that it feels like a proper neighborhood event. Held every Sunday in a combo indoor-outdoor space on the Upper West Side, the Bazaar hosts over 150 independent, rotating local vendors who sell everything from handmade holiday decor to vintage accessories to skincare. Plus, 100 percent of the event’s profits are donated to four local public schools that serve over 2,000 kids.

FAD Market Holiday Pop-Up will set up shop in the lobby of Empire Stores in Dumbo, also home to Time Out Market.

Location: Empire Stores, 55 Water Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201 (Dumbo) and St. Paul, 190 Court Street, Brooklyn, NY 11201 (Cobble Hill)

Dates: November 30 – December 20 (Dumbo) and December 5–6, 12–13, and 19–20 (Cobble Hill)

Why we love it: FAD (which stands for Fashion, Art, Design) will host double the markets this year, in two separate locations in Brooklyn. Dumbo, which will run continuously from November 30th until December 20th inside Empire Stores, will have a rotating selection of jewelry makers, ceramicists, and small-batch food purveyors, with about 35 vendors on weekends and 14 during the week. Cobble Hill’s pop-up, meanwhile, will run over three weekends in December at St. Paul church, with a brand-new crew of 70-plus makers selling giftables like apparel, home decor, and skincare.

Turkish jewelry, fondue baguettes, and artisan soaps are on offer at Columbus Circle's Central Park-adjacent Christmas market.

Location: Columbus Circle, New York, NY, 10019

Why we love it: Situated at one of the prettiest corners of Manhattan—smack between Columbus Circle and Central Park—this market would be worth the trip even if the vendors were hawking only touristy souvenirs. Luckily though, the selection here is carefully curated, with makers this year ranging from Seyahan’s Turkish-inspired jewelry to Fairy Greens Lavender Farm’s fragrant collection of candles, soaps, and body oils made with the dreamy plant. There’s also plenty to snack on: don’t miss first-time vendor Fondue Baguette selling—you guessed it—baguettes filled with cheese.

Location: Herald Square, New York, NY 10001

Field + Supply, one of upstate New York's premier makers' markets, has landed in the city for the first time this year with a weekend pop-up in the Starrett-Lehigh Building.

Location: Starrett-Lehigh Building, 601 W. 26th Street, New York, NY 10001

Why we love it: One of upstate New York’s premier makers’ markets returns to the city this year, much to the delight of anyone looking for chic home goods, artisanal jewelry, and much more. There will be 140-plus vendors at the two-day Field + Supply event in Chelsea, with products ranging from ceramics to textiles to specialty foods. And even if you’re shopped out, there’s plenty else to lure you, including a visit from Santa himself and retro tintype portraits.

Location: Iron23, 29 W. 23rd Street, New York, NY 10010

Why we love it: The ultimate one-stop-shop for foodies, Eater Under Wraps, returns for a one-day-only market this year in Chelsea. Brands like Pepsi, Reese’s, and Kahlúa will host activations, along with food and drink samples from local spots like Shania's Max Bet and Nishaan, and, naturally, a robust, curated selection of gifts chosen by Eater’s own editors.

#6245. Can you save money with a theme park annual pass? We did the math

Annual passes to major U.S. theme parks like Walt Disney World, Universal Orlando Resort, SeaWorld and Legoland come with a long list of benefits. You can visit as often as you like; you get discounts on extras like parking, merchandise and dining; and your pass often comes with access to special events throughout the year.

Theme park annual passes also come with a hefty price tag that can climb upward of $1,000. Because of this, it can be easy to assume an annual pass is only worth the cost if you live near one of these parks and can visit every week.

As an out-of-state resident who has held an annual pass to Universal Orlando Resort since 2020, I can assure you that assumption is incorrect. But you don't have to take my word for it.

I calculated the break-even point for 10 theme parks across the country to help you decide whether it's an option worth looking into. For consistency, I based these calculations on each park's top-tier pass and the lowest one-day ticket prices, using park-to-park tickets at resorts with multiple parks, since annual passes include park-to-park access.

Because these calculations are based on one-day tickets, you would still need to determine whether you could save money with an annual pass by considering the ticket cost on the date(s) of your visit (most parks have variable pricing), how many trips you take each year and the number of days you visit per trip.

**About 6 once you factor in the cost of free parking and the Express passes

Disney World offers several annual passes, but only one, the Disney Incredi-Pass, is available to out-of-state residents. The Disney Incredi-Pass has no blockout dates and includes complimentary theme park parking.

If you were to visit only on the cheapest days of the year, you would need to visit nine times each year to realize the value of a Disney World annual pass as a non-Florida resident. When you factor in shopping and dining discounts and free parking, you can probably break even after eight visits. But if you were to visit on the more expensive days, you could break even in closer to six days.

Related: Bluey, Buzz and Grogu: Opening dates for new Disney World and Disneyland attractions in 2026

Remember, though, this comparison is based on the one-day ticket price. If you plan to spend eight days at Disney World broken up between one or two visits per year, you could potentially do better to buy a multiday park hopper ticket versus an annual pass. Because Disney uses variable ticket pricing and tickets get less expensive as you add more days, you have to do the math to find out which is best for you.

Don't worry, the math on most other parks isn't quite as involved.

Disneyland's top-tier pass is called the Inspire Key. At $1,899 per year, this pass has blackout dates during the weeks of Christmas and New Year's Eve, and it includes free standard parking and unlimited Disney PhotoPass downloads.

The Inspire Key pass can pay for itself after 11 visits, since the lowest park hopper tickets start at $179.

Related: How Disneyland's newest ride proves that 'progress is impossible without change'

As with Disney World, the number of visits required to break even would decrease if you visited on more expensive days, and you could still save money by purchasing multiday tickets.

Universal Orlando has several annual pass options, but the 2-Park Premier Pass is the easiest to use and has the most benefits. You get park-to-park admission between Universal Studios Florida and Universal Islands of Adventure, complimentary skip-the-line Express passes after 4 p.m., complimentary valet and prime parking, one free ticket to Halloween Horror Nights, early park admission and several valuable discounts.

If you were to visit during the holidays when one-day park-to-park tickets climb as high as $255, you can break even after four days. It's also worth doing the calculations with the included Halloween Horror Nights ticket, which starts at $99. When you factor that in, you can break even after five visits.

Related: Epic Universe tips: 11 ways to spend less time in line and have more fun

A six-day park-to-park ticket that also includes access to Universal Epic Universe is only $550.99 per person, so if you only plan to visit once per year for six days, you would save significantly by purchasing a multiday ticket versus an annual pass.

Universal Studios Hollywood only has one park, making the math here easier to calculate. The park's Platinum Annual Pass has no blockout dates and includes free general parking most of the year, one Halloween Horror Nights ticket and Express skip-the-line access after 3 p.m.

You'd technically have to visit 6.0025 times to break even, but if you include the free parking and after-3 p.m. Express passes, we can safely say you break even after six visits.

Related: Thrills for all ages: 6 best rides at Universal Studios Hollywood

Similar to Universal Orlando, you can break even sooner if you factor in the cost of a Halloween Horror Nights ticket, which starts at $77 per person. When you factor that in, plus those other perks, you can break even after approximately five one-day visits.

This is where things get a little bit fun (in my opinion, anyway). Legoland's Premium Annual Pass includes visits to more than 20 Merlin attractions across the country, including Legoland, Peppa Pig Park, Sea Life Aquarium, Madame Tussauds wax museum and more. A lot of these parks are in theme park hubs like Florida, California and Texas, so you likely aren't too far from one or multiple locations.

In this case, you don't need to plan multiple visits to a single park to see the value in an annual pass. You can visit multiple locations around the country with no blockout dates, free parking and four free "Bring-a-Friend" tickets (one ticket per quarter), which make the math very appealing.

If you assign a $69 value to the "Bring-A-Friend" tickets, four per year would equal $276, just $23 less than the total annual pass cost. So, if you were to visit one of the 20+ parks nationwide four times per year (once per quarter) and bring a friend or family member with you, you'd save money with an annual pass before even factoring in free parking and other discounts.

This is another instance where you can access multiple parks with a single annual pass. SeaWorld Orlando's Platinum Pass includes unlimited admission to 11 parks across the country with no blockout dates. These include all SeaWorld and Busch Gardens parks, as well as their affiliated water parks. You also get eight free guest tickets, free photos and free preferred parking.

A few notes here. You can't use all eight free guest tickets at the same time and they are limited to select parks. SeaWorld allows you to use a certain number of tickets during different calendar windows throughout the year. But if you were to visit these parks eight times per year and bring a friend, you would save more than $600 by purchasing an annual pass.

It's also worth noting that SeaWorld San Diego's Platinum Pass is only $201 on sale, and its lowest one-day ticket costs $64.99, so you'd break even after just four visits. While it provides the passholder access to the same 11 parks, its guest passes can only be used at the California parks.

Opened in July 2026, Universal Kids Resort is the newest park on this list. The park recently started selling annual passes, with the Gold Annual Pass being its top-tier offering. The Gold pass has no blockout dates and includes regular self-parking.

Assuming you visit on five separate days and only visit on the least expensive days, you would break even after five visits. But because the Gold Pass also includes free parking and other discounts, you could potentially break even in four one-day visits. Because the park also sells discounted multiday tickets, the above math only makes sense if you were to visit on five nonconsecutive days.

You don't need to live in Florida or California to have access to award-winning theme parks. Holiday World in Santa Claus, Indiana, consistently wins awards for its cleanliness, water park and thrilling coasters. Holiday World's Platinum Pass has no blockout dates, early entry for select attractions and discounted "Bring-a-Friend" tickets.

Holiday World already offers free parking, sunscreen and soft drinks, so you won't get additional discounts there. You would break even after four one-day visits, assuming you purchase the lowest-cost tickets.

Dollywood's top-of-the-line pass is a Diamond Season Pass (a very fitting name for our bright and shining queen Dolly Parton, if you ask me). With it, you get unlimited visits, complimentary parking, Time Saver skip-the-line access for the first hour of each day, a 20% discount on shopping and dining, and four free "Bring-a-Friend" tickets.

Dollywood handles its "Bring-a-Friend" tickets differently. You can use them one at a time or all four at once. If you brought four friends with you during your first visit after buying your annual pass, you would have more than covered the cost of your pass. In fact, you could save about $110 by purchasing an annual pass instead of five one-day tickets (you and four friends). Any future visits that year are just a bonus. Just one of the million reasons to love Dollywood.

Silver Dollar City and Dollywood are owned by the same parent company (Herschend Family Entertainment), but their annual passes work quite differently. Silver Dollar City's Diamond Pass includes unlimited visits to the park and White Water water park, eight free "Bring A Friend" tickets (to be used during specific redemption windows at Silver Dollar City or White Water), a bonus "Bring-a-Friend" ticket you can use on any day and $29.99 tickets for friends and family.

Even though you can't use all of your "Bring-a-Friend" tickets at one time, you only need to visit with a guest twice to break even with an annual pass before even digging into the savings you would find from in-park discounts.

In addition to the advertised benefits, there is a level of convenience that comes with being a passholder. You can pop in for a few hours without feeling like you wasted money on a full-day ticket, and you feel like a more valuable guest when you visit. I often get things like priority parade seating, fun freebies and passholder-only discounts of up to 70% off merchandise.

No amount of math matters unless you know you will actually use and enjoy the benefits of being a passholder. Use these calculations as a jumping-off point to decide if you are ready to be a passholder.

#6244. Where to Find 15 of Philly's Best Cheesesteaks, According to a Longtime Local

The City of Brotherly Love is filled with meat-and-cheese sandwich lovers. Philadelphia is defined by the big three: Hoagies (loaded Italian and chicken cutlet sandwiches), roast pork (with garlicky broccoli rabe and sharp provolone), and cheesesteaks.

The cheesesteak's story began in the 1930s in South Philadelphia but has become a staple at corner shops across the region, given the gourmet remix by award-winning chefs, and even inspired international outposts in Tokyo and London. I've been eating cheesesteaks since my college days, and as a Philly lifer, I've got plenty of opinions. Consider this your beginner’s guide.

Cheesesteaks are as much a part of Philly's late-night food culture as they are a daytime attraction, especially on weekends and game days. Expect long lines, limited seating, and plenty of takeout orders at popular spots, and bring cash—many old-school shops don't accept cards. Like New York's pizza slice culture, cheesesteaks are typically eaten on the go or at a nearby outdoor table. Grab extra napkins and come hungry.

A classic Philly cheesesteak starts with thinly sliced ribeye steak, melted cheese, and a long Italian roll. But no two shops make it exactly the same, and everyone has their preferences.

The meat: Some shops finely chop their ribeye on the grill, while others leave it in thin slices or longer strips. It comes down to whether you prefer a finely chopped, cheesy mixture or more substantial bites of steak.

The cheese and toppings: American, Cheez Whiz, and provolone are the traditional choices. In Philly, you'll hear people order their preferred cheese "wit" or "without," referring to fried onions. For example, "Whiz wit" means Cheez Whiz with onions, while "American without" means American cheese without onions. Other popular toppings include mushrooms, sweet or hot peppers, which you can often request on the side.

The bread: A good cheesesteak roll is typically long and Italian-style, sometimes seeded, with a lightly crunchy crust and soft interior—similar to New Orleans French bread. Some shops scoop out the excess bread to make more room for the steak and cheese, while others leave the roll intact. Either way, the bread needs to hold up to all that juicy filling.

John's Roast Pork has a signature sandwich of the same name.

John’s on East Snyder Avenue has been a neighborhood fixture for nearly a century, thanks to the Bucci family. The James Beard Award-winning shop has also been voted Best Cheesesteak multiple times, known for its hefty portions of finely chopped, crispy ribeye steak served on crusty rolls sourced from nearby Carangi’s or Sarcone’s. Choose from American, provolone, or Cooper Sharp cheese. Expect long lines, but there’s outdoor seating and a semi-enclosed dining area where you can dig in. And if you’ve got the appetite, don’t leave without trying their signature roast pork sandwich.

You’ve probably heard the hype or seen the long lines on 9th Street. Every cheesesteak at Angelo’s is made with house-baked, crusty bread and fresh, peppery ribeye steak, with your choice of Cooper Sharp or the increasingly popular long-hot-pepper-infused Cheez Whiz. Since its Italian Market debut, the Michelin Bib Gourmand-recognized shop has expanded beyond its Italian Street location, including an outpost at a food hall in Wilmington, Delaware and a ghost kitchen deeper in South Philly, with more locations on the horizon.

400 South St. Philadelphia, PA 19147431 N. 62nd St. Philadelphia, PA 19151

Philadelphia is lucky to have two Jim’s Steaks, each with its own personality. The 50-year-old Jim’s South Street is where all walks of life congregate late into the night, plotting their orders (definitely get the famous Whiz wit), scrambling for cash (there’s an ATM inside that sometimes works), and hollering at motorbikes cruising by. Inside, there’s a first-floor diner-style dining room and a second floor adorned with rare mosaics by the late legendary Philadelphia artist Isaiah Zagar, whose Philadelphia’s Magic Gardens is just a few blocks west. Over in West Philly, Jim’s West—the original location, now under different ownership—sits on a residential corner where O.G.s line up to bring cheesesteaks home to family and friends or score a $20 combo special: a beef or chicken cheesesteak, a drink, and a side of banana pudding.

517 South St. Philadelphia, PA 19147337 South St. Philadelphia, PA 19147

Recently featured in season six of Abbott Elementary, the nearly 50-year-old Ishkabibble’s has long attracted celebrities, locals, and tourists alike, often captured on camera by local photographer South Street Sam. The shop helped popularize chicken cheesesteaks and hot pepper-and-onion Spanish fries, eventually expanding to a second, larger location with additional seating just two blocks away. Chicken cheesesteaks are the name of the game here, with nearly a dozen variations, including Pizza (mozzarella and pizza sauce), South Philly (roasted peppers, spinach, and provolone), and Broccoli (melted cheese and steamed broccoli). Wash it all down with their famous Gremlin, a half-grape soda, half-lemonade concoction. Trust us.

What began as a Northeast Philly corner shop in 1949 has changed owners, locations, and names over the decades, but one thing remains: its signature thinly sliced ribeye cheesesteaks, grilled to order with or without onions on fresh Liscio's rolls delivered daily. In 2013, the renamed shop landed at Fishtown's buzzy corner of Girard and Frankford avenues, transforming into a family-friendly, '50s-style diner with an expanded menu. Alongside its classic cheesesteaks, you'll find vegetarian versions with onions and mushrooms, gluten-free roll options, crinkle-cut fries, egg creams, and sundaes.

1338 S. 10th Street Philadelphia, PA 19147

Got cheesesteak FOMO because you're vegan? Or have plant-based loved ones who want in on the Philly experience? Triangle Tavern, a neighborhood bar on East Passyunk Avenue, has you covered. Most of the menu is vegetarian or vegan, including its only cheesesteak, which was crowned Best Vegan Cheesesteak in Philly by the American Vegan Center in 2019. The winning sandwich features locally owned Blackbird Foods' seitan, fried onions, and a Carangi Bakery roll, all smothered in house-made vegan Whiz (a blend of Daiya vegan cheddar, Tofutti cream cheese, miso, nutritional yeast, and seasonings).

For decades, Robert Perry has cultivated a community of artists, musicians, creatives, and beer lovers at this two-story rock-and-roll bar known for its sticker- and graffiti-covered walls. Affectionately called TMoms by locals, Tattooed Mom welcomes meat lovers and plant-based eaters alike with a savory, gooey vegan cheesesteak. Chunks of seitan and plant-based smoked Gouda replace the traditional steak and Whiz, all tucked into a crusty roll from local bakery Merzbacher's of Germantown. Even better, you can snag one for just $7 on Meatless Mondays.

4540 Baltimore Ave. Philadelphia, PA 19143

A West Philly institution, this husband-and-wife-run Ethiopian restaurant and bar is known for its mashup of East African and Philly staples, particularly its berbere-spiced beef cheesesteaks, served since 1996. Thinly sliced beef is coated in an earthy, fiery blend of chili peppers, coriander, ginger, cardamom, nutmeg, and allspice, then tossed with onions and melted American cheese. The result is a juicy, boldly seasoned cheesesteak with a kick.

1600 W. Girard Ave. Philadelphia, PA 19130

Fairmount may not be the first neighborhood that comes to mind for a Philly cheesesteak, but it's home to an 8,500-square-foot indoor mini golf course serving pan-Asian-inspired bar food. Opened in 2021 by three longtime friends, Libertee Grounds has a playful menu to match, including an Indian-inspired Lamb Kheema cheesesteak made with a masala-rubbed lamb and ribeye blend, melted Cooper Sharp, caramelized onions, and cilantro-lime aioli on a seeded long roll. It comes with fries, but for an extra kick, add pickled Fresno peppers or miso Cooper Sharp cheese Whiz.

3101 Tasker St. Philadelphia, PA 191453401 Walnut St. Franklin's Table Food Hall, Philadelphia, PA 191042563 Trenton Ave. Philadelphia, PA 19125

What began as a food cart in 2022 has grown into multiple Philadelphia locations for Korea Taqueria, where chef-owners Alexander Sherack and Rene Lopez blend traditional Korean flavors with Mexican street food staples. Their Korean-Mexican mashups include a signature slow-burn spicy bulgogi cheesesteak featuring thinly sliced halal ribeye marinated in bulgogi sauce, melted Cooper Sharp, gochujang mayo, and scallions on a seeded Liscio's hoagie roll. Add cucumber kimchi for an extra tangy crunch.

Dalessandro's sits in Roxborough, in the city's northwest outskirts.

Husband-and-wife team Steve and Margie Kotridis have kept this Northwest Philly cheesesteak shop humming with hungry customers since taking over in 2008. Now one of three Michelin Bib Gourmand-recognized cheesesteak shops in Philadelphia, alongside Del Rossi's and Angelo's, Dalessandro's is known for its juicy, gooey, squishy sandwiches. Finely minced ribeye, melted cheese, and generously diced onions meld together inside Amoroso's hearth-baked rolls (another local favorite bakery), which soak up all that goodness. Better yet, toppings are free. Grab your cheesesteak to go and, weather permitting, enjoy it beneath the trees at the park across the street.

3653 Germantown Ave.Philadelphia, PA 19140

This North Philly cheesesteak shop is a celebrity in its own right, having appeared in Creed and Creed II and attracted famous fans like Philly's own Colman Domingo. Since 1994, crowds have lined up beneath its glowing red neon sign near the Broad and Erie transit hub for finely chopped "100% sirloin steak," served in half, whole (12-inch), or Giant (two-foot) portions. Order yours Whiz wit (ketchup is a popular addition here), grab some cheese fries, and join the regulars eating off the hoods of their cars. Those in the know head next door to Eagle Bar for a beer before calling it a night.

3020 S. Broad St. Philadelphia, Pennsylvania 19145

Heading down to the stadiums for a game? Consider Skinny Joey's your pre- or post-game cheesesteak fix. Former inmate turned podcaster turned restaurateur Joey Merlino has entered Philly's competitive cheesesteak scene, offering six beef and chicken variations that draw long lines of customers and parked cars along Broad Street on weekends. And he's not stopping there: Merlino has expanded to the Jersey Shore with a Wildwood outpost.

Competition and tradition run deep in Philly's cheesesteak scene, a challenge Nish Patel embraced when he took over Del Rossi's in 2020. He helped usher in a new wave of cheesesteak making by focusing on better ingredients and technique rather than reinventing the classic sandwich. First came a house-baked roll with a crunchy crust and pillowy-soft interior. Next, pasture-raised, hormone-free, hand-cut ribeye steak, followed by melted Cooper Sharp American cheese and onions. The upgrades paid off: Del Rossi's earned Michelin Bib Gourmand recognition in 2026.

One of Philly's newest cheesesteak sensations, Sal Burgese's Backyard Cravings began as pandemic-era home cooking for friends, family, and a few lucky guests at his South Philly rowhome. What started in his backyard grew into tailgating parties and, eventually, his first brick-and-mortar shop in October 2026. Like Del Rossi's, the focus here is on quality ingredients and cooking from scratch. The $20+ cheesesteak has a generous portion of finely chopped, salt-and-pepper-seasoned beef, onions, and creamy Cooper Sharp cheese on a long, crisp, sesame-seeded roll with a soft, scooped-out center. Burgese's cheesesteaks have drawn sold-out crowds wherever he's served them, so for now, the Eagles “Kelly Green” and cream-colored corner spot sells them only on weekends.

#6243. I Visited China as an American Without a Visa—Here’s How You Can Do It Too

Last month, I visited China as an American—without going through a multi-week visa application process. This is thanks to a recent policy introduced in 2024 that allows certain travelers to visit China for a maximum of 10 days while transiting between one country and another. Though the rule can feel intimidating in theory, it’s relatively straightforward in practice as long as you prepare accordingly.

Officially called the “240-Hour Visa-Free Transit Policy," the program is part of China’s goal to attract more inbound international travelers, according to Mei Zhang, the founder of WildChina and a Condé Nast Traveler travel specialist. “The idea is to make visiting China an easier decision,” Zhang says. “Most people are daunted by the idea of queuing for a visa at the Chinese consulate. Removing that step makes it easier for people to come.”

And even though the policy is designed for transiting between countries, 10 days is still enough time for a meaningful visit. “Beyond the quick business visits or short stopovers people may associate with China, ten days gives travelers time to explore several destinations, experience the culture, and develop a deeper appreciation for the country,” says Catherine Heald, CNT specialist and founder of Remote Lands, which specializes in travel to Asia.

However, because the program is relatively new, not all airline or airport staff are familiar with it—which almost resulted in me being denied boarding. To help you avoid ending up in a similar situation, here’s what travelers should know before booking your flight to China, so you too can see the Forbidden City in Beijing, the futuristic skyline glowing along the Bund in Shanghai, the terracotta warriors in Xi'an, and the mountainous megacity of Chongqing.

Officially called the “240-Hour Visa-Free Transit Policy,” this new rule was first introduced by China’s National Immigration Administration in December 2024. It permits a traveler to visit China without obtaining a visa ahead of time as long as the total length of their stay in the country does not exceed 240 hours. “It’s a great policy that has driven the growth of international travelers to China,” says Zhang, “but you do need to read the fine print before using it.”

The fine print: First of all, the operative word is transit. You have to enter China from one country, then leave it for another, different country. For example, flying from the US to China, then from China to Japan is allowed. However, going from the US to China, then back to the US, is not. Hong Kong, Macao, and Taiwan count as separate destinations for this policy, so a trip that goes from Hong Kong to mainland China to Taiwan would qualify for a visa-free transit in China that does not last longer than 10 days.

Second: Only holders of passports from 57 countries, including the United States, can take advantage of this policy. See the full list here. And third: You have to enter and exit via designated ports. The full list is here, and it conveniently includes the cities you might visit on a first-time visit to China, like Beijing, Shanghai, and Chengdu. If you want to travel beyond the areas permitted by the transit policy, you’ll have to apply for a Chinese visa.

“Remember that you can enter and leave through the same eligible Chinese city or choose different eligible cities,” says Heald of Remote Lands. So you could come to China through Shanghai, spend three days there, then take the high-speed train to Beijing, stay for another three days, then depart for a third destination like nearby South Korea to make the most out of your trip.

The Forbidden City was the Chinese imperial palace from the Ming dynasty to the end of the Qing dynasty (1420-1912).

To try the transit policy for myself, I kept my first-ever trip to China simple. I arrived in Shanghai on September 30 and departed on October 5, entering and exiting through the same qualifying port, Shanghai Pudong International Airport (PVG). I stayed in the country for a total of five nights, well under the 240-hour limit. (For what it’s worth, I stayed at the good-looking PuLi Shanghai, the very cool Upper House Shanghai, and the historically rich Capella Shanghai, Jian Ye Li, to explore different parts of the city.)

I’m an American citizen, so my US passport made me eligible for the transit policy. As for my routing, I departed from Paris, where I live, on a direct flight to Shanghai; from there I flew onward to Manila. The logic is that this made my visit to China count as a long layover since my final destination was actually the Philippines.

As you prepare your itinerary, check—and double check—that your passport, routing, entry and departure ports in China, and destinations within China all qualify under the 240-hour visa-free transit policy before you make your bookings. The list of qualifying passports and entry-exit ports in China can be found here.

Once you have all your confirmation info, it’s a good idea to get organized and put together a folder with all your bookings as proof of your plans to stay no more than 10 days in China. “Carry printed copies of your confirmed onward tickets, hotel reservations, and itinerary,” Heald says. She also recommends calling your airline before departure and confirming your transit eligibility with them. You might even print the official page describing the policy (again, here!) so you can present it to anyone you encounter, like a check-in agent, who might be unfamiliar with the relatively new 10-day rule.

Consider this your heads up, says Zhang: “It’s a great policy but sometimes the implementation on the ground can be uneven.” For an added layer of security, consider booking your travel to China with local tour operators or travel specialists like WildChina or Remote Lands. They can design a trip that will definitely qualify for the transit policy, and can help you out in case you run into issues while you’re traveling.

Well, I did none of the above. I arrived at Paris-Charles de Gaulle for my flight to Shanghai without any printed confirmations of my onward ticket to Manila, my three hotel stays, or the official policy from the Chinese National Immigration Administration’s official website.

The Air France check-in agent asked me to present my Chinese visa, which, of course, I did not have. I tried to explain in French that I could go to China through this new policy, but the agent insisted, “Non, c’est pas possible.” Foolishly, I plugged “10-day visa-free transit China” into Google on my phone and presented the results to him. He sighed, switched to English, and said, “That is not official. That is AI Overview.”

I asked if there was anyone at Air France I could talk to, and the agent shook his head. Maybe he softened when he saw the panic creep across my face because he then phoned a colleague, an Air France agent who was Chinese. The other agent explained that I was correct, there is indeed a new 10-day transit policy, and all I had to do was present my onward ticket to the Philippines, which I did have saved as a screenshot on my phone.

May my failure to properly prepare be your reminder to print out everything, including your flight and accommodation info, as well as the official visa-free transit policy. If there was ever a time to be a type-A traveler, it’s this.

Once in China, the process becomes much smoother. All international travelers are required to fill out a digital arrival form, whether they have a visa or not. The form asks if you have a visa for China and, when you select no, offers a drop-down menu where you can declare that you are visiting through the 240-hour visa-free transit policy. Once that’s done, the form gives you a QR code that confirms you’ve completed the form; screenshot this code, just in case. Then go through the immigration line, approach the immigration officer, and present whatever is asked of you, like that QR code or your onward ticket, when prompted. That’s it!

For my journey, I got to Pudong Airport in Shanghai, logged onto the airport Wi-Fi, completed the form, and went into the immigration line. They didn’t ask for the QR code but they did ask for my ticket to Manila. Once everything looked good to them, they stamped my passport with a transit visa—a little sticker that declared my date of entry into China and when they expected me to leave. I was cleared to go, and I stepped into the duty-free shopping area, located right before baggage claim, feeling giddy and satisfied that it all worked out.

Zhang says working with a travel company could help relieve some of the stress on the arrival side too: “WildChina normally would book a VIP airport pickup if any of our travelers are using the 10-day transit visa. This way, an airport concierge would meet the guests at the gate and walk them through the visa step-by-step. This eases the stress of facing an unfamiliar bureaucratic process.”

One of the things that greatly intimidated me about visiting China was how different the tech is. There’s no Uber or Google Maps, which has been very helpful for me on my solo travels in new-to-me countries. The very fine teams at PuLi Shanghai and Upper House Shanghai helped me get set up with the right apps, and I was zipping around the city in no time. (For a map app, Apple Maps worked like a charm, to my surprise.) Here are tips for what Chinese apps to download before traveling.

First, set up Alipay, which is a do-it-all app and a total lifeline in China. You can link an international bank card and use it for all payments everywhere you go; call a DiDi car (China’s equivalent of Uber or Lyft), use its translation tool, and more. “Alipay is part of everyday life here,” Zhang says. “At most restaurants, you can scan the QR code on your table with Alipay, choose your dishes—already translated on the interface—and pay through the app.” Be sure to set it up and link your bank account or card before you arrive in China; some verification steps require authorization via your phone number, which you may not have access to while in the country.

Second, everyone in China is on WeChat, so you’d do well to download that too; it’s how I communicated with the guest experiences team at Capella Shanghai, Jian Ye Li, who took me on cultural tours in the hotel’s neighborhood. Think of it as Chinese WhatsApp.

And to stay connected online, Heald suggests checking if your existing carrier offers roaming in mainland China (helpful for any verification texts you may need to receive). Otherwise, get a compatible travel eSIM that explicitly covers it. A home carrier or a travel eSIM will allow you to connect to sites like Google Workplace and apps like Instagram that you would not be able to normally access through the internet while in China. For my phone, Airalo, a travel eSIM, and Free, my French home carrier, worked perfectly.

“If you'll be using a laptop or tablet on Wi-Fi and need access to services such as Google, WhatsApp, or Instagram, install a VPN and arrange any paid subscription before you leave,” Zhang says. “Downloading and setting it up can be much trickier once you're in China.” I, for one, used Astrill VPN to stay connected on my laptop to sites like Gmail and YouTube.

And finally, both Zhang and Heald recommend keeping an open mind. “China can feel very different from what you know,” Heald says. “Give yourself the chance to observe, ask questions and learn, rather than expecting everything to feel familiar.” Zhang adds, “That's part of getting to know a place. Don’t be afraid to ask for help or start a conversation, even if you only have a few words in common. You'll often find people are curious about you too, and pleased that you've come to see where they live.”

#6242. Once a Filipino Party Isle, Boracay Has Reinvented Itself

“Fun and sunshine, there's enough for everyone,” says a neon sign before me at the discotheque Club Tropicana on Boracay, a four-square-mile island at the heart of the Philippines. The lyrics are from a buoyant 1983 song, also called “Club Tropicana,” by Wham!. But tonight's playlist is cribbed from the 2010s. As midnight nears, Jennifer Lopez's voice sounds over the speakers, “If you're a party freak, then step on the floor.” So I twirl under a disco ball with gleeful strangers in bikini tops, cargo shorts, and Havaianas flip-flops, beers and gin and tonics in hand.

The effect is transportive. I'm flung 10 years into the past, back when Boracay was the locus of an exuberant, if at times debauched, nightlife scene on the creatively named White Beach. Crowds raved until sunrise and woke up on some of the world's softest sand. They had budget hostels and three-star inns, 24-hour shops, water sports and boats, and eateries of all stripes to keep them entertained until nightfall. Then came the parties, VIP bottle service, and the voice of Kesha speak-singing over sound systems, “Tick-tock on the clock, but the party don't stop, no.”

The thing is, it did. Boracay had to shed its hedonistic streak after a series of closures curtailed tourism. First there was the government-imposed cleanup in 2018 ordered by then president Rodrigo Duterte to correct rampant overdevelopment and environmental negligence. Then there was the COVID-19 shutdown from 2020 to 2022, when the Philippines was closed to foreigners. Boracay lost an estimated $845 million in tourism revenue in 2020 alone and counted only 260,000 visitors. Compare that with 2017, when it raked in roughly $1.1 billion by welcoming more than 2 million travelers who dug their toes into a White Beach clogged with the debris of multiday concerts and ragers thrown by local hosts and corporate mega-sponsors. Broken bottles, cigarette butts, and waste—plastic and otherwise—came in and out with the tides.

The writer (right) aboard a paraw tour at White Beach

Despite growing up in Manila, about an hour away by plane, I never got to see “old” Boracay before immigrating to the United States in 2003. In the 1990s it was beloved for its rustic milieu and unfussy hospitality, though it was already a resort island with more than 100 hotels. My family knew it best in the '80s, when backpackers from Europe and the US began to arrive after the German writer Jens Peters called it, in his 1978 guidebook to the Philippines, “paradise on Earth.” In those halcyon days, paradise had no electricity or potable water. Ice was brought in from the mainland to chill San Miguel Pale Pilsens in Coleman coolers. Even my stepfather, a reluctant traveler, fondly remembers the Boracay of yore: “Your mother and I had only the sea and the stars.”

Boracay is changing yet again. Since 2022 it has vowed to revitalize its economy without sacrificing its environment. Laws now enforce a maximum of 19,000 tourists per day. Smoking, alcohol, littering, single-use plastics, and parties directly on the beach are forbidden. Visitors are not permitted without reservations at accredited lodgings—no more sleeping overnight on the sand. No longer raw as it once was, neither an unspoiled Eden nor a profligate Sodom, this grown-up Boracay is what I've come to see for the first time. As I gaze at the stars above a pristine White Beach, I think, So far, so good.

“Boracay was stuck in a mode,” says entrepreneur Nowie Potenciano as we have brunch at his restaurant Percy Seafood, part of his beachfront hotel Seaworthy Boracay. He's referring to both the island's party animal years and its old culinary scene. Back when sustainability and dairy alternatives weren't yet part of the vernacular, diners usually packed their own food from the cities or bought fresh fish at wet markets to have them grilled or fried at canteens called paluto, meaning “to have something cooked.” They remain part of Boracay's charm today, but now we also have the dishes on our table like mango and tuna ceviche, seafood tagine with prawns and mussels, and grouper marinated in sambal. Dessert is a mélange of coconut-pandan ice cream, mango cubes, and crispy rice from Coco Mama, another Potenciano venture. The entire treat is vegan, and I, lactose intolerant, am grateful.

A seafood platter at Percy Seafood, right on the beach

Pecho, a popular chicken dish at Island Chicken Inasal, served with frozen calamansi

The owner of multiple Boracay restaurants, Potenciano prioritizes sourcing locally. Mahi-mahi and grouper come from nearby Roxas City, oysters from marshy New Washington, and lobsters from the colorful reefs of Palawan. Last October he opened a new restaurant, Hello, Po, inspired by open-fire cooking and smoking traditions from all over the Philippines. As much as possible the ingredients come from Panay, the main island off which Boracay sits. “I want tourists to realize that Boracay is at the center of so much wealth in terms of food and culture,” he says. “It's not just another beach.”

That said, judging it solely as a beach, I get why Boracay is beloved. The sand is soft like confectioners' sugar. The shallows are so vast the waters are basically a giant kiddie pool. Behind a fence of palm trees, all tall and outstretched, as if they're fighting for a cab, there are countless bars, restaurants, canteens, shops, resorts, and hostels. They're divided into “stations” typified by vibe: Station 3, the backpackers haven; Station 2, the busy commercial hub; and Station 1, the home of high-end hotels. Yet wherever your accredited accommodations may be, you can park a blanket anywhere on White Beach. Everyone's welcome to do nothing but sit here and watch the blazing postcard-perfect sunsets.

But I do no such thing. Having missed out on Boracay's previous eras, I am anxious to play catch-up and pack my calendar with activities. While staying at The Lind Boracay, I board a paraw, a traditional outrigger sailboat, and zip along the shore with guides who balance on the watercraft with surprising grace. I go for a snorkeling safari (stunning) and my first try at paddleboarding (nauseating) at the sumptuous Shangri-La Boracay's private Punta Bunga Beach. In the clamorous whirl of D'Mall in Station 2, I shop at the boutique Hiyas, scoring a watch with a pearl bracelet, then grab lunch at Island Chicken Inasal Boracay for grilled birds marinated in calamansi. I have a cocktail at Exit Bar, where a band plays “Easy” (“Easy like Sunday morning…”). After dark the vibe shifts: A handsome, leathery, maybe Swedish DJ busts out his turntables. As I join the crowd untz-ing to the electro-house beat, a fog seems to roll in. It's smoke from cigarettes and vapor from vapes.

Though it leaves me breathless, this rapid-fire succession of capital-E experiences feels natural, like what one is meant to do here. On Boracay the surf shops, tiki bars, karaoke venues, and all-you-can-eat buffets are arranged like dominoes, each address falling into the next. One night I catch a band of dads singing Filipino love songs at Nigi Nigi Nu Noos, a down-home resto-bar with casitas, before I go to Rainbow Cafe and Lounge, where a drag queen performs to a RuPaul song, leaping from a chair and landing in an earth-shaking split. This cornucopia of options can be overwhelming to some and a boon to many. Travelers, alone or otherwise, choose their own adventures and curate vibes by the hour. After decades of being many things to many people, today's Boracay now has everything everywhere all at once.

More people are on the way. Visitor numbers are back to pre-closure levels and only increasing: 2.1 million travelers arrived in 2025, up 3.7 percent from the previous year. To handle them all, a new passenger terminal at Godofredo P. Ramos Airport in Caticlan, the gateway to Boracay, is meant to open in December. Domestic travelers currently outnumber the big spenders from abroad nearly five to one (the split was 50-50 before 2018). But there's still the sense, among business owners I meet, that Boracay is meant to represent the best of the Philippines—not just to foreigners but to ourselves as well.

That's the goal at Subo, a modern Filipino restaurant that straddles Stations 2 and 3. Its chef-owner, Jian Sacdalan, takes guests on a culinary field trip through the country's diverse regions with vegetable pinakbet from Luzon, pork belly pochero from Visayas, and coconut-rich sulu laksa from Mindanao. Subo gets a lot of, as Sacdalan calls them, “intros”—those being introduced to the Philippines for the first time. Staff instruct visitors to leave their flip-flops and Birkenstocks at the entrance. This is a Filipino house after all, and I feel my heart flutter when I'm made to do the same.

“And we get the balikbayans,” Sacdalan says, smiling. Translated literally: country returners, like me. “They long for our culture and heritage, and they get that here.”

When I have breakfast at True Home Hotel, I'm still wet and sandy from spending the already-warm day on White Beach. As co-owner and chef Peter Montemayor hands me Bacolod-style chorizo pudpud, garlic rice, and eggs, he says it's good I'm enjoying the beach. It's what brought him back here after working at resorts in Southeast Asia and the Caribbean: “I said, if I ever return, there's only Boracay.” Another balikbayan.

But Montemayor thinks not enough tourists are relishing White Beach, especially after all that's happened to clean it up. During the 2018 closure True Home Hotel shrank from nine rooms to three to comply with new regulations that forbid permanent structures within 98 feet of the shoreline. He's critical of the government's execution (locals who had to move residences or close businesses weren't supported financially) but admits, “When the island closed, it healed.”

He laments how today's tourists stay dry in the shade, viewing Boracay only through their cameras, or cram their schedules with shopping malls, kiteboarding, windsurfing, and booze cruises where water slides catapult passengers off a ship's stern. “Sounds like my itinerary,” I say, and he laughs. “The island's magic throughout all its iterations,” Montemayor responds, “is how it rewards you when you stand still.”

I taste that peace at Real Coffee and Tea Cafe, a diner in Station 2 styled like a bahay kubo, a stilt house with a thatch roof and bamboo walls. Nearly every surface is covered in sun-bleached photos of guests dating back to when it opened in 1996. The delightfully sour calamansi muffin, it's said, hasn't changed in 30 years. The place feels like a brush with what my family must have longed for: that placid and sweet vibe attached to a Boracay of the past—a contentedness with the here and now.

Inspired to take a breather, I find a spot on White Beach, use my shirt as a blanket, and make to watch the world go by. Instead I drift into a nap. I get to sleep on the sand after all. When I wake, I don't find I've missed out. There's still fun and sunshine. There's enough for everyone.

The pathway over the koi pond at Shangri-La Boracay

The part of White Beach with fewer folks and the softest sand is Station 1, home to Filipino-owned The Lind Boracay. Most of the 118 rooms have sea views, and some have private plunge pools; the brand will come to on-the-rise Philippine island Coron in 2027. The sumptuous Shangri-La Boracay is set on a secluded corner of the island, informally dubbed Station Zero. The 30-acre, 219-key resort has a spa, four restaurants, a PADI-certified water sports center for everything from diving to kitesurfing, and two beaches: the private Banyugan Beach and Punta Bunga Beach, which it shares with sleek Crimson Resort and Spa Boracay and lush Mövenpick Resort & Spa Boracay.

It's easy to fuel up everywhere on the island, especially Station 1: Percy does local seafood dishes; the cocktails at Hello Sailor spotlight Pinoy botanicals; and almost every dessert at Coco Mama is vegan. All are part of the sweet seven-room Seaworthy Boracay. The cozy True Home Hotel and Bistro, with three rooms and an all-day kitchen, is a few doors down. Get a calamansi muffin and an iced latte—there's oat milk—at Real Coffee and Tea Cafe, a 30-year-old oasis amid the hectic vibe of Station 2. In D'Mall, Island Chicken Inasal Boracay serves the titular barbecued bird, one of the region's specialties. At D'Mall's beachside entrance, find Exit Bar for sundowners that become all-nighters. The new Nigi Nigi Too, an eat-drink-and-stay all-in-one, is the latest iteration of a 36-year-old institution. On the border of backpacker haven Station 3 and commercial center Station 2, Subo (meaning “a bite” or “feed”) offers a primer on Filipino regional cuisines. Next door is Boracay Island Brewing Company, with locally made ales on tap.

For a taste of classic Boracay nightlife, hit the dance floors at intimate Club Tropicana, neon-lit Om Boracay, and epic Epic, a storied survivor of the island's closures. If you're looking for a dive-y feel, hit Rainbow Cafe and Lounge for some nibbles and drag shows, and Frendz Resort and Hostel Boracay for a spot of community karaoke (the crowd is young; request some current Top 40).

All of White Beach is yours to claim. Be respectful, do not litter, and leave only footprints.

#6241. United Unveils 14-Gate Concourse at Dulles

United and the Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority unveiled Washington Dulles International Airport’s first new concourse in nearly two decades on Monday. Concourse E opens to passengers Nov. 10, giving United 14 new gates at a hub where its departures have risen 30% since 2022.

The 435,000-square-foot concourse connects directly to the airport’s AeroTrain and has jet bridges at every gate. It can handle both domestic and international flights. The airports authority said existing gates were already fully in use several times a day, with passengers crowding waiting areas and concessions during peak periods.

The concourse also houses United’s second-largest United Club. The nearly 40,000-square-foot lounge seats more than 600 people and increases the airline’s total lounge space at Dulles by about 70%. New concessions include local businesses such as Good Company Doughnuts & Café and Honor Brewing.

“Washington Dulles is a critical part of United’s global network and growth strategy,” United CEO Scott Kirby said in a statement. The carrier currently offers more than 250 daily flights from Dulles to 135 destinations.

United has added six international destinations from the airport this year. It plans to begin international Airbus A321XLR service from Dulles in December with flights to Amsterdam and Dublin, followed by new service to Toulouse, France, and Milan in 2027.

Concourse E is the first phase of the broader Dulles Global Gateway program, which United and the airports authority estimate will involve more than $20 billion in investment. Later work is expected to add gates, expand the main terminal, and build a new U.S. Customs facility. The program also calls for extending the AeroTrain so the airport can eventually retire its mobile lounges.
