At The Points Guy, we’re always looking for simple ways to save money and earn more rewards. One of the easiest yet often overlooked tools is Chase Offers.

With just a few clicks, you can unlock targeted discounts and cash-back deals at brands you already use. These range from streaming services and restaurants to travel and retail purchases.

Even better, Chase Offers can often be combined with your card’s usual earning rates and shopping portals, helping you get more value from everyday spending.

Here’s how the program works and how to maximize it.

Chase Offers is a program available on eligible Chase debit and credit cards that gives cardholders access to targeted deals, similar to Amex Offers. These offers typically provide cash back or a percentage back as a statement credit when you make a qualifying purchase.

Like similar programs from other issuers, offers are personalized. That means the deals you see may differ from what someone else receives. You may also see different offers across your own Chase cards.

Most Chase-issued consumer and business credit and debit cards are eligible for Chase Offers if the primary cardholder has a U.S. address listed as their primary residence or place of business.

To see if Chase Offers is available for your card, check your Chase mobile app or log in at Chase's website.

For Chase credit cards, primary cardholders and authorized officers can view and add offers. Authorized users and employees can't add offers themselves, but they can redeem offers that have already been added to the account.

Some of the most popular eligible cards include:

Chase Offers are also available on many cobranded Chase credit cards, such as the (see rates and fees) and select United Airlines and Marriott Bonvoy cards.

Each card may offer different deals, so it's worth checking all your accounts if you hold more than one Chase card.

You can find available offers on the Chase website and on the Chase app. To view your available offers on the website, log in to your account and find "Chase Offers" on the right-hand panel.

Alternatively, you can click on "Benefits & travel" on the top panel and select "Chase Offers", as shown below. Note that the offers shown below may not be available to you.

To view your Chase Offers on the Chase mobile app, log in to your account and then scroll down toward the middle of the main account dashboard. You should see a section titled “Chase Offers” showing some of your current offers.

Either the website or app option will bring you to the offers currently available for you to browse.

Offerings change daily and typically feature various types of goods and services. You may see deals for:

Offers typically range from about 5% to 30% back or provide a fixed statement credit after meeting a spending requirement. For example, you might receive a $20 statement credit after spending $100 with a specific merchant.

Chase Offers can be an easy way to save on purchases you’re already making, which is something TPG staffers have seen firsthand across a range of everyday spending.

TPG travel writer Rachel Craft, for example, recently used an offer on her for 15% back at home improvement stores. She bundled supplies for a few projects she already had planned into a single purchase and received $33 back. Meanwhile, TPG principal spokesperson Clint Henderson earned an $85 statement credit on a DISH Network purchase using his World of Hyatt card.

TPG editor-in-chief Nick Ewen has also had success with Chase Offers. He recently earned $15.81 back on Trans-Siberian Orchestra tickets purchased through SeatGeek with his Chase Freedom Flex. Since the purchase also fell within one of the card's Q3 rotating quarterly bonus categories, he earned 5% cash back on top of his Chase Offer savings (on up to $1,500 in combined purchases each quarter, activation required).

And in an even bigger example of how these savings can add up, Nick earned a $125 statement credit through a Chase Offer on an IHG hotel stay booked through The Edit by Chase Travel℠, using his . By combining that offer with the card's The Edit and select hotels credits, he saved a total of $625 on the stay.

While individual savings may vary, these examples highlight how these targeted offers can add up, especially on purchases you already planned to make.

While you don’t have to enroll your card to start using the Chase Offers program, you do have to add each individual offer to your credit card. Adding them is easy — all you have to do is navigate to Chase Offers either online or through the Chase Mobile app and click “Add to card” on any available offer that interests you.

Alternatively, if you have a subscription to a service like MaxRewards Gold, your offers should be automatically activated for all linked cards.

Then, use your card at the specific merchant, and you should see a statement credit applied to your account within 30 days after your qualifying transaction posts, unless the offer terms state otherwise.

Once you arrive on the Chase Offers landing page, adding an offer to your account is very simple.

If you have multiple eligible Chase cards, you’ll see a “Choose your account” drop-down near the top of the screen. Note that if you have multiple sign-ins with Chase, such as one for your personal cards and one for business credit cards, you will only see cards associated with the account for which you’re currently signed in.

Again, note that the offers you see here may not be available for you.

Click on any offer to add it to your card. Then, use your card at the specific merchant and wait for your statement credit to post.

Once you find an offer you would like to use in the app, the process is similar to the website process.

You can click on “See all available deals” to see the rest of your offers. You’ll see a “Choose your account” drop-down near the top of the screen if you have multiple eligible Chase cards.

Click on any offers to add them to your card, use your card at the participating merchant and wait for your statement credit to post.

When you add an offer for a specific card, you must use that same card to redeem the offer. For example, if you add a Chase Offer to your , you must use that card to redeem that offer successfully.

Be sure to read the terms and conditions for each offer carefully. You only have a certain amount of time to use each offer, and many come with maximum earning limits. As long as you make your purchase by the expiration date, you should receive the credit even if the transaction posts after the expiration date.

Chase Offers are rewarded as a statement credit, even if you have a card that earns Ultimate Rewards points on regular spending.

One of the common threads among all Chase Offers is this condition: Payment must be made directly with the merchant. While you can still use services like mobile wallets and PayPal with Chase Offers, you can’t use third-party providers to make purchases.

Finally, Chase Offers are only available on eligible U.S.-issued Chase credit cards tied to U.S.-based accounts. However, some offers may still be valid at international merchants, particularly global brands like hotel chains, as long as the transaction is processed by the eligible merchant and charged to your enrolled card.

Since new offers are constantly added, it’s a good idea to go through your Chase Offers at least biweekly to review and add new offers. It doesn’t cost anything to add an offer and then not use it, so you can be pretty lenient with which offers you add.

If there’s even a tiny possibility that you’ll use an offer, you might as well add it to your card. If you use it, great; if not, it’s not a problem.

Chase Offers become significantly more valuable when you stack them with other rewards opportunities. This means combining an offer with a shopping portal and a credit card bonus category to earn multiple layers of rewards on the same purchase.

For example, imagine you’re booking a $200 stay at a Hyatt property. You could:

In this scenario, you’d earn 1,000 points through the portal, $10 cash back from your Freedom Flex and a $20 statement credit from the Chase Offer.

Instead of earning rewards from just one source, you’ve effectively tripled up on the same purchase.

Chase Offers are best used for purchases you were already planning to make. Like any coupon or sale, saving 10% on something you didn’t need isn’t actually saving money. But when used strategically, especially in combination with shopping portals and bonus categories, they can meaningfully boost your overall return.

*Earn 5% cash back in rotating categories for the first $1,500 in combined purchases each quarter; activation required.

Related: How I earned over 3,800 points and miles buying $180 worth of sports tickets with my Freedom Flex

Chase Offers is one of the easiest ways to save money on purchases you already plan to make. While the discounts may not always be large, they require minimal effort and can add up quickly.

By checking your offers regularly and combining them with bonus categories and shopping portals, you can turn everyday spending into meaningful savings over time.

#6239. Brisbane Gets Its Moment in the Sun

Late one afternoon last November, Ty Simon works the room at Golden Avenue. He laughs with a pair of men in suits, tops off the glasses for a table of women in flower-patterned dresses, squeezes shoulders, and nods and smiles his way across the rest of the floor. Waiters ferry wine and coffee and platters of hummus and salads between the kitchen and the split-level dining space. Sheets of bright Queensland sun pour in through the open walls. It's Tuesday, it's lunch, and the place is full, unrushed, and lovely; it feels good to be here. Golden Avenue opened in the middle of last year as the ninth restaurant from Simon and his wife, Milan-born Biànca Marchi-Simon, through their Anyday hospitality group, which started with the Asian-inflected Longtime and went on to include Agnes, a dimly lit open-flame spot that won Australia's Restaurant of the Year in 2023. When Simon returns to our table, I remark on the hospitality that I've just seen. “Here we take a community approach,” he says. “My goal has always been to make sure that the people who like us, love us.”

The community approach may be the key to his city's success. Brisbane—Australia's perpetually distant-third city—has long been reduced by the Aussies to a “big country town.” (Their words—not mine!) Though a good-natured and happy place, it lacked the natural beauty and trendsetting of Sydney and the cultish urban creativity of Melbourne. For decades Brisbane seemed to succumb to the belief that it could never compete. It lacked personality in its Central Business District (CBD) and had pretty much no public transport. Even geography worked against it: In a state prized for its coastline, Brisbane is nearly 50 miles from a surf beach. Locals would often zip overseas or migrate south, perhaps on the assumption that their ambition could never be realized at home. The big country town endured.

The astounding Kith and Kin, from Queensland artist Archie Moore, which won the Golden Lion at Venice’s 60th biennale, on display at GOMA

Then a shift began. The city council embarked on an ambitious rebranding in 2010 to position Brisbane as globally connected and dynamic, giving it the nickname of New World City (“It was about shedding the idea of being the poor cousin,” Simon says). The magnificent Gallery of Modern Art (GOMA) had opened just a few years before, attracting world-class works from the Pacific and beyond. The council leveraged the city's billion-dollar location, just north of the booming Gold Coast, with its high-rises and killer beaches, and south of the covetable Sunshine Coast, with the Great Barrier Reef just off its shores. Millions traveled in from all over each year for what lay on either side of Brisbane, so why not make the city bait for some of their money and time? Many Brisbanites, Simon included, began to grow this place together, creating a city that reflected their own ambitions—and themselves. In the 2010s the city developed sharply designed precincts filled with glamour shopping and higher-level dining, all under year-round sunshine and with Brisbane's noticeable good cheer and friendliness. In 2021 the IOC announced that Brisbane would host the summer Olympics in 2032, following Los Angeles.

And right around that same time, COVID hit. While the rest of Australia struggled with lockdown and tight regulations that dragged on, Queensland fared generally well, with looser rules and relatively low numbers of cases after the initial shutdowns. “We had Melburnians coming into Brisbane just to feel normal again,” says entrepreneur and developer Catherine Malouf.

Malouf may be the most recognizable face of Brisbane's new chapter. Her family is one of the key forces behind the James Street precinct, a fig-tree-studded melange of open-air coffee houses, Champagne bars, and high-end restaurants strung together with designer shops selling top local labels. “I wanted to create somewhere where we could have a good lunch, a glass of wine, and go shopping in a place that felt like the best of Australia,” she says as we eat grilled chicken and salads at her Hellenika restaurant. Stylish and elegant, Malouf exudes the kind of sophistication you may more often associate with the places she formerly called home, like Italy and California, but her good nature and easy friendliness is all Brisbane. In a sense she personifies the version of Brisbane she is invested in creating: global and chic but anchored in hometown charm. “It took me 20 years to come back and realize that this is the place I want to live in, and a lot of people have realized that too,” she says. “It is comfortable. It is easy.”

The precinct's architecture is heavy, concrete, and borderline Brutalist, but not at all ugly. It creates an aura of strength and permanence that's almost symbolic for the next chapter of a city whose heritage architecture was mostly knocked down and whose locals have often fled elsewhere for opportunity. And amid it all is the anchor of the precinct, The Calile, an urban resort hotel whose execution feels Aussie but whose ambition and hospitality would work in any major global city. Its opening—along with its smartly designed rooms and mezzanine-level pool, bars, and restaurants that spill over into the general precinct sidewalks—catapulted the James Street precinct onto the radars of international travelers. “We are very much an Aussie hotel, but we are increasingly hosting people from around the world,” Malouf says.

Designer Heidi Middleton inside her atelier, Artclub

The James Street precinct serves as a gateway to Australia. The stores here, high-end and, for the most part, independent, are nearly all Australian brands such as P. Johnson, St. Agni, and Brisbane's own Gail Sorronda. A centerpiece is Artclub, from fashion designer Heidi Middleton, which launched here last year. Like many of her fellow Brisbanites, Middleton left to start and grow a business whose ambitions, she felt, would never flourish in Brisbane. After spending decades in Europe and selling her globally renowned Sass & Bide, she alleviated her homesickness and moved back. Artclub is a sustainably minded fashion brand that focuses on small production and renewable materials. Middleton remarks that the key to the precinct's success is the curation: high-end and never high street. “They have created a genre that is all their own,” she says.

Brisbane is called the River City for the coffee-hued eponymous waterway that snakes through it. Like the James Street precinct, the river, too, has been a focus for a lot of redevelopment. The work here—walkways, bridges, cycling and jogging lanes, dining districts, and green spaces—has pulled the city together and been a catalyst for a revamped relationship between people and place. On the banks near the James Street precinct, where a once industrial wasteland lay abandoned and uninspired, now sits the reimagined Howard Smith Wharves, alive with breweries, green parks, and restaurants. It's located on the Brisbane Riverwalk, a network of overwater walkways that are dotted with bright red royal poinciana flame trees, which didn't exist 10 years ago. Along the walk sits Stanley, an excellent Chinese spot that conjures a Hong Kong evening parlor and was opened by Louis Tikaram, who made a name on the global culinary stage as executive chef of EP & LP in West Hollywood. A 15-minute stroll away is Supernormal, the only sister restaurant to the hit Melbourne joint of the same name, whose 2024 opening unofficially announced Brisbane as a serious foodie city.

A signature steamed dumpling basket from Stanley

Four new pedestrian bridges have opened to decrease car traffic, promote sustainable living, and solve some of the city's connectivity issues. The latest, Kangaroo Point Bridge, connects the suburb of Kangaroo Point to the CBD, and it's bookended with coffee bars and has green spaces so that pedestrians can relax while looking out over the water. Zigzagging underneath them all is the beloved CityCat ferry, which zips from bank to bank, chartering passengers throughout town and beyond. Stops include the wonderful South Bank cultural district, where you'll find GOMA and the Queensland Art Gallery (QAG). It chugs its way to West End, Brisbane's perennial counterculture neighborhood, which has a funky retro cinema, indie shops selling Japanese crafts and fashion, and solid food.

Take the ferry north and you'll arrive at Brisbane Powerhouse. A hulking industrial building that powered the city starting in the 1920s, it was reborn in 2000 as the city's contemporary art center, complete with sprawling grounds, rooftop areas, bars, restaurants, and untouched industrial spaces that can host interactive exhibitions. It's raw and cool, and its scale is enormous. When I meet Louise Bezzina there, she is in her second week as the Powerhouse's artistic director and CEO. Kind and unassuming, she is the type of person you might casually meet at a mutual friend's birthday dinner and, 15 minutes into the conversation, realize you are sitting next to someone brilliant. “As Australia develops it allows for more cities to grow—it is not just Sydney and Melbourne,” she says. “Brisbane has long been an untapped city of opportunity.”

She is part of the cohort of local leaders drilling into its potential. Prior to the Powerhouse, Bezzina was the creative director of Brisbane Festival, the largest international festival in Australia by attendance numbers, for which she secured the Jean Paul Gaultier show over creative capitals like Melbourne in 2024. “My edgy style suits Brisbane,” she believes. For her first project at the Powerhouse, she launched “Swingers: The Art of Minigolf,” an interactive statement on female empowerment in a male-dominated world, pegged to the origin story of the putting game, which was founded in the 19th century by Scottish women who had been banned from 18-hole golf on account of their gender; each of the nine holes here was designed by a different female-identifying artist. Bezzina has begun ideating plans to partner with Los Angeles and Pacific dance groups in the lead-up to (and handoff of) the Summer Olympic Games.

But to suggest that creativity is new to Brisbane would be misleading. Designer Lydia Pearson is a local loyalist who has long believed in the power of her hometown. “It used to be that if you wanted to be successful, you had to either leave or create it yourself,” she says. She chose the latter. In 1989 Pearson cofounded the fashion brand Easton Pearson with fellow designer Pamela Easton, which focused on circular fashion through textiles and hand embroidery. It took off, showing during Paris Fashion Week in 1999 and selling in 20 countries before the label closed in 2016. The following year the Museum of Brisbane acquired more than 3,000 pieces from the Easton Pearson archive and has put some of the items on permanent display. “The hard part was getting people to believe you could make a brand in Brisbane that wasn't simply a hibiscus-patterned dress,” Pearson says.

We meet in the leafy suburb of Red Hill, where she and her current partner, the artist Shilo Engelbrecht, work diligently to upcycle old fabrics into a new life through their label, ShiloLydia. This could mean turning an antique tablecloth into a sheer, soft dress, or reworking discarded linens into sharp shirts whose silhouettes could compete with any on a global catwalk. The work is slow, careful, and considered—a preservation effort as much as it is a creative one. The results are delicate and beautiful, a quiet and enduring counter to the louder creativity happening across the city.

Their studio sits inside a Queenslander, an old, iconic style of house that started to appear in Brisbane in the mid-1800s. The structures are wood, often colorful but always fragile, with large verandas designed to catch and route cooling breezes through the home. Queenslanders are delightful and charming, and have become recognizable to millions of viewers around the world who tune into Brisbane's most famous export, Bluey. The beloved animated show about Bluey, a blue heeler dog, who is likely known to more people around the world than her real-life fellow Brisbanite Jacob Elordi, is the creation of animator Joe Brumm. The show airs in 28 languages and more than 140 countries. For several years it was the most streamed show in the United States of any genre, and it has an empire worth $2 billion. Brisbane is a main character, and the city is unmistakable via the iconic Queenslander wood homes, the ibis birds pecking around, the sun and steep hills, the hours of imaginative outdoor play that Brumm says is modeled after his own upbringing in Queensland. Bluey resonates with parents and children of the world due to the heart and the humor at the show's core, something Brumm says defines Brisbane. “It is about the cheer that I feel when I come back,” he says. A good reminder, then, that a place's most resonant selling point is often something that can't be built.

True urban resort The Calile Hotel helped put Brisbane on the traveler map. The hotel has a phenomenal pool and fitness space; even if you're not staying here, swing by for its Lobby Bar and excellent restaurants, including Hellenika, which serves Greek favorites.

Inside a restored heritage Queenslander, the intimate Spicers Balfour Brisbane is well-located in New Farm: It's walking distance from the James Street precinct, the Howard Smith Wharves, and Brisbane Powerhouse.

The dimly lit, decidedly grown-up restaurant Agnes, which was named Australia's Best in 2023, is known for its exceptional wood-fired cooking of duck, steak, and more.

Housed inside a former church in West End, August is a nod to the reverence of Sunday lunch, with considerately prepared plates of Noosa snapper and Jerusalem artichoke risotto.

Sleek and light-flooded, the 15-month-old Middle Eastern spot Golden Avenue has great eggplant and grilled meats.

Do an outdoor table and load it up with all the dumplings and noodles you can order at superb riverside restaurant Stanley that feels like high-end Hong Kong parlor dining.

The Brisbane outpost of the hot Melbourne restaurant Supernormal has a glamorous dining room with large water-facing windows and a fun, Asian-inflected menu that leads with local produce and protein.

Located near the funky Fish Lane, Southside is the spot for dumplings and siu mai after strolling the museums of South Bank.

The French Exit, the newest venture from Ty and Biànca at Anyday, has Parisian-style interiors by star designer Tamsin Johnson and cool bars and dining rooms spread over multiple floors in a heritage building.

Brisbane's cultural hub is South Bank, with Gallery of Modern Art (GOMA) and other institutions featuring Indigenous, Australian, and Pacific Island artists. The riverfront Brisbane Powerhouse has ambitious and edgy festivals, exhibitions, and events throughout the year.

For the best Australian labels, head to the James Street precinct for objects from Dinosaur Designs; stylish dresses from St. Agni; and sustainable, one-off fashions from Heidi Middleton's atelier, Artclub. Over in Red Hill, drop into ShiloLydia as well as the other ateliers that share space in the same Queenslander. Shilo Engelbrecht also hosts collage and meditation workshops in her studio out back by appointment.

The best way to see (and travel) Brisbane is the CityCat ferry, which bounces between 22 stops along the river. But the city has made walking easier too. Stroll the overwater footpaths on the waterfront up to the gorgeous City Botanic Gardens. If you‘re keen for a longer walk after checking out the exhibitions at GOMA, find your way to West End for funky vintage shopping and phenomenal food.

There is no shortage of worthy weekend getaways from Brisbane, including the Gold Coast and Noosa on the Sunshine Coast. But drive an hour inland to the artsy, beautiful Tamborine Mountain for a lovely look at a lesser-explored side of Queensland. Stay at the chic, two-year-old Tamborine Boutique Hotel, where a pantry and bar stock local snacks. Have lunch at the petite Picnic Real Food Bar, and don't worry if it's already run out of the plump and delicious pies (everything is worth trying). Then head around the corner for local amaro tastings at Loborn. Restore yourself after mountain hikes at the floating Sol Elements spa, whose soaking baths and salt room all seem to hover over a lake.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6238. Why You Should Pack Your Hiking Boots on a Trip to St. Croix

The smell hit me out of nowhere: an uncanny whiff of sweaty socks. I instinctively glanced around for another hiker. My guide, local naturalist Olasee Davis, laughed and pointed to a thick brown seed pod lying on the trail. It had fallen from a West Indian locust, more commonly known as a stinking toe tree.

The culprit loomed farther down the trail, its massive limbs weaving a vaulted canopy overhead. “It tastes better than it smells,” Olasee said, picking up the pod and cracking it open on a rock to reveal the powdery pulp inside. I watched him take a bite but decided to pass. I suspected stinking toe fruit was an acquired taste, and with only a few days remaining on my trip to St. Croix, I'd save the acquiring for a future visit.

As we continued along, Olasee introduced me to other tropical evergreens, including the soursop, laden with spiky fruit, and the red manjack, much shorter and shrubbier, with brownish-red berries. Around the next bend he pointed out nonnative fruit trees: papaya from South America and mango from India. But he hadn't brought me here just for the botany. He'd brought me to understand why this forest matters.

As an ecologist, historian, and assistant professor at the University of the Virgin Islands, Olasee helped lead the effort to establish Maroon Sanctuary Territorial Park in 2025. Encompassing 2,469 acres in the northwest corner of St. Croix, the park protects part of Maroon Country, the island's steep, forested interior where people who had escaped slavery found refuge during the 1700s and early 1800s. The new park also safeguards former sugar plantations and mill sites, which have been slowly returning to nature since Denmark ended slavery in the Danish West Indies (present-day US Virgin Islands) in 1848. By that time more than 100,000 enslaved Africans had passed through the port of Christiansted on St. Croix, the largest of the islands, to be sold to plantation owners in the Danish Caribbean sugar economy.

Olasee and I were following an old plantation trail through one such former estate when he suddenly stopped and then scrambled up a steep embankment into the trees. I followed, brushing aside slender branches. Hidden beneath the understory, almost swallowed by spider lilies, was a burial ground. Most graves were marked with conch shells. Some were covered by low, weathered concrete slabs. One was marked by a headstone, its inscription softened by decades of moisture and lichen. The hidden cemetery wasn't an isolated discovery. For more than 40 years, Olasee has bushwhacked his way through Maroon Country to search for burial grounds and other traces of those who escaped slavery, documenting sites that would otherwise disappear beneath the forest. Now that it's been conserved as a territorial park, that work can continue in a more systematic, permanent way. Or as Olasee put it, “I could die in peace now.”

Travelers have traditionally come to the USVI for beach vacations and sailing charters; now Maroon Sanctuary is opening up another side to the islands. The park's founders are also building out an official trail network. The roughly 10 miles of trail that I explored with Olasee were a patchwork of former estate roads, plantation footpaths, and forgotten forest routes that he'd pieced together over decades. Soon these trails will be easier to navigate without needing someone like Olasee to lead the way. The next morning I met Kristina “Kitty” Edwards, director of the US Virgin Islands Division of Territorial Parks & Protected Areas, at a trailhead on the slopes of 1,165-foot Mount Eagle, the island's highest peak. We were about to hike the first official segment of the trail, a three-mile loop designed for hiking and mountain biking, which opened this past May. When completed, the trail system will wend 30 miles through the forested backcountry.

As excited as Kitty was to show off the new path, a first of its kind on the island, she wasn't in a hurry. “I'm a meanderer,” she said with a shrug and a smile. In the shirt-soaking heat of the tropics, I was grateful to take it slow. We ascended amid white-winged butterflies and yellow-breasted bananaquits. After an hour we reached the stone remnants of the old watchtower that marked the summit. A spur trail led us to an overlook where we paused to take in the 270-degree view, bookended by emerald peaks to our right and the inviting turquoise waters of Cane Bay to our left. It occurred to me that Maroon Sanctuary wasn't just about the land. The park's protected boundary extends all the way to the sea, helping shield Cane Bay's coral reefs and the nearby Annaly Bay tide pools from pollution and sediment.

A green sea turtle in the warm waters around St. Croix

I spent the next day reveling in those crystal waters. At Sweet Bottom Dive Center, I rented a mask and fins, and went snorkeling among the parrotfish, angelfish, and wrasse that inhabit the shallow reef just offshore. After watching a sea turtle munch on seagrass, I flipped over onto my back. Above the beach the densely forested peaks of Maroon Country rose in layers, a physical reminder of the many lives and histories held within.

The Waves at Cane Bay, an 11-room boutique hotel built into the rocky shoreline overlooking the bay, was reimagined in 2021 as a stylish oceanfront retreat with private patios, two bars, and the sustainable seafood restaurant Ama. The hotel is a four-minute walk to the beach at Cane Bay and a nine-minute drive to the new Mount Eagle trailhead.

Located directly across the road from Cane Bay, the Landing Beach Bar serves up Caribbean specialties like jerk chicken and fried plantains in a fun, convivial setting. Leatherback Brewing Company is St. Croix's first craft brewery and an unofficial headquarters for the island's mountain-biking community, complete with a full-service bike shop inside.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6237. We Keep Going Back To Germany. This Family Trip Reminded Me Why.

We landed in Zürich on SAS and drove to my in-law’s home in Southwest Germany, about an hour away.

There are border checks now as you enter Germany from France and Switzerland, though usually (I’m just saying…) when they see it’s white people they just waive you through.

And I’ll leave off the politics here (because I’d rather focus on getting our own house in order in the USA), but I think this picture says it all about Germany these days:

We tend to stop at DM (a drug store chain) at the start of each trip because it’s on the way home and we always come with a list since so many products here are cheaper and better than their American counterparts, even with the stronger Euro. One thing I like about DM (well, liked…) was that they had a free water dispenser with cups.

In Germany water is an annoyance when going out…most restaurants and coffee shops frown on tap water (unlike in France and the Netherlands), so you’re paying everywhere €5-8EUR for bottles you can buy for 50-80 Euro cents in the grocery store. It’s nice to “hydrate” at DM, but for TWO YEARS the water machine has been broken.

How in the heck can you not fix this for two years (unless, as I suppose, the point is that you don’t want to offer free water any longer)?!

It was a bit warm for the time of the year, but not unpleasant. How nice it was to be back and over the next several days we enjoyed a lot of quality time together, with good döner, coffee, and ice cream.

There was a fairly intense lighting storm that was just beautiful to sit out on the patio and watch:

One morning I decided to ride by myself to Basel for coffee…there was a new place I wanted to try called Mantila Coffee…it was SO GOOD (my new favorite coffee spot in Basel) and I had such a nice chat with the owner. I’m going to update my Basel Coffee post with a couple of places I tried on this trip.

Augustine was livid that biked to Basel without him, so we returned the next day (sadly Mantila is closed on Saturday), but we found another great place called Tinka. Augustine wanted his own coffee…I had a cortado, he had cappuccino, and then we split a delicious sparkling blood orange drink.

My father-in-law likes a restaurant called Gasthaus Krone in the hamlet of Lehnacker, located really right in the middle of the Schwarzwald (Black Forest). The food is delicious indeed.

One cool part of this trip is that my daughter finally got the hang of riding her bike herself…we just don’t feel it’s safe to ride bikes at home (due to fast drivers…see here for a laugh) but it was fun to see her so excited.

To celebrate, we had (more) ice cream together.

Among major hotel loyalty programs, Marriott Bonvoy offers some of the most attainable lifetime elite status tiers. I already have lifetime Gold Elite status with Marriott Bonvoy and will secure lifetime Platinum Elite status in three years.

If you're wondering if it's within reach for you, here's what you should know about Marriott lifetime status.

Marriott Bonvoy lets its members earn three tiers of lifetime elite status as follows:

Marriott also historically let members earn lifetime Titanium Elite status, but the program stopped offering it Dec. 31, 2018. Additionally, keep in mind that some Marriott brands don't offer a full qualifying night per eligible night stayed; for example, City Express, Four Points Flex and Protea Hotels award half an elite night credit per qualifying night, while StudioRes doesn't award any elite night credits.

The years of elite status don't need to be consecutive, and years spent at higher elite tiers count toward the requirements for lower lifetime tiers. Marriott status you get as a credit card perk counts toward the calculation of years in a specific elite status tier.

In addition to elite night credits earned from qualifying stays (which include qualifying award stays), elite night credits from credit cards and the five elite night credits you can select as an Annual Choice Benefit also count toward lifetime status.

Related: The complete guide to earning Marriott elite status with credit cards

Members with lifetime Marriott elite status enjoy the same benefits as members who earn these statuses annually, including waived points expiration. Plus, upon earning lifetime Platinum Elite status, you'll also get a complimentary gift and access to a webpage that looks back at your lifetime journey.

However, lifetime Platinum Elite status doesn't automatically qualify you for Annual Choice Benefits. You'll still need to earn 50 or 75 elite night credits in a calendar year to unlock these benefits.

And while lifetime members get the perks of the status they've earned, there's no guarantee that Marriott won't change the benefits of a particular status tier. So, if you earn lifetime Platinum Elite status, you'll get the current benefits of Platinum Elite instead of the benefits available at the time you secured lifetime status.

Marriott has made it easy to check your lifetime status progress. Go to the Marriott website, log in to your account, click your name in the upper-right corner and select "Overview." Then, click "Nights this year" on the left side of the page.

On the right side of the panel, you'll see your lifetime statistics.

This panel shows your lifetime nights, lifetime years with each status and how far you are from earning the next lifetime status tier.

Earning lifetime Marriott elite status can be relatively easy if you frequently stay with Marriott Bonvoy, hold a Marriott credit card that provides elite status and elite night credits, or both.

I'm looking forward to securing lifetime Platinum Elite status in three years. Although Marriott could change the benefits associated with each status tier, I'm excited about eventually enjoying Platinum Elite perks without requalifying each year.

#6234. American Airlines Makes Hotel Vouchers Easier To Get, But Warns Of Fewer Hotel Choices

American Airlines is updating how it provides hotel rooms, food credits, and transportation to passengers stranded by flight disruptions. Getting help without standing in another long line is welcome. But an internal memo also warns that employees may have fewer hotel choices to offer, which leaves me wondering whether a faster voucher will necessarily mean a better night.

View From The Wing highlights a November employee memo outlining changes to American’s Hotel, Meal and Transportation system, known internally as HMT.

American was already promoting automatic disruption vouchers in 2025. The question now is whether the latest changes make that assistance more reliable and easier to use.

I recently wrote about my American Airlines flight from Chicago to Los Angeles that nearly became an overnight stay.

A 7:10 p.m. departure slipped repeatedly until the posted departure time reached 11:55 p.m. The aircraft was there, but we had no pilots. Eventually, pilots arrived from Dallas and received a chorus of cheers from passengers who were thrilled we might actually get home.

During the wait, an Admirals Club agent offered me a hotel room if I wanted to rebook for the next day. The offer came with a caveat:

I appreciated having an option, but I wanted to get to Los Angeles. By that point, an airport hotel would have meant a short night followed by another trip through security and another flight.

But it is a reason why I appreciate this new rollout. Every minute spent waiting for an agent to arrange accommodation is a minute you cannot spend sleeping. If American can deliver a usable hotel offer to your phone promptly, that is a practical improvement.

“Frontline teams may see fewer hotel choices displayed than they are accustomed to seeing.”

Yes, a shorter list of suitable properties could work perfectly well and it is too early to say whether the remaining hotel options will be worse. But I’m not all that optimistic, here.

What happens when the available hotel is far from the airport, has no functioning shuttle at that hour, or cannot accommodate a family in an appropriate room.

We are not talking about putting every stranded passenger in a luxury hotel. But I do expect a clean room and a workable way to get there and back. A voucher is useful only if the accommodation behind it is suitable.

My agent’s Hilton comment was amusing, but it also captured the uncertainty. When you accept an airline-arranged room late at night, you may have little idea what you are getting.

Uber Central allows businesses to request rides for customers who do not have the Uber app. Riders receive trip details and a tracking link by text.

That could be particularly helpful for someone who rarely uses rideshare services or is already overwhelmed by a disrupted journey.

According to the reported instructions, however, hotel shuttles remain the first option, followed by Uber vouchers. Agent-arranged rides are intended for exceptions when those options do not meet the passenger’s needs. Broad availability of the new arrangement has not yet been established.

I hope agents have enough discretion to solve the actual problem. A hotel shuttle listed in a database is no help if it stopped running an hour ago…as a practical aside, before you leave the airport terminal call the hotel to make sure that the shuttle is running.

Under American’s published customer service plan, when a disruption is caused by the airline, assistance available upon request includes:

The plan also promises reimbursement of reasonable hotel costs if American cannot provide an approved hotel voucher (with an almost impossible caveat that such authorization must be obtained in writing). For disruptions beyond its control, such as weather, American generally leaves passengers responsible for their own accommodation and meals.

If you qualify for assistance and no automatic offer arrives, ask an agent. And if you get the food/beverage voucher, realize that the $12 won’t go very far (unless you are in Denver).

American Airlines deserves credit for making disruption assistance easier to deliver. Passengers who have already lost hours to a delay should not have to lose another hour obtaining a hotel voucher.

But fewer hotel choices could limit the usefulness of that improvement. I will judge the system by whether it gets stranded passengers into suitable rooms promptly, with transportation that actually works.

On my recent Chicago flight, I was thankful the pilots arrived and I never needed the hotel. Next time, I may not be so fortunate…(or maybe next time I will fly Delta or United).

#6232. Air France Takes Its 60th A220 as A318s Fly On

Air France took delivery of its 60th Airbus A220-300 on Friday, completing the order it placed in 2019 to replace its A318s, A319s and some A320s. The airline’s remaining A318s are still scheduled to fly through March 27, 2027.

The new A220, registered F-HOZJ and named Mimizan, arrived just over five years after Air France put the type into commercial service in October 2021. The airline says its 148-seat A220s now serve 50 destinations and have carried nearly 24 million passengers.

Air France had initially expected to have all 60 A220s in its fleet by 2025. The carrier has also pushed back the end of A318 flying. An August schedule update moved the last planned flights from Nov. 8 to March 27, according to AeroRoutes. The winter schedule includes A318 service from Paris Charles de Gaulle to destinations such as Barcelona, Dublin, and Rome.

Air France took delivery of its first A318 − the smallest A320 family variant − in October 2003 and went on to operate 18, the largest fleet of the type. Three remain active, according to fleet data from Planespotters.net.

The 60th delivery closes out the initial firm order, which also included 30 options and 30 purchase rights. Air France says its 61st A220 and subsequent deliveries will have Wi-Fi installed before entering commercial service. About 85% of the A220s already in service have the equipment, with the remaining installations due by February 2027.

#6231. What’s Your Airport Dwell Time? A Metric Businesses Think A Lot About

Dwell time, simply, is how long you spend in an airport, or airport space, before a flight. For most people, it’s not something they’ve ever actively really thought about.

For businesses in air travel and airports, like lounge operators, credit card companies or airlines, it’s one of the main things they think about. So what’s yours and what does it say about you?

Well, a lot. More importantly, the tracking of that dwell time has contributed to quite a lot of innovation in lounges and airports, with hopefully much more to come.

Build it and they will come. Who knew Kevin Costner knew so much about lounges?! In truth, if someone builds a lounge, everyone will come and ensuring it’s a good experience is an art form requiring math. Crowds can be hard to predict and most lounges are “too” full these days.

Knowing the average dwell time of a customer, and even a specific customer profile is one of the best tools lounges have to predict the flows of customers, including how much they’ll need to stock in food and drinks and everything else during peak times.

Even outside of lounges, knowing how long an air traveler spends in the airport is vital to understanding what kind of businesses, restaurants or concessions to offer. There’s a reason grab and go places do really, really well and get away with charging $12 for water.

Surprisingly to some, top tier frequent flyers typically have a really low dwell time compared to lower ranks or leisure travelers.

If an airline knows their lounge is full of top tiers that day, they can expect many people who won’t stay long. Whereas, if it’s a day with full flights and mostly leisure travel passengers, you can predict people will dwell far longer.

It makes sense. If you’re not used to the delights of a great airport lounge you come earlier, stay longer and take advantage of more. You also have less confidence in timings of the check in and security process, so you pad time in, in addition to the natural, “treat yourself” vibes.

If you do it all the time, every minute not in the airport is often seen as the win, so lounges are just a place to quickly reset and refresh before carrying on.

The first time I experienced a true first class lounge I think I got to the airport at the earliest possible interval. I had hours in there and of course, tried everything.

But I’ve been very lucky, I’ve experienced most lounges many times, been spoiled by the best many times, and unless there’s a real wow factor moment, I’m happiest spending as little time waiting in an airport as possible. Don’t get me wrong, I still indulge from time to time, but I’ve seen a huge dip in my own dwell average.

As I strolled through T2 at Heathrow this week en route to the United Club, it occurred to me that most of my recent lounge visits averaged about 30 minutes in total. In that 30 minutes I’d say I have a maximum of one drink, often little or no food, and mostly take advantage of the wifi and nice calm facilities.

I’ve gotten my time from curb to security at Heathrow down to a decent science and I like it that way. At other airports with even more predictable security and check in patterns, I’ll shave even more time off, often leaving no time for lounges at all.

And this raises a fair question: if everyone could truly model out their time from curb to airside, would they spend as long? Things like TSA PreCheck and CLEAR have been monumental in adding a layer of certainty to this process and I’d expect we’ll see more of it. Will more passengers change habits as they have better confidence in making their flight while cutting it fine?

Now of course, all bets are off when I travel with my kids. And that’s kind of the point. We think we’re very unique in our travel habits, but there are many variables of our travels which drop us into a fairly predictable pattern … and dwell time.

When lounge access is a marquee benefit of being a frequent flyer, but most top frequent flyers hardly leave any time for lounge dwelling, is that a real selling point?

In response, we’ve seen really clever pivots lately, including from Air Canada and Capital One. Each brand has created curated “grab and go” offerings in their lounges or lounge-like areas to offer passengers complimentary things which have tangible value — a nitro cold brew latte, or a nice pastry — for “free”, which they’re totally able to take on the road with them.

That’s a huge departure from the days of lounges with signs everywhere saying no outside food and drinks and no removing food or drinks from the lounge. People never paid attention anyway, and this now just creates a formalized and better thought out approach to catering to all traveler needs.

The big question is: what’s next for adding value to a travelers airport journey? Be sure to share your lounge and travel habits as well.

If you’ve been frustrated by soaring airfare, now may be your best chance to book flights without the sticker shock.

American Airlines just launched one of its biggest AAdvantage award sales of the year. And you'll want to act quickly: It’s only scheduled to be live for 72 hours.

American has put more than 1 million main cabin seats on sale for the winter months.

If holiday fares were out of your budget this year, this could be a chance to redeem miles for a long weekend getaway in the Caribbean in January — or to hit the ski slopes over President’s Day weekend in February.

American’s winter AAdvantage award sale covers flights from Jan. 11 through Feb. 28, 2027.

The deals are slated to run through 12:59 a.m. EST on Nov. 12.

These aren’t the cheapest AAdvantage award redemptions we’ve ever seen (a similar award sale last year offered award prices even lower than this year’s).

And some of these redemptions are in the range of what I typically look for in the quieter winter months.

The good news here is that these cheaper award prices are widely available. And that’s significant in a year where fares (and award prices) have surged.

As an AAdvantage member myself, I'd feel pretty good about booking at any of these price points.

You won’t find these discounted award prices on every flight, date or route. Instead, American simply says it’s discounting more than 1 million main cabin seats across its network.

Fortunately, there aren't blackout dates — which means you don't need to fly at 10 p.m. on a Tuesday to take advantage of this deal. There are options on Fridays, Sundays, peak long weekend travel days and during other popular times.

These deals apply to economy bookings; American is not offering up these discounts on premium economy, first class or business class.

However, these cheaper award redemptions could be a way to get a spot on the plane and then watch for a targeted upgraded offer to a premium seat.

You can find domestic bookings within the 48 contiguous U.S. states for as low as 8,000 miles one-way.

That includes longer transcontinental flights.

For instance, here’s a January flight from Philadelphia International Airport (PHL) to Los Angeles International Airport (LAX).

There are also short-haul international redemptions to warm-weather island destinations at that rate, too — like this February flight from Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA) to Turks and Caicos.

As a Raleigh-based flyer, I could book this Martin Luther King, Jr. weekend flight from North Carolina to Zurich, Switzerland, for 22,500 miles one-way.

There are a ton of AAdvantage redemptions to Europe at that price point, with options for both nonstop and connecting itineraries, depending on your final destination.

I also found pretty open award availability for 25,000 miles one-way.

#6229. Southwest Airlines Offers “Free” Same-Day Flight Changes, But There’s A Seat-Fee Trap

Southwest Airlines offers eligible passengers free same-day flight changes, but there is a catch if you paid separately for your seat. Asking an airport agent to make the change can leave that seat purchase nonrefundable, while making the change through the app, website, or telephone receives different treatment. Apparently, how you change your flight now matters almost as much as which flight you choose.

View From The Wing highlights a peculiar provision in Southwest’s seat refund and exchange policy.

For passengers who separately purchased a seat on their original flight, Southwest explicitly states:

“Same-day change requested at the airport: Seat purchased on original flight is non-refundable.”

But complete that same-day change through Southwest.com, the Southwest app, or by telephone, and the rules provide a way to apply the original seat payment toward a replacement or receive a refund when buying a more expensive seat.

You could be standing at the gate with your phone in hand, looking at an earlier departure. Whether you tap the screen or ask the employee in front of you for help could affect what happens to money you already spent.

The policy concerns seats purchased separately from the airfare. Here is how Southwest describes the treatment when you voluntarily switch flights:

For a hypothetical example, suppose you paid $40 for a seat and make a confirmed same-day change through the app. If the replacement seat costs $30, Southwest applies the original payment but does not return the $10 difference.

If the replacement costs $50, you pay $50 upfront and generally receive a separate $40 refund. You should therefore check that the refund actually arrives rather than assuming the system simply charged you the difference.

Under Southwest’s same-day change policy, the confirmed-change benefit is available with Choice, Choice Preferred, and Choice Extra fares, along with Getaways by Southwest vacation bookings.

You need an available seat on a flight between the same origin and destination airports on the same travel date. The change must occur at least 10 minutes before your original scheduled departure.

Basic passengers must upgrade to an eligible fare first (and A-List or A-List Preferred status alone does not make a Basic ticket eligible for a free confirmed same-day change)

So when it comes to standby, there are two separate things to check: whether you can switch flights without an additional airfare charge, and what happens to the seat you purchased.

Do not confuse a confirmed change with same-day standby.

A confirmed change secures your place on the replacement flight immediately. Standby means waiting for space to become available, often much closer to boarding or even after boarding commences if you are waiting for no-shows. Southwest’s seat policy says the original seat purchase becomes nonrefundable when standby clears, regardless of how you joined the list.

Using the app therefore does not solve the seat-payment issue for standby. The eligibility rules differ too. A-List and A-List Preferred members can qualify for standby on Basic fares, even though those fares do not qualify for free confirmed same-day changes.

Of course, switching flights does not guarantee the same seat. Someone who bought extra legroom on one departure cannot reasonably expect an identical seat to materialize on a replacement flight. But why should the channel used to request the change determine the treatment of the original payment?

If Southwest can apply or refund that purchase when I use its app, why should asking an airport employee produce a less favorable rule? There may be a systems explanation, but that does little for a passenger who reasonably assumes an agent can provide the same options available online. On the other hand, I would bet that an agent who assigns you a superior seat in these sorts of situations is not going to charge for it…any frequent Southwest travelers want to weigh in?

This also puts employees in an awkward position. A passenger asks for help, receives it, then discovers that handling the transaction another way could have preserved the value of a seat purchase. For an airline that built so much goodwill around simplicity, this seems like an unnecessarily complicated way to handle a relatively ordinary request.

If you paid separately for a Southwest seat and want to make a confirmed same-day flight change, check the app or website before asking an airport agent to process it. Telephone changes also receive the more favorable treatment outlined in the policy.

Compare the replacement seat cost and keep track of any refund due. If you are using standby, remember that the app does not preserve the refundability of your original seat purchase once you clear.

A free flight change can still have consequences for the extras you purchased. Southwest passengers now have another reason to read the fine print before accepting what sounds like a straightforward benefit.

#6228. New Credit Card Sets Annual Fee Dynamically, Based On Benefit Usage

Among savvy Redditors and credit card blogs, there’s a common thread with many recent credit card changes. “It feels like a coupon book” is often the consumer reaction, particularly as annual fees rise as justification for an increasing number of partner offer benefits, which if consumed in entirety could lead to more value.

Since many people simply won’t use all the benefits and partner offers being baked into the card, people increasingly feel like the annual fee rises are getting too steep. In a bold move, a new card launched today which offers a flexible annual fee, based only on the benefits you actually use.

Signed up for a card named after a precious or semi precious metal and shocked by the $450-$695 fee? You’re not alone.

To get your money back from such a fee, you’d need to take advantage of regular lounge access at airports, utilize your TSA PreCheck/Global Entry credit, maximize every monthly dining or entertainment credit and sign up for every other fee credit, which often requires a purchase.

To quell this issue, the new card is effectively a build your own card, card.

Despite the innovation, the card draws on the historical concept of the coupon book, where you only pay for the offers you tear out and redeem. The annual fee starts at zero, but as you actually redeem the cards benefits, you get billed accordingly. Your fee can be zero, or as high as $10,000 per year.

Done right, you can end up paying $650 in annual fees for about $800 worth of stuff, some of which you wanted and most of which, about $700 worth, you didn’t really want or need, but felt compelled to get, just because it’s there.

This model allows you to really dive into the classic coupon book, feeling like you’re really tearing offers out of the page, and simply leaving the ones you’re not using in the book. You’re only paying for the ones you rip out, but when there’s so many offers to choose from, the book just feels so compelling.

Obviously, it’s April 1st and no such card is coming to the market (yet, lol), but hopefully this light hearted amusement has been a helpful exercise in framing the true value you’re really extracting from your premium credit card, or conversely, the lack thereof.

Consider the things you’d actually purchase without the “offer” prompt and if that number still adds up to be more than the annual fee, you’re doing it right. If it doesn’t…

This method sounds as irritating as the coupon-book BS. As soon as you use a benefit, you are dinged for it.

#6227. Global Airlines Is “Fyre Festival”, Not Virgin Atlantic

Yesterday, a Hi-Fly charter airplane took off from Glasgow bound for New York, with Hi-Fly crews and pilots. If you read the papers, it was purportedly ‘Global Airlines’ maiden flight, even though there’s no regularly scheduled service, the pilots and crew weren’t theirs, they couldn’t legally sell airline tickets on their own website and they don’t have a license to operate.

In 2025, crazy things are par for the course, so that didn’t stop all sorts of promising headlines of a revolution in the skies. This is the airline that promised stunning innovation and joy in the air, and the press gave Global Airlines an early gift, by comparing the story to Richard Branson and Virgin Atlantic. That’s just insane, as you’ll soon read.

In reality, anyone can charter a plane and have Hi-Fly operate it, and anyone foolish enough can pay extra for a custom paint job with their logo, or more financially insane — buy a scrapyard A380 and be on the hook for its maintenance, while paying a third party to fly it.

The whole ‘Global’ pitch was that people love the Airbus A380, hate all the current global airline experiences ( really?) and airline services — and a revolution in the skies, can happen again. It sounded exciting. We all like to dream. Global’s first flight would be the testament to what air travel can be and something passengers love. So, how’d they do?

When Virgin Atlantic launched in 1984, the airline industry had been in a massively “beige” management consultant style, joy killer phase for a decade.

The fun “golden era” aircraft spaces and frills of the 60’s had largely been stripped out and bus travel comparisons were totally fair. Richard Branson’s light hearted approach to service and differentiated selling could shift dollars and votes — and measurably did.

Let me be very clear: that simplicity in differentiation is no longer the case. You cannot shift wallets and put butts in seats just by saying you have a cool airplane alone, or a bar on board (particularly when it’s just a beverage cart that says pub).

From leading (actually real) global airlines, passengers expect, at minimum, the following…

When “Global”, and by Global I really do legally, technically mean Hi-Fly the jet charter company which actually flew the scrapyard plane that “Global” bought, they did NOT have…

Travel blogger Noel Phillips shared some of the trip with his following. The following screen grabs are…. cute?

The truth is, Virgin Atlantic didn’t have nearly as gargantuan of a task in the 80’s as any airline coming to market does today. In the 80’s many airlines were stuck, did lack innovation and had a pool of largely uninspired talent, with no experience outside of the airline vertical. There also wasn’t this whole technology thing, as standard expectation.

That’s all so far from the case these days and most that are specialized in the airline world are wickedly sharp. Most new people I know at airlines now also come from major tech companies, other travel verticals or impactful innovation firms.

Airlines are getting pretty good at this ole’ air travel thing.

A differentiated approach to smiles on board and a little bit of extra focus on fun, food and drinks could really shift minds and mentalities in the 1980’s, but now you gotta back it up, baby.

Everyone likes to feel special and Virgin, forever, has made people feel special at a time without tech. I’d argue Virgin has taught Delta a lot about that, and it’s a contributing factor to Delta’s rise as a premium airline. It didn’t happen overnight, and what looks easy never is.

Getting people to fly with you is now about safety, reliability, excellence in mobile technology, schedule and personalization. Then fine, we can care about which champagne; or caterer or lounge style or airport, and which celebs like it. Yes, these legacy airlines can appear stuffy at times, but my god, can you not marvel at the technology revolution making air travel journeys excellent?

On real airlines, before I even arrive at the airport, I can use the NFC chip in my passport pressed against my phone to validate my document and bypass human interaction. I board a United, or any serious airline flight nowadays and see a notification that my bag is loaded onto a cart to be loaded on the plane, then again when it’s loaded onto the plane!

I hit the wifi and I’m connected sitting at the gate. If for some reason the flight is at all delayed, or connection in jeopardy, I can instantly rebook onto any other service at no charge, without talking to a soul, with just a tap on the app.

Their seag back screens have blockbuster movies, boxsets and everything else you could want for a one hour, or 15 hour journey. It’s all just standard now, not innovative.

The app navigates me through the airport and even tells me when my zone is boarding. AKA – stand the “f” back. The food is at least solid, the beverages are getting better because of their scale (buying power) and there are fewer poor customer service interactions because of how tech forward and seamless journeys are.

All the great, big airlines do this. This is like… baseline for a real player.

Tell me, or ask the Global Airlines CEO, James Asquith, where in the roadmap all of these essentials are? I want to make it clear that their priority for the last three years was a Soho House press conference about serving champagne in economy, maybe, “if they could get the economics right” rather than any of these basic things.

And in the end, they didn’t even deliver on the silly things they prioritized. The first Global flight wasn’t a remotely differentiated take on economy, business or first, as promised. It was 12 year old seats from another lackluster airline, without real refurb and even the long haul dignity of any seat back entertainment, which that airline which scrapped the plane offered.

If Richard Branson was at the helm, they never would’ve let that flight take off. Making a splash means at least doing one thing differently, right? An airline promising total innovation, A380 experience and differentiation cannot launch a flight which does not even meet the basic standards of budget carriers like Norse. You just can’t take off. You innovative something!

Let’s not forget that when Richard Branson formed Virgin Atlantic, he’d already founded a notable brand and number of businesses in the UK, was quite famous, and filed records and company books in a place where they are scrutinized. He was “real”, even if some was bluster. The public could and did use his businesses.

James Asquith’s only claim to fame, other than from the Instagram account he bought followers for, to fake fame — yes, factually — is that he was the “CEO” of Holiday Swap. Omg, so big time!

The business purports to be a home swap company, though there are no financial records of any legal merit in the West, and despite my damndest multi-year attempts, no record of actual customers. Simple use of Similar Web or review sites will help your own conclusions. You can read old blog posts for more musings. The rumors of what laundered through are scary. Maybe a real journalist can find out for us?

I actually think it’s dangerous to the public to compare these two people.

I’ve had the good fortune of meeting Richard Branson many times throughout the years and he’s always been wildly impressive. Wickedly sharp, analytical, funny and personable. It’s easy to put in a good shift for PR purposes, but I’ve observed levels of deep dive knowledge that no setup encounter can protect for — and genuine interest too. He cares about his people and he worries about the details.

I also have many people in my personal life connected to the Virgin Atlantic founder and I know of nothing but admiration and respect for the man, his company ethos and family. Business in the front, party in the back.

My only encounter with James Asquith was when he was fuming that he wasn’t invited on an airlines press trip, slid into my Instagram DM’s wanting me to blast them – and for us to be best buds as we roast a major (actual) global airline. That airline later confidentially told me he was banned from flying, due to his antics. I politely declined and he unfollowed me. It was soooo cool.

I guess if you can’t fly other airlines, you start your own?

So yeah, if you ever feel like putting your life in the hands of an airline without functioning entertainment screens, or WiFi, or regularly scheduled service, or new seats, or a mobile app, or an actual license to fly planes, definitely fly with Global. Oh, and no viable loyalty program either. Forget about earning points from daily spending and turning them into upgrades.

Those other “boring” airlines with all the bells and whistles above are clearly not ready to make travel great, with a new golden age, again.

Gilbert Ott is an ever curious traveler and one of the world's leading travel experts. His adventures take him all over the globe, often spanning over 200,000 miles a year and his travel exploits are regularly... More by Gilbert Ott

His intrusion and snide comment ab0ut Simon Calder was entirely unnecessary. I have little respect for Asquith as it is, he doesn’t seem to actually “do” anything other than post Insta’s of slamming Champagne, and buying an Instagram account for the new venture is downright deceptive. Prove me wrong, I’m all for new carriers, but part of me wants it to fail just because of the insufferable “CEO”.

‘Global Airlines’ reminds me of the line from ‘The Producers’: “Under the right circumstances, a [person] could make more money with a flop than he could with a hit.”

This is why many say “hire for personality and train for skill.” James Asquith has failed this test with his attitude and stands little chance of building a culture within his company that can grow to compete with the likes of Virgin. I was always concerned that this airline was launching without any unique selling points at all. Now to read that what little was brought in from China Southern does not even work: it’s for me very sad to read. Substantial funding was needed to get this far and there seems to have been very little planning around the customer experience. I raised 350k externally to launch my last business, and that was not easy for me to do. So to imagine the capital sums that will be wasted here for all the unforced errors made, it’s so disheartening given it was foreseeable! There are so many case studies, even from Virgin with Virgin Nigeria and Virgin America to review! James Asquith seems to be very lazy and entitled. A great opportunity not afforded to many better qualified people (not me), has been thrown away!

While I agree with everything in this article, I also feel like immediately criticizing new entrants and disrupters is not fair. There is not a single person in aviation that wants to see less A380’s, that want les competition transatlantic, or fewer carriers. I appreciate Global, I appreciate BOOM, and I think it is just as sensational to criticize Global as it is for them to put on a metaphorical Fyre Fest in the sky. This is responsible reporting, but let’s also at some recognize the feat that getting this particular plane in the sky, with people, to NY was. Aviation was built on the backs of visionaries and risk-takers, I hope we will continue to celebrate that spirit.

I’m genuinely surprised that yours seems to the the only objectively credible take on this fiasco. I’ve watched a couple of the first flight review videos and the aircraft and service are laughable, yet the internet is still awash with “great to see!” and “Go Global!”, all blindly ignoring the current capabilities of the competition summarised above as if they don’t matter.

At least it’s given us a good laugh over the last few years but someone is losing money (hard to call anything sunk into this shambles an “investment”) and I imagine the flag carriers will be delighted as it makes them look stellar by comparison. Got to seriously question the judgement of anyone that wanted to get involved with Global. It’s all been smoke and mirrors from day one.
