Among my friends and family, I see couples manage their finances and credit cards in many different ways. But across all the couples I know, I've found that two people can work together to earn more rewards and enjoy more benefits than they could individually.

So, here are some credit card strategies you should consider if you're part of a couple.

Couples who manage their finances separately will generally want separate credit card accounts. However, even if you manage your finances separately, you may want one or two cards you both use for shared expenses.

Likewise, even if you generally manage your finances jointly, having a few separate cards can be nice for purchasing surprise gifts.

You'll be approved or denied for a card based on your credit score and history, independent of your partner's credit score and history. But depending on your age and circumstances, you may also be able to include income from your partner that you can reasonably access when applying for a new card.

Some banks offer joint credit card accounts, which you apply for together and are jointly responsible for the bills. But joint accounts are relatively rare, so this article instead considers the more common situation in which one person opens an account and then adds their partner as an authorized user.

Primary account holders can make their partner (or anyone else) an authorized user on their account. Authorized users can make purchases on the account, but the primary cardholder is responsible for all the charges (including those made by authorized users).

Related: Here’s how my husband and I maximize each dollar we spend on household expenses

One of the biggest advantages couples have over solo travelers is access to more welcome offers. Specifically, each member of a couple could earn the welcome bonus on the same card if they each apply separately.

This can be particularly useful if you're earning welcome offers for a specific trip. You could use one person's welcome offer for hotel bookings and the other person's for flights. Or, you could each use your welcome offer to book an award flight for the same trip.

But while both partners can potentially earn welcome offers on the same card, it's still important to coordinate application timing and avoid taking on more minimum spending than you can comfortably manage. Plus, each individual must keep in mind issuer application restrictions, such as Chase's 5/24 rule, when deciding which cards to apply for and when to apply for them.

Related: Cards currently offering welcome bonuses of 100,000 points or more

If you and your partner each want to apply for a new card, you must decide whether to get the same cards or different cards.

The biggest reasons to get the same cards are an exceptional welcome offer or perks you'll each want.

For example, each member of a couple might want their own Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card if they frequently travel separately and value airport lounge access, especially since lounge access for authorized users now costs extra.

And I love that my husband and I each have our own , as this lets us use our anniversary night certificates for consecutive nights to make a two-night stay.

However, it often makes sense for couples to have complementary cards. By applying for different cards that complement what's in your partner's wallet, you can unlock better bonus-category coverage, different travel perks and access to different transferable rewards currencies.

This can be particularly useful if one person in a couple travels more frequently, as they may want to carry more cards with travel benefits, such as lounge access and airline or hotel elite status.

Be sure to weigh the combined annual fees against the benefits you'll actually use. And keep in mind that some cards let you share benefits with other travelers. For example, many airline credit cards offer a checked baggage benefit that extends to other travelers on your same reservation.

Related: Better together: The ultimate guide to the best credit card combinations

In some cases, you may want to add your partner as an authorized user on a card. This can be an easy choice when there's no fee. But it can also make sense to pay an authorized-user fee in some situations.

For example, many couples have one primary and pay $195 per additional Platinum card for each other family member (see rates and fees). By doing so, these family members can enjoy many of the Platinum Card's perks, including lounge access and select hotel elite statuses (enrollment is required for select benefits).

However, keep in mind that some benefits don't extend to authorized users. For example, purchases on additional Platinum Cards count toward many of the Platinum Card's statement credit benefits, such as up to $200 in airline incidental fee statement credits per calendar year (enrollment required). But additional Platinum Cards don't get their own statement credits.

So, while it might make sense for one partner to hold a premium travel card and add the other as an authorized user, it can make sense for both partners to independently hold cards that offer valuable benefits you'll use.

For example, my husband and I both hold several hotel credit cards, such as the (see rates and fees) and (see rates and fees), since their annual free night certificates and other perks provide ample value.

Adding your partner as an authorized user may also help them build credit if the issuer reports the account to credit bureaus and the account is managed responsibly. However, missed payments or high credit utilization could hurt their credit instead.

Related: 7 credit cards with the best authorized user benefits

Whether you and your partner earn the same currencies on your credit cards or different currencies, and whether you combine your finances or not, it makes sense to coordinate how you earn and redeem rewards.

Consider what types of rewards you should both be earning based on the trips you want to take. For example, if you have your sights set on visiting a far-flung international destination, spending on a Southwest credit card likely isn't the best choice. Instead, earning hotel points in a program with properties in your desired destination, airline miles with a program that serves that destination or transferable rewards is a better bet.

The benefit of both partners earning the same transferable currency is that you can each transfer to the airline or hotel program of your choice once you're ready to redeem. But there's also value in diversifying your earnings in case flight availability appears in a program that only some transferable currencies can access.

Before deciding which rewards to earn, consider how you'll redeem them together. Some credit card issuers let you move rewards between eligible household accounts, while some airline and hotel loyalty programs allow members to pool points or transfer them to each other. Even when you can't combine rewards, you may be able to use your points or miles to book travel for your partner.

Related: These 14 apps and websites make award redemptions easier to find

Couples have plenty of opportunities to earn more rewards and enjoy more credit card benefits by coordinating their credit card strategies. Whether you and your partner decide to get the same cards, hold complementary cards or add each other as authorized users, the best approach depends on your spending habits and travel goals.

My husband and I have found that having our own credit card accounts while coordinating which rewards we earn and redeem works well for us. But you don't need a wallet full of cards to benefit from a two-player strategy. Even a few carefully chosen cards can help you earn more rewards and enjoy more perks together.

Related: How to earn and use an IHG annual lounge membership

#6224. Virgin Atlantic Ups The Ante In India, As The World Dials In

This week, Virgin Atlantic celebrates 25 years of flying to India. In Virgin fashion, it’s doing so in style, with a joint announcement among partners Delta Airlines, Air France-KLM, and a new strategic partner IndiGo.

On the sidelines of the IATA Annual General Meeting, basically the UN General Assembly of airlines, the new strategic partnership for India was announced with very interesting nods to the future.

IndiGo carries more passengers in India than anyone else and will connect US and UK/European customers flying Virgin, Delta and Air France KLM onward in India, while also helping fill seats for these European and North American partners, as their own customers head West.

That’s probably a good thing, because with recent service additions, Virgin now flies a million seats a year to India and it sounds like others are piling on more flights too. It’s now one of the largest operators to India.

I’ve been bullish on India as the next great center of the world for a while now. It’s not necessarily that I’m at all intelligent, it’s just based on the fact that India is the world’s largest population. But, when Ed Bastian, Delta’s formidable CEO says it, people tend to listen. Bastian mentioned India being the most important aviation market globally now and signaled a return of direct services for the carrier as well.

Virgin has been a small step ahead, adding service regularly on their Delhi, Mumbai and Bangalore routes. IndiGo chose this alliance over formidable competition and this will certainly be a space to watch as more global airlines and alliances focus on India.

Geo-political activity points to India becoming a new manufacturing super power, in addition to its prolific work in tech, IT and customer service, not to mention blossoming tourism. These kind of globally connected businesses are big business, huge in fact, for corporate contracts and easy onward connectivity to regional sites is essential. The partnership makes sense.

In a somewhat rare and impressive signal of unity and seriousness towards India, Virgin Atlantic made their India crews part of the core Virgin family, rather than as contractors through a third party local company, known in aviation world as a GSA. This means Virgin’s India crews are a part of the full team, with benefits too.

When asked about loyalty implications of the new alliance, Virgin Atlantic CEO, Shai Weiss, noted a mutual passion for using loyalty to enhance guest experience far beyond just the earn and burn of points and miles. For future iterations, they’ve offered the following…

The MoU (memorandum of understanding) also creates a framework for deeper collaboration between the carriers on a bilateral and multilateral basis; contemplates commercial collaboration including network, loyalty, cargo and sales, subject to regulatory approvals; explores areas of non-commercial cooperation including aircraft maintenance, sustainability, training, ground handling; and acknowledges the need to develop advanced collaboration through use of technology to efficiently service joint customers.

IndiGo will provide onward connectivity for Virgin and the other strategic partners to 32 destinations, making it easier than ever to see Udaipur, Jaipur, Mumbai, Kashmir and delights further south in Bangalore and Goa.

I just returned from the lovely Leela Palace in Delhi, as I watched the news happen live.

To me, India is a country of joy. Even people with truly nothing seem to find positivity and it’s generally a way of life here. Hospitality is as warm and steeped in tradition as it comes, too. It’s hot, it’s humid, but it’s an experience unlike any other and that’s something that’s harder to say these days than I’d like.

The food, ugh. I adore. Sure, I’ll take a dosa from the South over a heavy curry from the North most days, but I love both and if you don’t love a good black daahl there’s something wrong with you.

In short, it’s already fairly easy to get to India but it’s about to get a whole lot easier and not just to hub cities too. More seats means more chances to use points, by the way!

#6223. Brit Arrested After Flight Attendant Finds Hidden Camera In Airplane Bathroom, Now Faces Voyeurism And Cover-Up Charges

A flight attendant discovered a hidden camera while using the lavatory on a Scoot flight from Japan to Singapore. A British passenger now faces charges of voyeurism and obstructing justice, with police alleging that he remotely activated the camera and later tried to erase evidence after realizing it had been found.

Hugh Lutley, a 52-year-old British national, was charged on November 5, 2026, following an incident aboard Scoot flight TR821 from Osaka (KIX) to Singapore (SIN) on October 7.

He faces one charge each of voyeurism and obstruction of justice. It appears Lutley intends to plead guilty, was offered bail of S$10,000, and has a pretrial conference scheduled for November 17 (which of course is not a conviction or a sentence).

The Singapore Police Force’s account describes an alleged attempt to record people inside an aircraft toilet. Police say the passenger concealed a camera in the lavatory, left, and activated its recording function through an application on his phone.

A cabin crew member subsequently used the lavatory and discovered the device. She removed it and immediately alerted a colleague. The passenger allegedly returned to retrieve the camera, found it missing, and deleted the application and related photographs from his phone in an attempt to avoid detection.

Police detained him when the flight arrived at Singapore Changi Airport and seized his phone and the camera.

Those are statutory maximums, but the alleged attempt to destroy evidence exposes him to a charge carrying a substantially longer maximum prison term than the underlying voyeurism charge.

I am thankful the flight attendant found the device and reported it. Discovering something like that while using the restroom must be deeply unsettling.

The published accounts do not establish how many people, if any, were recorded before the camera was discovered…the alleged installation and remote operation are disturbing enough.

Is this world so twisted that passengers must become amateur surveillance experts every time they use an airplane bathroom? If you notice an unfamiliar device or something suspicious, alert the crew promptly…yeah, I guess you should look around before you drop your drawers.

#6222. “You Can Have My Middle Seat!” Frontier Passenger Swipes Another Man’s Aisle Seat To Sit With His Wife, Crew Does Nothing

A Frontier Airlines passenger reportedly found another man sitting in his assigned aisle seat because that man wanted to sit beside his wife. The proposed solution? The displaced passenger could take a middle seat two rows behind him. According to a witness, a flight attendant became involved but did not resolve the situation, and the passenger ultimately gave up. If that account is accurate, the airline failed him and owes him more than an apology.

The seating dispute occurred aboard Frontier flight 1550 from Atlanta (ATL) to Jacksonville (JAX).

According to the witness, a passenger arrived at seat 28C and found another man occupying it beside his wife. When he pointed out the assignment, the seated passenger reportedly responded:

“Well, I wanted to sit next to my wife. You can have my middle seat (30E).”

The witness says a flight attendant heard what had happened, but the man remained in the aisle seat. The displaced passenger eventually accepted 30E, saying:

The original Reddit post has since been deleted, though the discussion remains. This is an unverified witness account on reddit…it might be all malarkey…but at worst it makes for an interesting theoretical discussion.

I have no objection to asking another passenger to switch seats. Sometimes couples end up separated despite trying to arrange seats together. But there is a proper way to ask. Start in your assigned seat, explain the situation, and accept the answer. Offering a comparable or better seat certainly helps and is something I view as a starting point.

Taking someone’s aisle seat before he arrives, then informing him that he can have your middle seat instead, turns a request into a confrontation: wanting to sit beside your spouse does not give you authority to make that decision for him.

Why not ask the person beside your assigned middle seat whether they would like to move forward and take your wife’s seat? That would at least give someone a genuine choice while leaving the unwilling passenger out of it.

But the broader problem is the alleged response by Frontier flight attendants. Especially on Frontier, which has totally unbundled fares and has made seat selection a major part of the booking process. The practice of charging for seat selection makes indifference to these disputes even harder to defend. Still, I’m suspicious because even on Frontier I find it difficult to fathom that the crew could reasonably leave the rightful occupant to negotiate for it.

I recognize that airlines sometimes must move passengers for operational or safety reasons. But that is quite different than allowing one traveler’s preference to override another’s confirmed seat assignment merely because he sat down first. If the witness’s account captures the full exchange, the straightforward response would have been to check the boarding passes and ask the man to return to his seat or be ejected from the flight. The crew could then explore a voluntary swap if someone wanted to help.

It is easy to read this story and declare that you would never surrender your seat.

I would have calmly asked the flight attendant to confirm my assignment and help me sit there. If that went nowhere, I would have asked whether another crew member or a gate agent could assist. And yes, I would have filmed it all.

But I also understand the exhaustion behind “I just want to get home.” Sometimes a passenger has already endured enough that a middle seat seems preferable to another argument.

That does not make him foolish and certainly does not establish that the swap was fair.

Frontier (or any carrier) should not create a situation in which the most persistent passenger gets what he wants while the more accommodating one absorbs the inconvenience. That rewards precisely the behavior crews should be discouraging.

This account comes from a witness, and the original post is no longer available. We should leave room for details that may be missing and be open to the possibility that this story is a fabrication.

But the principle is simple and it’s still worth repeating: you may ask someone to switch seats so you can sit with your spouse. You may not decide that his aisle seat is yours and that he should accept your middle seat instead.

When that happens, the crew should help resolve it. Airlines cannot spend the booking process telling us how valuable seat assignments are, then treat those assignments as optional once we board.

#6221. This Is The Summer To Tick Santorini Off The Bucket List

It’s June, and for perhaps the first time in modern history, Santorini isn’t crowded. Those earthquakes a good few months ago? Not even a flower pot was tipped over, yet incessant clickbait headlines managed to have a lasting impact.

And that’s a shame, because there’s been a lovely tourism revolution brewing there, where local hoteliers are bringing back the kind of experience and hospitality that you want to come back for over and over again.

As someone who goes at least once or twice a year, and will again very shortly, I can only advocate to tick it off the bucket list this summer, because you’ll never find prices, availability or an experience quite like it again for a while.

In the last 20 years, Santorini got totally overrun. Cruise tourism and day trip mania somewhat ruined a once idyllic, low-key fishing island and then Instagram and TikTok lit the match.

But now the TikTok crowd is in Mykonos and Santorini, as unequalled in beauty as ever, is lovely again. Hotels like The Vasilicos and Santorini Sky bring wildly different, delightfully luxurious and hospitality driven experiences to the island.

Beach clubs, yes Santorini’s beaches are underrated, have made a nice little mark on quieter coasts with great effect too. Assyrtiko, the local grape has hit the world stage as a darling of sommeliers in top restaurants and vineyards like Vassaltis offer stunning tasting experiences.

And the food? There’s no Nobu, or Scorpios here, so there are plenty of places to feel the benefit of European pricing, including a personal favorite at Kantouni.

The trouble with Santorini has historically been that many of the best hotels are small, they fill up quickly, and as they do, they charge a fortune. For the best, like the ones mentioned above, it’s still worth it. But this season, all across the board, prices are lower and even if you don’t care about price, many of the best which might typically be sold out for the season have rooms.

As an additional tailwind for travelers, flights between the US and Europe are quieter this summer, which means there’s deals to be had with both points and cash from major markets to Santorini. If you don’t see cheap flights to Santorini, try a major hub and booking an onward ticket separately.

Naturally, precaution is a good thing in life. But fear mongering for the sake of clicks is another beast and I can’t help but be fairly appalled by the many weeks and months of coverage and follow up coverage, reiterating a narrative of fear… despite no damage to anything, anywhere.

If you do bag a great deal this summer and visit one of my very favorite places, and use this great Santorini guide to make the most of your time, you can thank the media.

#6219. In Winter, Canada's Banff National Park is So Much More Than a Skiers' Paradise

My view from the foot of gleaming Victoria Glacier was straight out of a snow globe. Two shaggy ebony draft horses pulled a vintage sleigh along a powdery path that hugged the shores of frozen Lake Louise. Lycra-clad Nordic skiers glided across the snow-dusted ice, navigating around life-size snowmen. In the far distance a ray of sun glinted off the turret of an ice-sculpted castle, a mini version of the grand Fairmont Chateau Lake Louise hotel, which stands sentinel over this unbelievably pretty patch of wilderness in Banff National Park. A soft gust of wind swirled a flurry of flakes across the scene. The winter wonderland in front of me was magical enough to make even the most die-hard snowbirds reconsider the season.

I've always felt winter could be approached in two ways: You could be lazy and binge Netflix for three months, or you could be sporty and get after it in the mountains. But a weeklong trip to the Banff and Lake Louise region of Alberta opened my eyes to a gratifying middle ground. This area is a true winter playground, where you could downhill-ski or engage with the elements in so many other ways: snowshoeing, going for a horse-drawn sleigh ride, or watching the snowflakes fall while you're soaking in an outdoor hot tub. My time ended up being more about appreciating nature than conquering it on the slopes.

A seat with a view inside Fairmont Chateau Lake Louise

I arrived in early January on the tail of one of the area's snowiest Decembers on record, though you couldn't tell from the landscape around Calgary airport. Umber-hued prairies and agricultural land surround the gateway city, and it wasn't until 40 minutes into my 90-minute drive west on the Trans-Canada Highway that the Great Plains transitioned to the Canadian Rockies and the sky started nuking snow.

Home to SkiBig3—a trio of resorts that include Banff Sunshine, Lake Louise Ski Resort, and the mom-and-pop Mount Norquay—Banff National Park was the place to be during a winter in which most of the American West suffered a snow drought. In my 20s I would have driven straight from the airport to the ski slopes. Now in my mid-40s, with an unpredictable knee, back-to-back, bell-to-bell days have lost their appeal. But the childlike joy of playing in the snow has not. And Fairmont Chateau Lake Louise was the perfect base for “soft” winter adventure.

The resort's address, in the heart of Banff National Park overlooking glacier-fed Lake Louise, envelops guests in nature. No surprise—Lake Louise was originally developed for outdoor tourism. In 1885, after the last spike of the Canadian Pacific Railway was driven in, future company president William Cornelius Van Horne built hotels along the route. Among the first, the Banff Springs Hotel was designed for horseback sightseeing. The Chalet at Lake Louise, a humble log cabin, was marketed as a destination for fishing, canoeing, and alpinism. Van Horne hired Swiss guides to teach his guests to safely navigate the mountains, and they are partially responsible for introducing locals to the sport of skiing.

A horse-drawn sleigh ride around Lake Louise

In 1925 the original Chalet, which had been damaged in a fire, was reimagined as Fairmont Chateau Lake Louise, a grand, Renaissance Revival–style resort with 539 rooms and suites. Today, a century after opening, some characteristics—like its staff dressed in lederhosen-inspired uniforms and its fondue-focused restaurant, Walliser Stube—nod to the original Swiss influence, and the lobby-level Guide's Cabin, decorated with vintage photos and stocked with books on alpine living, continues the property's mountaineering legacy. Through the hotel, guests can sign up for snowshoe hikes or Bavarian curling lessons and rent ice skates and Nordic skis.

My first morning, I met guide Kevin Kirkpatrick at the cabin for an activity called Powderfest Snowshoeing. I've long found snowshoeing a little snoozy and worried how we'd fill the allotted three hours. The activity's name, it turned out, wasn't a cutesy marketing ploy. The resort has seven snowshoe trails, but because there was a base of 61 inches and another foot of fresh powder, we went “off-roading.”

Leaving behind the groomed lakeshore trail, we trekked up the shoulder of Fairview Mountain, and all signs of civilization disappeared as we entered a frosted forest straight out of a Dr. Seuss story. “Really get in there and explore,” he encouraged as we wandered past fir and larch trees bent at cartoonish angles, their limbs heaving with snow. I followed him up a massive mound of powder only to catch the metal cleat of my snowshoe on a branch and topple backward, leaving an imprint like a gigantic snow angel.

Time flew as Kirkpatrick shared wisdom on everything from the current weather anomaly to how, in 1882, Edwin Hunter, a member of the Stoney Nakoda, first led a young European wrangler, Tom Wilson, to what the Indigenous people of this area called Ho-run-num-nay (Lake of the Little Fishes). He chose to ignore the name and anointed it Emerald Lake for its jewel-colored waters. Two years later the government changed the moniker to Louise to honor a daughter of Queen Victoria, Princess Louise Caroline Alberta.

An ice climber on the Lake Louise Lakeshore Trail

I returned to the hotel thoroughly exhausted from hours of high-stepping and grateful that I was booked for a session at Basin Glacial Waters, Fairmont's new, guests-only thermal bathhouse. Designed by Italian architect Matteo Thun, the building, with floor-to-ceiling windows that frame the lake and towering peaks at every turn, feels like part of the landscape. This is the epitome of nature bathing, I thought as I took in the views from the hot-stone room, silent salt chamber, and indoor-outdoor vitality pool.

I didn't think it was possible to distract me from the dramatic vista, but Basin's signature Aufguss sauna ritual, the conclusion to my multisensory journey, was impossible to ignore. This choreographed sauna performance popular across Europe has only recently been introduced to North American spas. For 15 minutes our sauna master, Kyan Van Haasteren, a young, blond Dutchman, theatrically waved a towel over scorching sauna stones to waft steam toward me and 32 other guests. He danced around the 185-degree-Fahrenheit space to an upbeat soundtrack of Luis Fonsi while smashing snowballs scented with aromatic oils over the hot stones to release the fragrance of Siberian fir. It felt more like a Vegas show than a wellness ritual, but the entertainment took my mind off the discomfort of the heat. I exited in a sweaty daze and willed myself to follow Van Haasteren's lead and dunk myself into the outdoor cold plunge. In seconds the tingling numbness gave way to a heady euphoria. I looked up to see the start of a steady snow spiraling down, one that wouldn't let up until late the next day.

I may not be a first-to-last-chair skier any longer, but I'm still motivated to score fresh tracks on a powder day. By 8 a.m. the next morning, I was on the complimentary Fairmont shuttle with a throng of stoked skiers for the 10-minute transfer to Lake Louise Ski Resort. With three ways up the front of the mountain, there's rarely a line. And once you're on the mountain, it's easy to spread out. With this season's addition of Richardson's Ridge, 200 acres of beginner- and intermediate-friendly glades and groomers, the resort owns bragging rights as the third biggest ski area in Canada, with 4,200 acres of skiable terrain. Throughout the day I experienced moments that felt more like backcountry than resort riding, especially in the rowdy inbounds steeps of the West Bowl.

Gearing up to snowshoe at Fairmont Chateau Lake Louise

I spent the morning lapping bowl runs off the Summit Chair, but in the afternoon the visibility disappeared, making a drop down black diamond Rodney's Ridge downright vertigo-inducing. I'd gotten my fix of SkiBig3's “Prosecco Powder” (wonderfully light, dry snow), and I won't lie—the other incentive that got me up and out early was the promise of lunch at Whitehorn Bistro. The acclaimed views from this upscale, on-mountain restaurant were obscured, but that didn't damper the deliciousness of its farm-to-table dishes, like pickled beet carpaccio with goat cheese and crispy duck with black cherry jus.

With a solid half day of riding under my belt, I left the resort to work off my lunch on the Nordic trails of the Lake Louise campground with Clare McCann, the high-energy owner of Bikescape. Her lighthearted guiding philosophy was an ideal match for my novice cross-country ski skills and the tricky conditions. Heavy wet snow would cement our skis to the ground the minute we stopped propelling forward. “Shimmy, shimmy, shimmy, glide,” she repeated like a mantra as we haltingly made our way around the four-mile Bow River Loop. The trail was so silent that the only sound was my retro SkiBig3 pass flapping on the side of my jacket.

Those words stuck with me as I drove 50 minutes southeast to the town of Banff. Compared with Lake Louise, it's a bustling tourism hub, but thanks to strict design guidelines, the businesses downtown—even the Starbucks and the McDonald's—are housed in intentionally rustic spaces built from local stone and wood. Over the last few years, new businesses have enlivened the downtown area. Some of these arrivals include locavore-focused restaurants Good Folk and Farm & Fire, and the 67-room boutique Kenrick Hotel, a hip remodel of the former High Country Inn that added a third-wave coffee shop, a thermal circuit spa, and a stellar Italian restaurant, The Fat Ox. Even the classic sticky-floored late-night club, the Dusty Boot Saloon & Dance Hall, has been reinvented as Banff's take on Jackson Hole's Million Dollar Cowboy Bar, complete with a shiny, boot-shaped disco ball and a karaoke room.

I kept things old-school and checked in to Fairmont Banff Springs, nicknamed the Castle in the Rockies for its Scottish-baronial-style architecture and perch overlooking the town. The hotel was another vision of railway executive Van Horne, who famously said, “If we can't export the scenery, we'll import the tourists.”

Today Banff National Park sees more than 4.25 million visitors every year; nearly two thirds come during summer. But a week into my trip, I began to think that winter might be the more enchanting season. On my final day I joined Discover Banff Tours on an excursion to Johnston Canyon for its Icewalk experience. In the parking lot our guide, Jeff Doherty, outfitted our group of six in Yaktrax—ice-gripping cleats that attach to shoes—then had us briskly hike a half mile over slick paths and bridges to the lower falls before the big bus tour groups arrived.

The canyon was pure quietude, and we had it to ourselves. When the pace slowed, I was able to admire the feathery moss suspended in frost on the forest floor, the icy old man's beard lichen dangling from the trees, and, most of all, the frozen ribbons of electric blue cascades. About a mile of slippery uphill trail led us to the upper falls, a stream of water plunging behind a veil of ice. I stood in front of Mother Nature's ice sculpture in awe. “It's like seeing the Mona Lisa alone in the Louvre,” said Doherty. “In summer you'd be elbowing iPhones out of the way for a view, let alone a photo.”

A few weeks after I'd returned home to Colorado, I read that Alberta had been hit by a warm spell that doused the mountains in rain, turning the slopes into sheets of ice. Some friends had taken their family on a ski trip per my recommendation. When I asked about their vacation, they told me they hadn't skied once, but they had the best time dogsledding, night tubing, and ice-skating. In an age when weather is unforgivingly unpredictable, Banff, with its buffet of activities, might be the closest thing to a guaranteed winter escape, no matter your preferred pace of adventure. My trip showed me that winter isn't just about high-voltage powder days at the ski resort. It can be enjoyed at a slower pace. I was even inspired to buy a pair of my own snowshoes.

Direct flights to Calgary International Airport are available from more than a dozen major US hubs. Banff National Park is an easy 90-minute drive west on the Trans-Canada Highway.

Lakefront grande dame Fairmont Chateau Lake Louise offers every imaginable snowy activity, from horse-drawn sleigh rides to curling. In winter an outdoor bar built from 240 blocks of ice serves mulled wine and spiked cocoa. Only hotel guests have access to Basin Glacial Waters, a sprawling thermal bathhouse. Don't miss the excellent hotel bookshop, curated with out-of-print editions on the area's mountaineering history.

One of the park's first hotels, Fairmont Banff Springs, recently added a new wing of larger, family-friendly suites with bunk beds and adjoining rooms. An on-site skating rink has a pop-up sugar shack that serves maple treats, and the adventure center rents fat-tire bikes and arranges guided evening snowshoe tours. Of the 13 dining venues, 1888 Chophouse, known for its Alberta Wagyu, is a standout.

A refreshing boutique alternative to Banff's palatial resorts, the reimagined Kenrick Hotel has an outpost of Calgary's Analog Coffee, a guests-only hydrotherapy spa that stays open until midnight, and one of the town's top tables, Alpine Italian–inspired Fat Ox.

Tucked away on Sulphur Mountain, 320-room resort Rimrock Banff, Emblems Collection debuted a sleek makeover last summer. The first property in Accor's new über-luxe Emblems Collection features a bathhouse of saunas, glacial plunges, and infinity pools, plus a cocktail-forward vinyl listening room and in-house guides who can take guests on glacier treks and ice canyon walks.

Reservations are a must at white-tablecloth Dining Room at the Post Hotel and Spa, known for its 25,000-plus-bottle wine cellar and European-inspired menu of dishes like roasted chateaubriand and Dover sole with saffron beurre blanc.

The house-made sourdough alone makes it worth pausing on a powder day for lunch at ski-in, ski-out restaurant Whitehorn Bistro off the Grizzly Gondola of Lake Louise Ski Resort. On a bluebird day request a patio seat.

The Dusty Boot Saloon and Dance Hall was recently spiffed up and turned into an Old West saloon with a stage for live music and a menu of excellent cocktails, like the Cattleman's Old Fashioned, and elevated bar food, including addictive popcorn chicken and shrimp spiked with wasabi peas.

At Good Folk, hearty breakfast dishes like banana caramel French toast will fuel your day's adventure. In the evening the menu showcases the local bounty in dishes like Alberta wild boar chop and a decadent bison burger topped with smoked cheddar and pepper bacon.

Johnston Canyon, a labyrinth of limestone rocks and cascades, sees a fraction of the visitors in winter than in summer. But to make sure you have the frozen falls to yourself, book the morning Icewalk experience with Discover Banff Tours.

Local outfitter Bikescape runs beginner-friendly Nordic ski tours on the trails within Banff National Park as well as electric fat-tire bike tours that include a backcountry lunch.

Sit back and enjoy the views of Lake Louise from the seat of a horse-drawn sled. Brewsters Lake Louise Stables runs hour-long trips that follow the lake path; evening tours under the stars are extra special.

SkiBig3's resorts offer something for everyone. Family-friendly Mount Norquay has night skiing and a thrilling tubing park. Every chairlift on the front side of Lake Louise Ski Resort has both an easy (green) and challenging (black) way down. Sunshine Mountain Lodge at Banff Sunshine Village has the area's only ski-in, ski-out lodging, and its big alpine views make you feel like you're downhilling in Europe.

For the perfect detour en route to Calgary International Airport, Everwild Canmore, a new Nordic spa at the Everwild hotel in the town of Canmore, features a DIY outdoor thermal circuit as well as five-elements rituals, ranging from an herbal steam cleanse to an Aufguss ceremony. The spa lounge serves a shareable charcuterie and cheese board for two along with cocktails.

#6218. Wander.com: Best Luxury Take On Airbnb (With Real Value Too?)

At first, the big hotel chains of the world laughed off Airbnb and vacation rentals. No seriously, they did. Now, they all compete in the vacation rental business and act like it was always the plan.

The problem for the traveler, is that almost all of the newer entrants just plug into a massive pipeline of already existing vacation homes and apartments and pop them on their own branded website with no added luxury, differentiation, amenity or expertise in curation.

There’s no huge unlock of new places or highly curated places that you could virtually always stamp as worth recommending to a friend, the way you’d rate an Aman, St. Regis, or Four Seasons hotel.

This is precisely where Wander.com comes in, and it’s by far my favorite luxe vacation rental platform to date. The fact that it’s boutique and limited is what makes it, at least for me. And, the $350 off Wander promo code doesn’t hurt either.

Wander is a vacation rental company which truly hand picks every property that it lists, and has the exclusive listing on. Crucially, each of the vacation properties undergoes a sort of ‘Wander’ transformation to conform with brand standards for wifi, amenity, style and vibe.

It’s above my pay-grade as a blogger on this topic, but it seems like Wander co-invests in the real estate portfolio’s, or partners with owners in a unique way that’s far more integrated than others.

Where are they? Most Wander.com properties are scattered across the US, from the shores of Malibu to the great National Parks in Wyoming and all along the Eastern seaboard too. Hawaii is also a recent addition. New destinations keep popping up!

Each of their properties feels uniquely wonderful and aspirational, and I’d say all have a very modern and contemporary slant to luxury. Grandma’s cabinets are not in any of these homes, but Tesla chargers are. One nice touch: each Wander offers a dedicated workspace with desk, chair, monitors and lightning fast wifi.

I completely respect that all tastes are individual, but the interiors and setups of these homes much more reflect my personal tastes, more minimalist chic, than many less curated vacation rental options.

Most Wander properties are around $1000 a night. Some will be half that, some will be double. On its face, that’s intimidating to many, but when you factor in the number of bedrooms and features it’s really reasonable. Families, or multi-family get togethers… amazing.

All Wander.com properties are at least two bedrooms and many are four, five or even twelve. One is an entire island with multiple residential complexes. For me, I love these sort of getaways for catching up with family or friends, and I never mind when other people are contributing too.

We’ve had some of our best ever vacations renting a house in Palm Springs for weeks or months at a time. Often, family or friends want in too, so we split the house and end up with two bedrooms each for under $500 per night.

We’ve used these bonus rooms and features to socialize or catch up with people in the serenity of the home, not annoyed by service, crowded pools or tight room setups. For a longer stay, I absolutely hate having to rely on a hotel kitchen for every meal. I love to hit a local market and grill with family or guests.

Wander is offering $350 off first bookings, which is a great way to get started. To browse the homes, you simply download the Wander app and start doom scrolling. When you find one you’re ready to book, the process is very self explanatory and easy to share with others.

I’m personally a fan of virtually California vacation and the properties offered on the platform cover everything from Palm Springs to Napa and all in between in stunning form. The $350 off is a solid discount and combined with new property discounts, which are frequent, there is a lot to love. You can browse Wander and download the app here.

If you don’t see the Wander.com discount in your account, you can add promo code AKFVDFD7 once the app is downloaded.

#6217. Inside Washington Dulles’ New Concourse E, Light Years Ahead Of United’s “Temporary” Gates

Concourse E at Washington Dulles International Airport is now open for business and it’s a beautiful terminal that stands in stark contrast to the “temporary” C and D Concourse that United Airlines has used since the mid-1980s.

I was present for the ribbon-cutting yesterday, which featured United executives Andrew Nocella (Executive Vice President and Chief Commercial Officer) and Toby Enqvist (Global Chief Operations Officer) as well as Virginia Governor Abigail Spanberger and U.S. Senator Tim Kaine and a number of other elected officials and airport leaders. Steven Bradbury, President Trump’s Deputy Secretary for Transportation, also spoke.

While everyone is going to play nice at these sort of events, I was happy to see Republicans and Democrats talking together about investing infrastructure, one of the many opportunities for bipartisan collaboration as the new Congress assumes power. There’s reasonable discussions over cost overruns and the massive time and money drain this project has been already, but it has to be done and maybe just maybe everyone can come together to accelerate this project and hold everyone more accountable.

But my main point here it to showcase the beautiful new terminal. It’s world class without a comparison, but we cannot help but compare it to the C/D Gates and it’s truly night and day; the difference between first world and third world.

First, it’s very easy to reach. Take the train to the C gates stations and now instead of walking a half miles back to the terminal, you can simply walk upstairs to the new terminal:

There’s plenty of natural light and and the Untied Club is conveniently located on at the top of the stairs/escalators on the right side. Many new concessionaires are slated to open, with several highlighting local food and beverage options from Northern Virginia.

And yes, the mobile lounges remain. Passengers arriving on an international flight will still be directed to a mobile lounge and driven to the mid-field immigration facility. Eventually, a new facility will be opened in Concourse E.

This is phase one. The terminal expansion will continue in 1-2 more phases and the entire concourse will not be done until the end of the decade, at the earliest (sad, but predictable).

I wrote about the new United Club here. It’s posh and United will also build a new Polaris Lounge in this Concourse.

Bottom line: it’s a bright new day for Washington Dulls and the new terminal expansion is a fitting upgrade for the capital city of the United States.

I know how it works and have experienced the current state of affairs more times than I can count.

And that the train is only accessible to people who have gone through security and do not have their checked luggage with them, right? so to do what you want, you’d clear immigration and customs, re-check your luggage, then go through security at E, then take a train to the main terminal, then re-claim your luggage at a carousel? That’s preferible to just getting on a mobile lounge and going through immigration and customs at the main terminal? Really?

Really like the that they kept the font from the main terminal building. The new terminal looks just like A/B, which is a good thing.

I like the cues from the check-in building in the columns and windows. Well done keeping it Dulles.

#6216. Editor's Letter: Introducing Our Winter Travel Issue

It was a long and hot summer, and I welcomed the cooler weather as soon as the leaves started to turn. My closet full of coats and jackets had sat sadly neglected for many months; the new boots I bought in April on a clearance rack are only now about to get their moment. I'm excited for the Christmas lights in London and New York, the festive trees, chestnuts roasting on street corners—and yes, my Christmas wish list (featuring a dangerous number of watches and pieces of jewelry) is ready too. There is something about the winter that still feels exotic and enthralling to me. I saw snow a few times in Kashmir as a kid, but the first real blizzard I encountered was when I was a freshman in college in Pennsylvania. It was late at night, but my roommate dragged me out of bed to make snow angels. I still remember lying on my back, waving my arms around—the sensation of cold all along my body was surreal, as was the way in which white feathery bits floated down from the sky. I recall thinking, What a strange but wonderful feeling! I discovered two things quickly: One, I was a terrible skier. And, two, I loved après-ski—to be nursing hot chocolate by crackling fireplaces and snuggled in blankets.

Our story on Banff perfectly encapsulates the promise of winter: the adventure, the exhilaration, the romance of a landscape transformed overnight. But equally seductive is the prospect of winter sun. Come January I'll happily trade snow boots for sandals and fly to Tenerife, Spain, or Boracay, in the Philippines, or Brisbane, Australia. That dose of vitamin D is essential by then, when the Christmas lights have come down and everything seems gray and empty. At that point I need a beach—and something colorful and sparkly to wear on it. So often I close my eyes and return to the end-of-year trips I've made to Maldives, Indonesia, Mexico, and remembered the sunrises, the sound of the waves, the palm trees swaying in the breeze, the fiery red chiles, and fresh coconut water. It's been a strange year. But as we navigate the final months ahead, this issue is filled with reasons to feel excited about what comes next. I hope it gives you plenty to dream about—and somewhere to go.

United MileagePlus has four published elite tiers: Premier Silver, Premier Gold, Premier Platinum and Premier 1K. Benefits and qualification requirements vary by tier and are subject to change, so review United’s current program rules.

You earn Premier status by collecting Premier qualifying points (PQPs) and meeting United’s other requirements, including taking a minimum number of United-operated flights each calendar year. United has announced that beginning in 2027, PQPs will become the sole qualifying metric.

PQPs are earned solely for the purpose of qualifying for elite status, and they are separate from MileagePlus miles. You cannot redeem PQPs for award flights. How you earn them depends on factors such as the airline operating the flight and how you book, and earning rules are subject to change.

United cobranded credit cards do not provide elite status on their own. Eligible card spending may earn PQPs, up to limits that vary by card. Earning rates, caps and offers are subject to the issuer’s terms and can change.

Having elite status with an airline can make a significant difference in your travel experience. Shorter lines, faster service, complimentary upgrades, international lounge access and other benefits can easily make stressful trips more seamless. But these perks don't come without a cost, and United MileagePlus overhauled how members earn status in 2026.

This guide will evaluate United Airlines Premier status and break down the different status tiers, how to earn them and whether their perks are worth the effort for United flyers.

Related: Your guide to United MileagePlus

When you choose to fly United and add your MileagePlus number to your booking, in addition to earning miles, you also earn points toward Premier status. Depending on your status tier, elite perks range from complimentary first-class upgrades on most domestic flights (depending on availability) to earning bonus miles that can be redeemed for future travel.

United currently has two ways for members to climb the Premier status ladder:

PQPs are based on a combination of your spending on flights and on eligible United credit cards.

Starting in 2027, PQPs will become the sole elite status metric. As part of those changes, top-tier Premier 1K status will also become even tougher to earn.

The old metrics are still in place through the end of 2026, so we will cover both options.

Apply here for a limited-time offer on the — Earn up to 90,000 bonus miles and 500 PQP: Earn 500 PQP after your first purchase and 80,000 bonus miles after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Plus, earn 10,000 bonus miles after adding an authorized user in the first three months from account opening (see rates and fees).

Related: Why United's elite status changes are bad news for many flyers

Anyone can create a United MileagePlus account for free online. Once you take off on your elite status expedition, you’ll have four official elite status tiers to work toward:

There’s also an unpublished exclusive tier called Global Services, which can only be achieved by flying 4 million miles or receiving a personal invitation.

Here's an overview of what you'll need to earn each status tier before and after the changes.

One requirement that is not changing: You must take at least four flights operated by United or United Express in a calendar year to qualify for any status tier.

When you reach any elite status tier, it is valid for the remainder of the calendar year, the entirety of the following year, and the first month of the year after. For instance, if you reach status requirements anytime in 2026, you will hold the status through Jan. 31, 2028. So, the sooner you earn elite status, the longer you can enjoy the benefits.

Now, let's dive into how to earn PQPs (and, through the end of 2026, PQFs).

Related: Earn MileagePlus miles with United’s airline, hotel and credit card partners

The classic way to earn PQPs is via your spending on flights. The earning rate depends on which airline operates the flight and whether you book it with cash or miles. PQPs are awarded to the passenger, not the person who buys the ticket.

Earn 1 PQP for every 6 award miles on MileagePlus partner airlines, up to a maximum of 500 PQPs per flight in economy and premium economy and 1,000 PQPs per flight in first and business class.

You can also earn PQPs through spending on United's cobranded credit cards. None of these cards provide complimentary elite status, but you’ll earn PQPs on everyday purchases (up to a certain amount), and some cards offer PQPs as part of the welcome bonus.

The information for the United Club Business Card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

Although United is making it harder to earn status in 2027, it is also giving existing elite members a boost toward next year's status. If you hold elite status and an eligible United credit card (or open one by Dec. 31, 2026), you will receive 5% of the PQPs required for your current status level at the start of 2027:

Related: The ultimate guide to earning elite status with United cards

The perks of United loyalty get more and more appealing as you climb the Premier status ladder. You'll also earn more MileagePlus miles on United purchases as you gain status, though the number of miles you'll earn also depends on whether you hold a United credit card.

When you reach the Gold tier, you'll receive all the perks of Silver as well as:

At Platinum, you can enjoy all the benefits of Gold, plus:

Members who get all the way to the top are rewarded with the Platinum benefits listed above, in addition to:

On top of the various metrics for earning miles and status, United MileagePlus awards something called PlusPoints, a separate currency available only to Platinum and 1K members.

PlusPoints were originally used for seat upgrades, though these have become harder to get in recent years as demand has skyrocketed. That’s why United introduced several new ways to redeem your PlusPoints, including for bonus miles, PQPs, TravelBank cash and gifting Premier status to other MileagePlus members.

Related: When does airline elite status expire?

Elite status can certainly make travel more comfortable and convenient. If you regularly travel with United or its partner airlines and/or spend significantly on a cobranded credit card, you may find it relatively easy to earn Premier status. And it can be a savvy way to maximize your travel.

Plus, this means you’ll also be earning plenty of United miles, which you can redeem for United award flights — all while enjoying your elite status benefits.

However, it’s not worth pursuing status when you can’t enjoy the benefits you’ve worked hard to earn. Be sure to consider United’s route map, its presence at your home airport and how easy it is to get to your desired destinations. If United and its partner airlines don’t fly where you live or where you want to travel, you won’t get much use from Premier status. You may be better off pursuing status with a different program, such as Delta SkyMiles or American AAdvantage.

Finally, remember that Premier status does not provide domestic lounge access when traveling with United. If this benefit is important to you, consider applying for the , which provides United Club access and perks such as two free checked bags and Premier Access travel services.

Related: Complete guide to United’s fare classes

Earning elite status, especially a top-tier status like Premier 1K, is no easy feat and requires countless hours on planes and thousands of dollars spent. Understanding the cost and perks of United’s elite status is important to determine if it is right for you — especially since United is making status harder to earn in 2027.

#6214. My First “New” Chase Sapphire Reserve Travel Redemption Blew My Mind

There’s… a lot… of coverage surrounding the revamped Chase Sapphire Reserve Card. As per usual these days, the hot takes are plentiful and people are fired up. It’s either the apocalypse or the beginning of something great, depending on which attention seeker you read. As a long time cardholder, I’m really intrigued by the new changes.

The changes really fit my profile and sure, the card will cost more, but I won’t have to introduce any behavior change to get more, unlike some other cards. I’ll do most of my spending on this card. I’m a keeper just from the fee credit and earning multipliers.

Well, if my first Chase Sapphire Reserve redemption is any indicator, this card may single handedly change the redemption game and just about everyone should take note — including airline and hotel transfer partners. It’s already a huge win.

Chase Travel’s ‘The Edit’ is a curated selection of nice hotels, which offer benefits similar to those provided by a travel agent or other luxury credit card booking platform. When booking a ‘The Edit’ property, you can expect breakfast for two, a $100 F&B credit, late check out and an upgrade subject to availability.

Which leads me to the important bit! With the revamped Sapphire Reserve Card, there’s a new “Points Boost” feature, which offers up to two cents per point (25,000 points would cover $500, etc) for some flight or hotel purchases.

This can be amazing value, with flights of $3,000 being grabbed for just 150,000 points, with no taxes and fees and the ability to still earn frequent flyer miles and elite status points, since the airline treats it like a cash ticket.

Previously, the Sapphire Reserve card offered a steady point redemption opportunity directly on Chase Travel at 1.5 cents per point (100,000 points would cover $1500, etc). But with the new version, some travel purchases you want to redeem for will either offer less value than before, the same, or more, with this new ‘Points Boost’ at 2 cents per point. We like more!

I am in New York and wanted to do a little staycation, so I fired up Chase Travel and found one of my more reliable upper mid-scale hotels, The Thompson Central Park was on as part of ‘The Edit’. My two options became a very clear singular, third option.

Typically, I’d consider paying cash or transferring my points from Chase to Hyatt to pay for a stay like this. Hyatt has “fixed” points rates, meaning the points price is largely irrespective of the cash price and only changes by seasonal dates. For this season, it was 25,000 points per night for the Thompson Central Park.

If I were to transfer my points, I’d get a free night (the cash rate was around $500) and have a really solid points redemption at exactly two cents per point. I’m not loyal to any hotel chain really, so I wouldn’t get any breakfast or “elite” benefits, but a free night is a free night.

BUT — Chase Travel had a ‘Points Boost’ option to book the hotel directly on their platform and not transfer points to Hyatt. Chase Travel was offering this property for circa 25,000 points and that would cover the $500 cash rate, but unlike transferring points to Hyatt, because I was redeeming a ‘The Edit’ property on Chase Travel, I’d receive…

Yep, by NOT transferring my points (and dealing with the fractured transfer journey) I was able to get myself basically $200 in additional value added to my stay with the breakfast and $100 property credit, not factoring in the value of late check out or a category room upgrade. In addition, I’ll be able to earn elite nights and Hyatt Points on the stay.

A mere 25,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards Points got me a “free” $500 hotel night, breakfast for two, and $100 to spend at the hotel. That’s a pretty stunning redemption, giving more than two cents per point of value and still allowing me to earn on the stay, unlike when you transfer your points to a loyalty program. I wish I could’ve stayed longer.

For the first time I can remember, transferring points to Hyatt was not the best option here and that’s something to stand up and take notice of.

If Chase can keep up this Points Boost game, it can really send ripples through rewards. For the first time, people can easily receive tremendous value for their points through a credit card portal while still earning elite status and points with the hotel or airline of their choosing.

You can check out the new 100,000 point + 500 travel credit offer for the Sapphire Reserve. It’s 200,000 points for Sapphire Reserve Business Cards.

#6213. U.S. Marine Calls Alaska Airlines Employee “Anti-Military” After Being Denied A Free Upgrade

A United States Marine Corps member says an Alaska Airlines employee was “anti-military” after declining his request for a free extra-legroom upgrade. He also alleges that the employee was rude and accused him of lying about previous upgrades. Those are separate complaints, and I think they deserve separate answers. Everyone deserves courteous service. Military service, however, does not entitle someone to a better seat.

The Instagram algorithim placed Taylor Yontz at the top of my feed this morning, where he describes an encounter at Portland International Airport. According to his account, he saw roughly 30 unassigned seats on the seat map and requested a complimentary move to an extra-legroom seat. He says he is 6 feet 4 inches tall, regularly makes this request, and receives an upgrade about nine times out of 10.

This time, he says, the employee told him free military upgrades were against policy. He alleges the agent spoke with disgust and accused him of lying when he mentioned previous complimentary upgrades. The employee offered a paid move, which he declined at $150.

You can listen to his side of the story here:

Alaska publishes a substantial list of military and veteran benefits. These include:

Complimentary upgrades based solely on military service are not among the listed benefits. So at the outset, there is no policy for upgrading service members when space is available, which even Yontz concedes.

I don’t blame him for asking, especially because he is 6’4″. Sitting in economy class is difficult enough for an average-sized person…it’s brutal for someone that tall.

But “it can’t hurt to ask” needs to leave room for the employee to decline. Otherwise, it becomes a test the agent can pass only by giving something away. Yontz strikes me as highly-entiteld to suggest that he should be given this upgrade because he has in the past, as if it’s standard procedure.

We’ll talk about the Alaska Airlines employee below, but by arguing that you’ve been upgraded in the past and therefore you should today, entitlement is on full display.

If an agent actually accused him of lying about previous upgrades, I would find that inappropriate (I’m not convinced, but it is certainly possible). The employee should have politely explained the current policy without assumptions about past interaction the passenger has had with the airline.

There is no contradiction between “another employee upgraded me before” and “I cannot provide that upgrade today” and Alaska should examine his complaint about insulting language on its own merits.

But even if the employee handled the conversation poorly, that would establish poor service, not necessarily hostility toward military members. And even if it was one agent being hostile (again, certainly possible), it’s still a different matter than whether the upgrade should have been denied.

I appreciate the sacrifices military members and their families make. Airlines can recognize those sacrifices through practical benefits, and Alaska offers several. But I hate to see that appreciation reduced to whether an airport employee hands over a seat upgrade…Yontz’s conduct is unbecoming of a member of the U.S. military (and I was one too, thank you very much).

If one agent makes an exception, the next agent should not face an accusation of prejudice for following the published rules. That creates an incentive to stop offering discretionary favors altogether. Accepting a kind gesture with gratitude leaves room for someone else to receive one later. Treating it as the minimum acceptable response makes it harder for employees to exercise generosity without creating expectations their colleagues must then manage.

The practical result of this whole brouhaha should be a memo to gate agents that no one is to be upgraded for free.

If the Alaska Airlines employee was insulting, the passenger has every reason to complain about that conduct. He did not need to receive an upgrade to deserve a respectful conversation.

But declining a complimentary extra-legroom seat does not, on its own, make an employee anti-military. Alaska’s published benefits do not promise that upgrade, and previous exceptions do not change that.

To all travelers: ask politely, enjoy the upgrade if it happens, but if it does not, a declined upgrade is not evidence that someone disrespects you, no matter what uniform you wear.

I often tell people that the best unkept secret with Avios is, in fact, the Avios app. Separate to the British Airways app, the Avios app allows users to set flight alerts and goals, but also gives a heads up about opportunities before they appear anywhere else.

Case in point: before a press release had even hit my inbox, the Avios app alerted me that an ‘Avios only’ flight had just launched. This isn’t the first time Avios has launched a flight only bookable with points, but it is the first time they’ve done one to CAPE TOWN, during peak winter break time.

British Airways and Avios have collaborated on a flight only bookable with Avios, where every seat on the plane is available for sale with points. First, business, premium and economy, all available using Avios. The flights depart as follows…

As noted, these flights are now bookable and if history repeats itself, they won’t be available for long. This plane only has 8 seats in first, so get in quick! #6211. United Airlines Executive Says Iconic Dulles Mobile Lounges Will Retire, But “Won’t Be Forgotten.” What Comes Next?

United Airlines wants Washington Dulles to move beyond its mobile lounges. But when I asked Andrew Nocella whether he actually likes them, his response suggested that retirement may not mean disappearance. Could one become a bar or café? Could a limited transportation role survive? His answer left room for some speculation.

During a press gaggle at Washington Dulles yesterday, I asked United Airlines Executive Vice President and Chief Commercial Officer Andrew Nocella a simple question: does he like the people movers? (it was in the context of their future place at an evolving IAD).

“I love it,” he responded, before explaining:

“The people movers, of course, is part of my history. I can remember, back in the day, coming out to the aircraft through the people mover, so it’s part of my history. But I do understand the need to evolve and change and innovate. And the people movers need to be innovated out. There are better ways to do it. But it will be an important part of the history of Dulles Airport and I can assure you that People Moves, while they will be retired, they won’t be forgotten.”

These vehicles are technically known as mobile lounges, though people movers is a fitting description too and I’ve called them “moon buggies” for years. Whatever you call them, I found that last assurance intriguing, even if we should be careful not to read too much into it.

Nocella did not announce a preservation project or describe a future use. But promising they will not be forgotten invites the question: how might Dulles preserve something so closely associated with the airport while finally moving beyond the need to use it?

My favorite possibility is turning one into a bar or café.

Imagine a retired mobile lounge parked in a suitable location, with its distinctive shape preserved and the interior converted into somewhere to have a drink while watching aircraft. Keep some of the original seating,  add photographs explaining its history, and suddenly an airport frustration becomes an attraction.

I would happily stop for a cappuccino. I suspect plenty of aviation enthusiasts would make a point of visiting too.

There would obviously be practical questions about access, utilities, and where to put it…maybe the wheels would have to be removed. A vehicle designed to transport passengers is not automatically suitable for operating a restaurant. But as a concept, it strikes me as a fun way to preserve a piece of Dulles without requiring anyone to ride it to immigration.

Nostalgia becomes much easier to appreciate when you can choose whether to participate!

Think how cool it would be to take one of these and put it inside the new Polaris Lounge in Concourse E that will be coming in the years ahead.

Another possibility is that the mobile lounges disappear from most journeys but continue in a narrower role.

I wonder, for example, whether there might be a useful way to run passengers between the D and E gates during the airport’s lengthy transition. Could a mobile lounge provide a convenient connection while the rest of the concourse development catches up? It woudl certainly save a lot of walking.

That is a question, not something Nocella proposed and I do realize that keeping an aging fleet operating for a limited purpose could undermine the savings and simplicity that retirement is supposed to deliver.

Still, “retired” can mean different things. Retired from routine passenger service would not necessarily preclude an occasional special ride or some other carefully limited use.

Of course, “won’t be forgotten” may mean something much less elaborate.

A preserved vehicle, a display in the terminal, or a design reference inside a future lounge could honor the mobile lounges without retaining their transportation function.

I would prefer preserving at least one actual vehicle rather than relying exclusively on photographs. These machines are unusual enough that future travelers should have an opportunity to see what generations of Dulles passengers experienced. I still love them and will always love them.

Nocella’s answer was affectionate, but clear about the need for change. He did not offer a retirement date or reveal what remembering the mobile lounges will look like.

But I do hope that assurance becomes something tangible. A mobile lounge café or bar would get my vote, preferably inside the new Polaris Lounge. A useful transitional shuttle or occasional heritage ride could be interesting too and much easier to maintain than a vintage aircraft.

For years, passengers have boarded these vehicles because they had to. It would be wonderful if Dulles eventually gave us a reason to step inside one because we wanted to.

What would you do with a retired Dulles mobile lounge?

#6210. United Adds Four Domestic Routes

United added four domestic routes to its 2027 schedule last week, a spokesperson confirmed to AirlineGeeks. Three of the new flights will depart from the carrier’s California hubs.

The airline will begin seasonal service from Los Angeles and San Francisco to Traverse City, Michigan, on June 19. Both routes will operate with Boeing 737-800s on Saturdays through Sept. 11, with additional flights on select Wednesdays. The additions will give Cherry Capital Airport nonstop service to all seven of United’s mainland hubs.

These additional routes were first flagged as part of last week’s Cirium Diio schedule update.

United will also fly year-round between San Francisco and Jacksonville, Florida, beginning March 29. The carrier will operate the route on Mondays and Fridays with a Boeing 737-800. Jacksonville Aviation Authority CEO Mark VanLoh said the Bay Area was “one of our largest unserved markets.”

San Francisco will become United’s sixth hub with nonstop service from Jacksonville.

The first of the four routes will start March 4, when United adds twice-daily flights between Lancaster, Pennsylvania, and Washington Dulles. The service restores a connection previously flown by Southern Airways Express. Southern’s Dulles flights ended in June when SkyWest began flying between Lancaster and Chicago O’Hare under the United Express banner as part of a federal Essential Air Service contract.

#6209. Frontier Begins First Class Ticket Sales

Frontier on Tuesday opened reservations for its upcoming First Class, which is set to debut in March 2027.

The new seats have up to 37 inches of pitch, the carrier said, and will be arranged in a two-by-two configuration at the front of the cabin. Installations are already underway. Reservations are available now for travel beginning March 5.

Frontier first announced plans to add a First Class product in late 2024.

The airline will also add extra-legroom seating, with up to 34 inches of pitch, in rows three through eight. These seats will be available with Frontier’s Premium bundle, which includes a carry-on bag and priority boarding.

Frontier plans to roll out two additional perks through 2027 – in-seat USB-C power at every seat in the first eight rows, and Starlink wireless internet service. The carrier decided on Starlink in July; it will be the first airline in the U.S. to use a new system managed directly by Starlink, officials said at the time.

“We’re transforming what customers can expect when they fly Frontier,” Bobby Schroeter, chief marketing officer at Frontier, said in a news release. “First Class seating, more room to stretch out, in-seat power, and fast, reliable Starlink Wi-Fi will bring a new level of comfort and convenience to flying with us.”

#6208. Frontier Airlines Starts Selling First Class From $129. I Am Seriously Considering Booking It.

Frontier Airlines is now selling its new first class seats, with wider seating and no middle seats in the first two rows. Extra-legroom seating, USB-C power, and Starlink internet are also part of the cabin transformation. I welcome the investment, though a better seat will only get Frontier so far if the rest of the experience does not improve alongside it.

Installation is underway, with completion expected March 5, 2027. Reservations are open for travel beginning that day.

Promotional pricing requires purchasing the flight and bundle together by November 16, 2026, at 11:59 pm ET, for select nonstop domestic departures March 5–April 5, 2027. Availability is limited.

USB-C power is planned for the first eight rows. Both power and Starlink installations begin in 2027 and progress aircraft by aircraft throughout the year. Booking the new seat does not mean every other advertised improvement will be available on your flight.

For me, reliable internet and the ability to keep a laptop charged substantially determine how useful a flight is. A comfortable seat is welcome, but on a daytime trip I also must get work done…it is an essential part of the package.

I have to say, I’m quite excited about these developments.

As much as I loved warmed mixed nuts, a hot meal, and sparkling water saved with lime and ice in a glass…the Frontier network is respectable and a comfortable seat with Wi-Fi and power are more important. If Frontier can charge half or what American or United are asking on the same route, I’m totally up for flying Frontier more.

The bigger question is whether Frontier can persuade passengers to pay more and then give them a reason to come back.

A first class seat loses much of its appeal if a cancellation leaves you with poor alternatives or resolving an ordinary problem becomes an ordeal…two areas where traditional network carriers still have a huge advantage. Selling a premium product raises expectations even when the price is relatively low.

I do not expect Frontier to become a full-service airline simply because it installs eight larger seats. But I would expect the airline to understand that passengers purchasing those seats are buying some relief from the compromises associated with budget travel, again myself included.

That makes this an opportunity. If Frontier can offer a comfortable seat at a sensible total price and deliver dependable transportation and maybe a little bit more service than the “Big Front Seat” on Spirit Airlines, I think there is a market for it.

Frontier Airlines is moving forward with first class, and I welcome more choice at the front of the aircraft. The new seats could make the airline more attractive to passengers who value comfort but remain sensitive to price, like me. Even the extra legroom seats are something I would consider, with Starlink being an even bigger game-changer.

While I would happily try it, the real test will be whether Frontier delivers an experience that makes me want to book it again. A larger seat with Starlink can get someone through the door…but Frontier must deliver that.
