If you've ever rented a car, you've probably been asked whether you want to pay extra for insurance at the counter. But depending on which credit card you have, you may already have some coverage.

Many travel rewards credit cards offer rental car insurance that can protect you against theft or damage to your rental vehicle, potentially saving you from paying extra for the rental company's collision damage waiver.

Here's how credit card rental car insurance works, what it covers and which cards offer some of the best protection.

These cards offer primary rental car coverage on eligible rentals. Coverage can vary by card, rental location and purpose.

The information for the United Club Business has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

These cards offer primary car rental insurance, as long as you use your card to pay for the entire rental. Note that this isn’t an exhaustive list; you may find other cards offering primary insurance.

The , and each provide primary car rental insurance for rentals of up to 31 consecutive days. The personal cards are primary, while the business card is primary in the U.S. only for business rentals.

This policy covers theft, damage, valid loss-of-use charges, administrative fees and reasonable towing charges due to covered theft or damage.

Policy details vary slightly among the three cards, though. A key difference is the total amount that can be reimbursed for damages caused by theft or collision:

To learn more about each card, read our full reviews for the Sapphire Preferred, Sapphire Reserve and Sapphire Reserve for Business.

The Capital One Venture X and Venture X Business both offer primary rental car insurance, though the coverage terms differ.

The personal Venture X provides reimbursement for theft and collision damage up to the actual cash value of eligible rental vehicles with an original manufacturer's suggested retail price of $75,000 or less. Coverage applies to rentals of up to 15 consecutive days in your country of residence or 31 consecutive days elsewhere.

Meanwhile, the Venture X Business provides primary coverage for eligible rentals made primarily for business purposes, covering theft and collision damage subject to the policy's valuation limits. Rentals of up to 31 consecutive days are eligible for coverage.

To learn more, read our full reviews of the Venture X and Venture X Business.

Learn more: Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card

Learn more: Capital One Venture X Business

Four of the Ink Business cards from Chase offer primary insurance when you rent for business purposes, providing reimbursement for theft and collision damage for most rental vehicles with an MSRP of $125,000 or less.

Each card provides reimbursement of up to $60,000 for theft and collision damage.

To learn more, read our guide to the Chase Ink Business cards.

United’s cobranded cards offer primary car rental insurance, though the business versions are primary only when you rent for business purposes. You need to decline the rental company’s collision insurance and charge the entire rental cost to your card.

This insurance provides reimbursement of up to $60,000 for theft and collision damage for most rental vehicles with an MSRP of $125,000 or less.

To learn more, read our guide to the United cards.

Among the most important factors here is making sure you pay for your entire car rental bill with a credit card that has an auto collision damage waiver included in its benefits. You'll also want to decline any insurance offer from your rental car company.

Of course, terms and conditions vary, so always check your card's specific policies before you rent. This way, if you run into a problem, you'll know what's covered and what's not.

If you don’t follow these requirements, your credit card car rental insurance won’t take effect.

Related: All you need to know about using a debit card to rent a car

The car rental insurance from your credit card is technically called an “auto rental collision damage waiver.” This benefit provides reimbursement for damage due to collision or theft. The cash amount your card's insurance policy will cover can vary, so check your card's guide to benefits for specific details.

While some cards also cover loss-of-use and towing charges assessed by the rental company, policies from other credit cards only cover physical damage or theft of the rental vehicle. Knowing what your card will cover is important before you use it.

Additionally, some rental types and locations may not be eligible for coverage. Keep the following provisions in mind if you rely on credit card car rental insurance benefits:

If you have doubts about your car's eligibility, it's best practice to call the customer service number on your card. You can get more information and confirm that your policy covers your rental vehicle type in the country you’ll be visiting.

Related: My experience with Turo: Car rental convenience at a great price

Another important distinction is the difference between primary and secondary car rental insurance, as your card could offer one type or the other. Both types of insurance usually have maximum coverage amounts, so make sure these meet or exceed the total value of the car you’re renting.

If you get into an accident with your rental car and have primary insurance, you only need to file one claim. Generally, primary insurance will reimburse you for the rental car’s cash value or the cost to repair it, whichever is less.

Secondary insurance is different because it only reimburses you for the amount not covered by other types of insurance, such as travel insurance or personal car insurance. However, if you don’t own a car or carry a car insurance policy, most secondary insurance from credit cards will become primary.

Select American Express cards include secondary coverage for damage to or theft of an eligible rental car. If you want primary coverage, you can enroll an eligible Amex card in Premium Car Rental Protection before you rent. Amex charges a flat fee per eligible rental paid for with the enrolled card.

Related: Secondary rental car insurance: Best cards and what's covered

Many consumers focus on the number of points or miles they can earn and redeem when choosing a travel rewards card, but travel protections such as rental car insurance can also provide significant value.

However, reviewing your card’s policy details is essential to understand what is (and isn’t) covered. Don’t assume you’re covered for every possible mishap when you pay for a car rental with a credit card that offers insurance, as many exceptions and exclusions apply.

Ensure you know the details and how they relate to your rental location, vehicle type, length of rental period and other important issues so you won’t be surprised by a bill if your rental car has a problem.

#6206. Headed to Puerto Rico? These Beaches Belong on Your Bucket List

My father grew up on Puerto Rico's west coast, where beach days began with a barefoot walk to the sand around the neighborhoods of Isabela or Aguadilla and often ended wherever the waves happened to be breaking next. I grew up on stories of salty hair, sun-warmed sand, and long, glittering afternoons in the water. Eventually, I started following in his footsteps, exploring the island’s beaches for myself and discovering just how many different shades of paradise fit along its 300 miles of coastline. There are the rollicking Atlantic surf breaks at Jobos and Middles, the impossibly blue waters and colorful fishing boats of Crash Boat, the mangrove-fringed coastline around La Parguera, and the powdery white sands of Culebra's Flamenco Beach. Some days call for a boat ride out to Culebrita’s secluded Tortuga Beach; others are better spent under the palms in Luquillo, with a plate of fresh seafood and a cold Medalla from the nearby kiosks.

The island is filled with beaches, all with a slightly different personality. Whether your plan is to wake up early and arrive with a surfboard, head out on a boat ride, snorkel, or lounge on the sand with absolutely no plans at all, I've got a rec for you. From well-loved surf towns to far-flung island hideaways, these are the best beaches in Puerto Rico worth building a trip around—plus, where to stay when you get there.

Head to dreamy Playa Jobos (or Jobos Beach)…

…for local vibes, sublime swells, a colorful coast

Head to Culebra, a lush island off the east coast, and you'll find Flamenco Beach, a gorgeous white-sand beach that's just over one mile long. It sits inside a broad, horseshoe-shaped bay, where the curve of the land shields the coastline from heavy Atlantic swells, so the water remains calm and clear for long stretches. The layers of color can be seen overhead: pale green near the shore, then deeper blue as the floor drops away. A quintessential tropical beach, the sand here is as fine as flour, remarkably pale and cool. While the shore is relatively short, it is wide enough that you can always find a spot to claim as your own, even on busy peak weekends.

Not to mention, the beach was ranked one of the top 50 beaches in the world for 2026—the Caribbean gem landed the 41st spot globally and 10th in North America on The World’s 50 Best Beaches list for 2026.

Jobos Beach is one of those stretches that captures the easygoing, salt-in-your-hair spirit of Puerto Rico’s northwest coast. Tucked into Isabela’s Bajuras neighborhood, the sandy bay is framed by a rocky headland, with a well-known reef break that draws local surfers and visiting wave-chasers alike. Even if you don't surf, there's plenty to keep you busy here: watch the lineup from the shore, book a lesson with Moku Surf Shop, or settle in at one of the beachside restaurants next door for fresh seafood and a table with an ocean view. The surrounding stretch of coast is dotted with little places to eat and drink, so it's easy to make an afternoon of it, whether you're coming straight from the water or just looking for a laid-back lunch with a view. Jobos is a proper surf beach, though, not a reliably calm swimming cove; strong currents and changing conditions are part of the picture, so take care before heading in.

The path to this beach is a bit of a trek: Starting in Ceiba, a small town to the northeast of the main island, travelers will need to take a ferry to Culebra followed by another 30-minute boat ride via water taxi or tour group to Culebrita (little Culebra). But trust that the ride is well worth the reward of unspoiled paradise—it's even sea-turtle-approved. The beach's name Tortuga nods to the herds of turtles that visit its shores from February to August and make for superb snorkeling companions. Above water, the beach welcomes a Robinson Crusoe variety of fun with its lush untamed jungles and powder-soft white sands. Make sure to grab everything you'll need for a few hours of fun—because of Tortuga's removed location, you won't find amenities like bathrooms or food stands close by.

The piers here were initially built so the US military could quickly recover downed airmen from Ramey Air Force Base, thus explaining the name, “Crash Boat Beach.” Located on the west side of the island in Aguadilla, this beach's past life as a military outpost feels far behind it—dinghies and fishing boats of all shapes, shades, and sizes line the highlighter-painted piers and the unofficial soundtrack of the shore comes from the speakers and boomboxes pulsing to reggaeton beats. Whether you're here to party at some of the best bars in Puerto Rico or enjoy the calmer life that carries on at sea, visitors are welcome to take their sweet time here, thanks to the well-stocked kiosks of water sports pavilions, umbrella rentals, and food stands, selling any wares you might need for a long day at the beach.

A one-mile crescent that arcs along the island's northern coast, Pine Grove provides a taste of the Atlantic's stronger waves, making it one of Puerto Rico's most popular surf spots for those just starting out. Especially during the month of December, the east side of this beach tends to catch consistent three-to-four-foot swells, making it a great place for beginners to learn how to surf. The convenient location is a welcome bonus; as a beach in Isla Verde, Pine Grove is a mere five minutes away from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport (SJU), so you can hit the sands as soon as you're wheels down in the Caribbean.

Where to stay near Pine Grove Surfing Beach:

Vieques is a six-mile skip to the southeast of the main island, and once dubbed, “La Isla Nena” by Puerto Rican poet Luis Llorens Torres—this island plays the role of darling little sister perfectly. And where better to experience the island's charms than on one of its beaches? La Chiva is a part of the Vieques National Wildlife Refuge, where a few steps to your left may lead you to a forest of mangroves, a few to the right, a stunning coastal lagoon. Take it all in surrounded by the friendly company of wild horses, sea turtles, manatees, and diving seabirds. Stretching out for one and a half miles, this is a leisurely walk along the beach that's begging to be taken. If you're enticed to do more in the clear-as-glass turquoise waters, head off to nearby Chiva Bay, one of the best snorkeling spots in Puerto Rico.

Also known as Balneario La Monserrate, Luquillo Beach is so much more than its 12 miles of golden sands, tranquil waters, and fanning palms—though all of the above are fabulous. The beach borders El Yunque National Forest, the only rainforest registered in the US National Parks system. If you're searching to pack your itinerary with more than swimming, surfing, and snorkeling, head for the mountains: For can't-miss sights, journey up the main road to La Coca waterfall for a cool mist and Yokahú Tower, an observation tower where you can behold the entire forest floor before you.

Technically, La Parguera has no beaches. But you won't miss any other shores after spending a day at these cays. Rent out a small boat or book with a local tour operator to explore the mild seas. Cays like Mata La Gata have shaded picnic areas for a casual lunch in paradise, while the gin-clear waters at Cayo Caracoles have natural walking paths lined with mangroves. Pressed for time and only able to visit one? Plan an after-hours trip to La Parguera's bioluminescent bay—one of three in Puerto Rico, and the only one visitors are permitted to swim in—which lights up an electric blue as you swim through the clouds of plankton that sparkle like glitter against the dark blue water.

This is one for the snorkelers. For a strong chance of seeing bus-sized manta rays, sea turtles, and marine life in every other form and flavor, look no further than in Tamarindo's welcoming waters. For those who aren't looking to paddle too far, the serene ocean in these parts is ideal for young families and those of all ages who'd rather just dip their feet in. While the entertainment and dining scene is virtually nonexistent, the opportunities for relaxation and reconnecting with nature are unparalleled.

This gallery has been updated with new information since its original publish date.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6205. Why Singapore Airlines Is Saving Its New Premium Economy Seat For The Boeing 777-9

Singapore Airlines(SQ) is about to sell two very different premium economy cabins under one name, and it has already decided which aircraft will get the better one. When the carrier detailed its next-generation KrisWorld system on October 22, as covered by Mainly Miles, one detail stood out: the all-new premium economy seat, with a screen of up to 16 inches (41 cm), is bound only for the Boeing 777-9. The 41 Airbus A350s undergoing the S$1.1 billion retrofit will retain their existing Premium Economy seats, albeit with a refresh.

That leaves an obvious question: why spend more than a billion Singapore dollars rebuilding the A350 cabins while leaving the premium economy largely as it is? Singapore has now provided more clues, including the fact that the new seats are certified for the 777-9 but not yet for the A350. The available evidence also points to a substantial new seat-development program and a retrofit focused on the cabins with the greatest revenue potential. The distinction matters: what follows separates what Singapore has confirmed from what the evidence suggests.

The announcement was broader than premium economy. CAPA summarized it as a package of inflight enhancements, but the detail that matters here comes from Executive Traveller: the A350s will get only a “refresh” of their current premium economy seat, while an all-new design goes to the 777-9. According to SeatCompare, the annex to Singapore’s release lists the 777-9 as the aircraft carrying all four new cabin products, meaning first, business, premium economy and economy. On November 6, Singapore confirmed the aircraft split: the Boeing 777-9 will introduce all four new long-haul cabin products, while the A350 retrofit focuses on the new First and Business Class products and retains the existing Premium Economy seat.

The new premium economy seat has now been confirmed with a 16-inch (41 cm) 4K screen, Bluetooth audio, USB-C connectivity, a 40-inch (102 cm) seat pitch, 9 inches (23 cm) of recline and a 19-inch (48 cm) seat width. Singapore says selected aircraft will receive 4K OLED displays, so even the new product may not be completely uniform across the fleet. The seat itself is being supplied by Collins Aerospace, with Factorydesign responsible for the design, replacing the earlier reports that only described its manufacturer and business-class lineage as unconfirmed. Leaving the seat on the A350 unchanged is not new, either. Singapore launched premium economy in August 2015 after a two-year program, which SilverKris, the airline’s own magazine, put at close to $80 million. That seat is now more than 11 years old. SeatCompare argues the contrast will be stark: on a 777-9 the premium economy screen will be bigger than the business-class screens of a generation ago, while an A350 passenger keeps the screen that cabin has always had.

The split between the two aircraft is easier to understand when viewed against the program’s original timetable. The new seats were developed for the 777-9, but Boeing's delays forced Singapore to find another way to introduce at least part of the cabin package. That decision explains why the A350 retrofit looks the way it does.

The cabin program was tied to the 777-9 long before Singapore announced the A350 retrofit. Reports trace the work to 2018, with a launch expected around 2021, as Live From A Lounge noted. The aircraft's development schedule, however, took a very different turn. The 777-9 first flew in January 2020 and, according to Simple Flying, still was not certified as of a Farnborough 2026 report, with Boeing now targeting a first delivery to Lufthansa in 2027, about seven years behind the original schedule. Mainly Miles counts it as the fifth delay since the type’s launch at the Dubai Airshow in November 2013.

The delay carried real costs. As early as May 2023, CEO Goh Choon Phong acknowledged that Singapore would have to extend the life of some aircraft, particularly the older Boeing 777-300ERs, because the 777-9 was late, as Mainly Miles recalls. By November 2024, Singapore had run out of patience. It announced a S$1.1 billion retrofit, roughly $835 million at the time, according to View from the Wing, that would put the first and business class designs meant for the 777-9 onto 41 long-haul A350-900s instead. The airline ordered 20 of the type in February 2017 and added 11 more in February 2021, as Executive Traveller has documented, and those 31 jets are meant to receive the same first and business class designs plus all-new premium economy and economy seats.

Moving the first and business class products to the A350s gave Singapore a way to use much of the work already completed for the 777-9. It did not solve every cabin question, though. Premium economy was left out of that transfer, and the aircraft configurations help explain why the airline may have chosen to concentrate its investment elsewhere.

More space, better meals, and none of the business class price tag — but only if you know which airline to book.

Singapore has not publicly explained why premium economy is being treated differently, so the following is analysis rather than the airline's stated rationale. One possible explanation is that the retrofit prioritizes the cabins with the greatest revenue potential. The program covers 34 long-haul A350-900s, each with 42 business, 24 premium economy and 192 economy seats, and seven ultra-long-range A350-900s that will gain first class for the first time, with four suites alongside 70 business and 58 premium economy seats.

When Singapore resumed nonstop flights to Los Angeles in 2018, Malay Mail reported a two-class layout of 67 business and 94 premium economy seats. That configuration is not merely a historical snapshot: Singapore's current Airbus A350-900ULR seat map still lists 67 business class and 94 premium economy seats. It is therefore the appropriate baseline for comparison with the announced retrofit. On the planned layout, premium economy loses 36 seats, while business gains three and first class gains four suites. A senior executive had told Malay Mail that same year that business class sold easily on the nearly 19-hour flights to the United States, while premium economy had to be priced very attractively.

The capacity changes are only part of the picture. The retrofit schedule has also become less certain. Mainly Miles reported in May that the first retrofitted long-haul A350 had slipped to the first quarter of 2027, with the ultra-long-range jets and their new first class left without a committed date. Mainly Miles reads the certification problem as likely involving first class. A program already running late has little room for a second major seat, and that points to a bigger question: how big a project is this premium economy seat?

Singapore Airlines has now confirmed who is behind its new Premium Economy seat. According to the airline'sNovember 6 announcement, Collins Aerospace will manufacture it, with Factorydesign handling the design. The seat will offer a 40-inch (102 cm) pitch, 19-inch (48 cm) width and 9-inch (23 cm) recline, along with adjustable leg and footrests. Passengers will also get a screen of up to 16 inches (41 cm), with 4K resolution and Bluetooth audio. Selected aircraft will feature OLED displays.

So why won't the A350 receive it? Singapore Airlines has made clear that it makes cabin investment decisions separately for each aircraft type. As Chief Commercial Officer Lee Lik Hsin toldThe Straits Times, the airline considers the requirements of each cabin within each fleet. There is also a certification issue. The new 777-9 seats have already cleared certification, while the A350 installations are still awaiting regulatory approval. Consequently, the 41 A350s in the S$1.1 billion retrofit will retain their existing Premium Economy seats while receiving the new business class product and, on the ULR version, a new first class cabin.

Mainly Miles has already reported that Singapore postponed the start of the ultra-long-range retrofit downtime, and every additional seat type installed during that hangar visit adds certification work and supply risk to aircraft that cannot afford to sit idle. All of that development work needs an aircraft to enter service. For Singapore, that means waiting for the 777-9, whose delivery schedule remains uncertain.

This brand-new link contributes to the airline having record flights and seats to Australia. Find out more here!

The airline's stated timeline points to 2027 for the arrival of 777-9s fitted with the new premium economy seat. That is the optimistic end of the current range. View from the Wing thinks 2028 is more likely, since Singapore is not among the first 777-9 customers. The numbers support the caution. Mainly Miles noted that Singapore’s fleet plan showed no 777-9 deliveries in the 12 months to March 31, 2027, with Emirates, Qatar Airways and Lufthansa ahead in line, which means no Singapore 777-9 before April 2027 at the earliest. According to Simple Flying, airlines wary of further delays are already locking in 777-9 production slots. Its separate analysis of the 777-9 and A350-1000 counts more than 520 firm orders for the 777-9, led by Emirates with 270 aircraft and Qatar Airways with 124, which shows how crowded the line is.

Passengers are likely to encounter the new cabin designs on the A350 before they see the 777-9. The same outlet reports that the first retrofitted A350 is expected to debut the new first and business class products in early 2027, ahead of any 777-9. The 777-300ERs that the new jets will replace are not scheduled to receive the new cabins either, according to the same outlet, so their premium economy stays as it is. More details are close: AsiaOne reports that Singapore will unveil the new first and business class seats on November 7.

The timing matters because the airline could soon be selling two noticeably different products under the same premium economy label. That creates a customer-facing issue Singapore has yet to address: how will passengers know which version they are booking?

The A350 retrofit is a bet that the 777-9 will arrive before the gap becomes a problem. Singapore has separated the two programs on purpose: the A350s get a refresh of the 2015 seat, and the new seat waits for the aircraft it was designed around. Whether that holds as a short bridge or a lasting split depends on Boeing’s delivery line and on A350 certification, and the airline controls neither.

The clearest test is the installed base. On the planned layouts, 34 long-haul A350s carry 24 premium economy seats each and seven ultra-long-range jets carry 58, about 1,220 seats with the older hardware. The 31 ordered 777-9s, at 36 premium economy seats each, would carry about 1,115 of the new seats, and that is only once the whole order has been delivered (the seat totals are my arithmetic from the published layouts). So the new product starts as the minority one, with no 777-9 deliveries in Singapore’s fleet plan before April 2027. Even among the new jets, View from the Wing reports the first 12 aircraft get conventional 4K screens and the later 19 get OLED. The thing to check is whether Singapore’s first 777-9 handover lands in 2027, as the airline maintains, or in 2028, as View from the Wing expects.

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

Mainly Miles has reported that Singapore has not ruled out bringing some of the new features to the A350 later. As AirlineRatings noted, the launch of the new seat depends on one unpredictable factor, and that factor is Boeing’s schedule. Two signals will show whether the split is temporary: any A350 certification news for the new seat, and whether Singapore starts telling passengers which premium economy they are booking. If neither appears before the first 777-9 does, the two-tier product stops being a transition.

#6204. The Best Ski Resorts in the US and Canada: 2026 Readers’ Choice Awards

For our 39th annual Reader’s Choice Awards, voters weighed in on their favorite ski resorts in North America—including the US and Canada. Big Sky’s decade-long transformation has paid off, landing the Montana resort in the top spot this year. But Colorado reigns as the top US ski destination, with 10 resorts making our top 30. Meanwhile, six East Coast resorts were recognized, including Mont-Tremblant in Quebec, Canada. And in the western US, new enhancements at Alyeska Resort helped get Alaska back on the list.

From Taos to Telluride and Stowe to SilverStar, these ski resorts were picked by our readers as the best in North America for their trails, lodges, lifts, and après-ski scenes. Whether you’re a powder hound or après ski devotee, these ski resorts ticked all your boxes.

View the 2025 Readers' Choice Awards winners for best ski resorts as a list with scores for the United States here and Canada here.

Aspen-Snowmass’s four mountains are each wildly unique, and Buttermilk might be the most playful. More like one giant terrain park, it’s home to seven different parks for everyone from beginners to pros. Its 22-foot Zaugg-cut Superpipe is the stage for star-studded sporting competitions including X Games Aspen and The Snow League. But Buttermilk is also the mountain for easygoing beginner terrain and awesomely intense trails for uphillers—those showoffs practicing the cardio-busting trend of trekking up a mountain on skis.

Where to stay: Just a free, five-minute shuttle ride away in downtown Aspen at your pick of great hotels, including the Little Nell, Limelight Aspen, St. Regis Aspen, and Hotel Jerome.

Stats: 8 lifts and 44 trails. One-day lift tickets average from $189; on the Ikon Pass and Mountain Collective.

The longest continually operating ski resort in Colorado, Winter Park is a Rocky Mountain playground known for its varied terrain and consistent snowfall (roughly 350 inches a year). It’s also one of Colorado’s most accessible mountains. Located just 67 miles west of Denver, it’s an easy drive from the airport, or take the Amtrak Winter Park Express ski train and get dropped off just steps from the lifts. This season, the resort is more than doubling snowmaking on a key base trail, again improving upon its recent $40 million snowmaking system upgrade. Families continue to find tons of value. Back this season, kids can nab a free ski or snowboard rental with a three-day adult gear rental package and every kid 14 and younger who signs up for a Winter Park Ski and Ride School lesson gets a free lift ticket for the day. The Gondola is free to everyone after 4 p.m. every Thursday through Saturday from mid-December through the end of March. That means you can wrap up the day at Mountaintop Après at Sunspot Lodge whether you skied or not.

Where to stay: Zephyr Mountain Lodge has studios, 1, 2, and 3-bedroom condos with full kitchens. In town, Gravity Haus Winter Park offers co-working spaces as well as gear demos and rentals. A-Frame Club is an Instagram-sensation with its 31 A-Frame cabins and historic saloon.

Stats: 23 lifts, 171 designated trails and 1,212 acres of off-piste terrain. One-day lift tickets from $108; on the Ikon Pass.

Where to stay: The Park Hyatt Beaver Creek Resort and Spa is fresh off a $20 million renovation. Other favorites include The Westin Riverfront Resort & Spa Avon, Vail Valley, The Osprey, a RockResort, and the Ritz-Carlton, Bachelor Gulch.

Stats: 24 lifts for 167 trails. One-day lift tickets from $116; on the Epic Pass.

Skiing in Alaska is a different experience than anywhere in the lower 48. Located just 40 miles southeast of Anchorage, Alyeska’s terrain is uniquely Alaskan, boasting everything from high alpine to the steep faces the 49th state is known for. Experts can push their limits, but with over 55 percent intermediate terrain, tree skiing, wide open groomed runs, and a lower mountain venue perfect for beginners, Alyeska caters to all ability levels. Aside from resort skiing, Alyeska serves as a backcountry basecamp offering guided ski touring, cat skiing, or heli skiing with top-notch outfits like SMG Alaska. And when it comes to après-ski, a trip to the mountaintop Bore Tide Bar for an off-menu Fizz cocktail is an Alyeska ritual.

Where to stay: The 299-room Alyeska Resort has eight dining venues, including stellar sushi spot Sakura and fine dining restaurant, Seven Glaciers, with its panoramic views. The eighth-floor Black Diamond Club feels like a hotel-within-a-hotel thanks to perks like a private lounge that serves complimentary breakfast and après bites. The resort’s 50,000-square-foot, indoor-outdoor Nordic spa is the perfect place to spend a down day.

Stats: 7 lifts for 76 runs, with an additional 1,400 vertical feet accessible via hike-to terrain when conditions allow. One-day lift tickets from $77; on the Ikon Pass.

Tamarack’s primarily east-facing slopes receive an average of 300 inches of snowfall annually. Readers love the diversity of terrain, which welcomes everyone from beginners and families to experts and powder chasers. The resort’s 2,000 mountain acres and 2,800 feet of vertical deliver everything from open bowls, steeps and signature cornice drops to high-speed corduroy groomers, natural tree-skiing glades and three terrain parks. At 6,700 feet, the new Mid-Mountain Lodge crowns the top of Tamarack Express with panoramic dining and event space, while a vibrant alpine-style village anchors the base with lodging, dining, and après. And Tamarack's Nordic trail system winds through open meadows and forested terrain for classic and skate skiing, snowshoeing, and fat biking.

Where to stay: Tamarack Resort has accommodations ranging from studios to four-bedroom penthouses plus amenities such as a pool, hot tubs and gear valet. The Lodge at Osprey Meadows is steps from the lifts and has studios and two- and three-bedroom condos.

Stats: 7 lifts for 59 runs. One-day lift tickets from $99; Ikon Pass Bonus Mountain

Founded by the late Robert Redford in 1969, Sundance Mountain Resort is a beloved escape tucked into Utah’s Wasatch Mountains at the base of the 12,000-foot Mount Timpanogos in Provo Canyon. Steep bowls give experienced skiers a thrill, while a third of the runs are green and beginner-friendly. Just an hour from Salt Lake City (hello, easy airport access!), the 5,000 acres of protected wilderness that surround the resort will help you find solitude. This season’s debut of Electric Horseman, a high-speed quad, marks the first phase of Sundance’s back mountain expansion, adding 60-plus acres of terrain and bringing the resort to 605 skiable acres. At the heart of the terrain expansion is Storyteller, a new signature ridgeline run carved from the terrain formerly known as the Far East Ridgeline. An additional 100 acres of terrain are planned for the 2027-2028 winter season. Off the slopes, guests can explore the resort’s renowned Art Studio & Gallery (think silversmithing and pottery classes), or unwind at the Spa and The Springs.

Where to stay: The Inn at Sundance Mountain Resort, which opened in January 2026, introduced ski-in/ski-out hotel accommodations to the resort for the first time, with 63 thoughtfully designed rooms in the heart of the village.

Stats: 10 lifts for 72 trails. One-day pass is $169.

Spanning six peaks and over 3,000 acres in the Yampa Valley, Steamboat is revered for its tree skiing, trademarked Champagne Powder snow, and family-friendly amenities. But many folks keep coming back for its deep Western roots and a down-home vibe that extends from the mountain to the town. A multiyear, multimillion-dollar redevelopment has reimagined Steamboat. The base area now features Wild Blue, a high speed ten-person gondola that takes skiers and riders from the base to the top of Sunshine Peak in 13 minutes, plus Skeeter's ice rink, and the Range Food & Drink Hall. Beginners can hone their skills mid-mountain at Greenhorn Ranch with natural feature-based instruction, while experts can test their mettle on 655 acres of challenging terrain in Mahogany Ridge and Fish Creek Canyon. One of the most accessible resorts in the Rockies, Steamboat is served by 18 major U.S. cities including Portland, Austin, and Houston.

Where to stay: The Steamboat Grand is a favorite for its massive heated pool and hot tubs. Ski-in/ski-out Sheraton Steamboat Resort Villas is conveniently located next to Christie Peak Express. Gravity Haus is an affordable, slopeside boutique stay. The Amble opened this summer and has 42 residences and resort amenities.

Stats: 23 lifts for 184g trails. One-day lift tickets from $131; on the Ikon Pass.

Of the four mountains that make up Aspen Snowmass, the ultimate rite of passage is here at Aspen Highlands’ massive Highland Bowl. Here’s how to do it: Hike some 45 minutes to the top of the bowl, soak in rewarding 360-degree views that include the twin-peaked Maroon Bells and own the drop into almost 2,500 feet of steep bowl skiing. Reward yourself at mid-mountain with the Merry-Go-Round’s signature Boomerang Burger, topped with onion rings, pastrami bacon and grilled cheese buns.

Where to stay: The Little Nell for five-star service and a great spa or its more casual sister property, Limelight Aspen. That Gant for apartment-style residences with full kitchens.

Stats: 5 lifts for 144 trails. One-day lift tickets from $189; on the Ikon Pass and Mountain Collective pass.

With nearly 5,000 acres of diverse terrain, Heavenly offers the best of both California and Nevada skiing and riding including wide-open groomers, glades, and 1,600-foot mogul runs. Sparkling Lake Tahoe views, an average of 300 days of sunshine a year, and high-energy events and après make Heavenly a dream getaway for your party crew that is always looking for the next adventure. The unique Skyline Trail is a must-do run, taking in majestic mountain landscapes, flat valleys, and lake panoramas while crossing from California to Nevada. Plus, the Heavenly Village is located in the heart of South Lake Tahoe, surrounded by snow-based activities and restaurants, and fun events throughout the winter season. If the views of Lake Tahoe inspire you on the slopes, a trip to the shore is just minutes away.

Where to stay: Basecamp Tahoe South is just a four-minute walk to the gondola and offers a variety of rooms from bunks to luxe tents. Zalanta Resort at the Village is steps away from Heavenly Village and residence-style rooms include gourmet kitchens and private balconies. Lakefront Edgewood Tahoe Resort has a partnership with Ski Butlers to have gear delivered directly to your room.

Stats: 27 lifts for 111 trails. One-day lift ticket from $115; on the Epic Pass.

A winter haven for East Coasters, this Poconos resort’s snow-making capacity could cover the George Washington Bridge with one foot of snow in 24 hours. The mountain’s 900-foot vertical drop is great training before venturing to bigger mountains in the West. More than half of the mountain, however, is covered in beginner-friendly greens. Families love the amenities, including one of the country’s largest snow-tubing park, an indoor water park, and a plethora of dining options including ski-in/ski-out Trail’s End Pub & Grille, known for its creative burgers and craft beer, and Alpine Outpost, a new grab-and-go spot along the Coolmoor teaching trail.

Where to stay: Camelback Lodge, the only ski-in/ski out resort in the Poconos, recently refurbished 453 guest rooms that come in 16 different configurations including bunk rooms and a suite that can sleep up to 14 guests.

Stats: 14 lifts for 45 trails. One-day lift tickets from $78; on the Ikon Pass.

Hard-core skiers who live for hike-to terrain and super steeps have always been fans of Taos Ski Valley. But a revitalized base area with an ice-skating rink, improvements to beginner and intermediate terrain, and $3 million in glading and expanding snowmaking capacity have made this New Mexico mountain destination way more family friendly. Taos Ski Valley leans into sustainability, equity, and inclusivity as the first ski resort in the world to have been B-Corp certified, and one of a few to be Certified CarbonNeutral®. The challenging terrain of Kachina Peak and the moguls of Al’s Run are the big draw for experts. This season ups the resort’s luxury appeal with the introduction of Taos by Belvedere, a fully hosted, all-inclusive mountain experience that features slopeside penthouse accommodations, a private chef, privately guided skiing, restorative wellness therapies, and insider access to local experiences. For dining, the Bavarian is an institution known for its brats and German beers (they also host a sleigh ride dinner during the winter), and newcomer Corner Office gives the state its first natural wine bar. Down days are far from dull thanks to surrounding cultural attractions including the Taos Pueblo UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Where to stay: Located adjacent to Lift 1, The Blake offers a variety of accommodation options that include hotel rooms, suites, penthouses, and condos; decor blends rustic European architecture with one of North America’s finest collections of Southwestern art, including original works by Georgia O’Keeffe.

Stats: 13 lifts for 110 trails. One-day lift tickets from $75; on the Ikon Pass and Mountain Collective pass.

The largest of the SkiBig3 resorts in UNESCO-designated Banff National Park earns its keep with 4,200 acres spanning four different mountain faces and a solid mix of beginner, intermediate, and expert runs from every chair. Here’s what else makes it a dream for all walks of skiers: steeps backed by an awe-inspiring wilderness, bowls dusted in famously dry powder, four terrain parks for beginners to experts, and long cruisers—one of which winds on for five miles. The ‘West Bowl’ is a freeride playground with some 480 wilderness acres to explore. And the recent addition of the Juniper Express Quad provides an ideal learning zone for beginner and intermediate skiers and riders looking to advance their skills. This season, Lake Louise is enhancing its recently opened Richardson’s Ridge terrain with new groomed runs, glades, and improved snowmaking, alongside a major Top of the World chair upgrade designed to increase capacity and reliability.

Where to stay: Located lakeside in Banff National Park, Fairmont Chateau Lake Louise looks like a fairytale castle and its new Basin Glacier Waters Thermal Wellness Spa will have you wishing for a down day to spend soaking in its healing waters. A member of Relais & Châteaux, Post Hotel & Spa has a saltwater pool and is known for its extensive wine cellar and talented culinary team.

Stats: 13 lifts for 169 runs and back bowls. One-day SkiBig3 lift tickets from $172; on the Ikon Pass and Mountain Collective pass.

Nestled on the northern edge of British Columbia’s North Okanagan wine region, SilverStar is one of Canada’s best-kept secrets, with 3,065 skiable acres that receive 275-plus inches of annual snowfall. Guests can skip the rental car and take one of the regular shuttles from Kelowna International Airport, just 55 minutes away. The resort has exceptionally groomed terrain for all abilities and families appreciate that kids age 5 and under receive free lift tickets all season. Alpine skiing is just one of many winter activities on offer. You’ll also find 65 miles of groomed cross-country ski trails, 9 miles of fat-tire bike trails, 4 snow tubing lanes, and a natural skating pond. The dining experiences, such as the Ravenwood snowshoe raclette dinner and the Paradise Camp snow cat dinner tour, are not-to-be-missed. And La Stella, a new Italian spot with wood-fired pizzas debuts this season.

Where to stay: SilverStar’s mid-mountain location means most accommodations are ski-in/ski-out. Snowbird Lodge, Silver Creek Lodge, and Lord Aberdeen have prime locations in the heart of the village, steps from the Summit Express Gondola. Firelight Lodge offers convenient access to the Nordic trail heads.

Stats: 10 lifts for 132 runs. One-day lift ticket from $119; on the Ikon Pass.

Originally known as Little Gap Ski Area when it opened in 1977, the resort changed its name in 1989 to better reflect the grandeur of our mountain. With a vertical drop of 1,082 feet, Blue Mountain boasts the highest elevation in Pennsylvania. Whether you’re a beginner or expert, you’ll find the perfect challenge on the mountain’s 171 acres. You can conquer 15 green, 6 blue, 16 black diamond, and 3 double black diamond trails across the region’s most varied terrain. Home to the East Coast’s largest snowmaking system, the mountain delivers some of the most consistent conditions all season long in the mid-Atlantic region. For lunch with gorgeous views, pop into Slopeside Pub & Grill for wood-fired pizzas and hearty sammys like chicken cheesesteaks. For a quick, grab-and-go bite, swing by the new spud truck, serving up loaded baked potatoes.

Where to stay: Blue Mountain-area Airbnb rentals are the way to go here.

Stats: 15 lifts for 40 trails; One-day lift ticket from $48; on the Ikon Pass.

American Express Membership Rewards aren't just for travel anymore. Sports fans now have another way to put their points to use.

As of today, some American Express cardmembers can transfer Membership Rewards points to FanCash, the rewards currency of sports merchandise retailer Fanatics.

The new transfer option is part of a broader partnership between American Express and Fanatics, which also unveiled additional details about its upcoming cobranded credit card.

Eligible U.S. cardmembers can now transfer Membership Rewards points to FanCash at a rate of 1,000 points for $10 in FanCash, giving you a redemption value of 1 cent per point. You can find this option in the newly added Lifestyle section of Amex's transfer partners page.

Simply enter your Fanatics credentials to link your account, which only takes a few seconds.

Once transferred, FanCash can be used toward eligible purchases across the Fanatics ecosystem, including sports apparel, trading cards, collectibles and tickets.

However, this isn't necessarily the best use of your Amex points. At 1 cent apiece, you'd be getting just half of TPG's valuation of Membership Rewards points at 2 cents each, a value you can potentially achieve by transferring points to Amex's airline and hotel partners.

Still, this gives sports fans another option for redeeming their points, particularly if they don't have any upcoming travel plans.

Related: Best ways to use Amex Membership Rewards points

As announced earlier this year, American Express and Fanatics are also teaming up on a new cobranded credit card designed for sports fans.

The upcoming Fanatics American Express® Card will have no annual fee and earn 5% FanCash on eligible purchases across the Fanatics ecosystem, or 8% or more when shopping through the Fanatics app.

The card will also offer sports-focused perks and more than 500 trading card-inspired designs featuring professional athletes.

It's not yet available for applications, but interested consumers can join the waitlist.

The information for the Fanatics American Express Card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

The ability to transfer Amex points to FanCash gives sports fans another way to use their rewards, but the 1-cent-per-point value may not appeal to travelers looking to maximize their Membership Rewards points.

For those who regularly shop with Fanatics, however, the new transfer option could be a convenient way to put unused points toward their next purchase.

Related: American Express Membership Rewards: How to earn, redeem and transfer points

It’s no secret that Away is one of our team's favorite luggage brands. With its thoughtfully designed suitcases and sleek essentials, the brand has become synonymous with effortless movement, whether you’re heading out on a quick city escape or a long-haul adventure.

If you’ve been waiting to invest in your next travel companion, know that verified Away promo codes can help you save on signature styles—from up to $100 off select luggage bundles to 20% off sale items. Whether you’re planning a cross-country road trip or a flight abroad, these savings make it easier to pack stylishly and travel smarter.

Black Friday is still a few weeks away, but some of Away's sales are already live. Shoppers can save up to 20% off when they bundle items—a great deal for travelers ready to upgrade their entire luggage lineup, or who are gift shopping for a few different travelers. There are a whole bunch of options that can help cut down on any holiday decision fatigue—the best-selling Jetsetter bundle is $200 off, with sets like the Work From Anywhere bundle or the Best Selling bundle almost $100 off. There's also a build your own bundle option for those looking with specific items in mind.

Whichever route you go, you can rest easy knowing each piece is crafted for travelers who value both form and function: hard-shell suitcases that glide seamlessly through terminals, compact carry-ons with convenient compartments, and travel bags that make packing feel like an art.

New customers, listen up: Away often offers a 10% off coupon on first orders when you sign up for emails and texts. This coupon code is not currently being offered, but keep your eyes peeled for its return. Once signed up, you'll stay in the loop on the latest launches and collabs, special events, and more. To snag the deal, head to Away's homepage and keep an out for a pop-up, then enter your information to sign up.

Away is making travel more accessible for those who give back to their communities with a 10% discount for veterans, active military members, medical personnel, teachers, and students. Whether you're a student preparing for a semester abroad or a teacher gearing up for a well-deserved getaway, this offer makes premium luggage more affordable. Simply verify your status through ID.me, and you’re all set to enjoy stylish, durable travel essentials at a discounted price. For more details, visit Away’s Hero Discounts.

Sharing your love of travel has its perks with Away’s $40 off referral offer. When you introduce a friend to the brand, they’ll receive $40 off their first purchase of $125 or more—and once their order is complete, you’ll get $40 off your next one, too. The best part? You can earn up to $200 in rewards by referring as many as five friends. To claim the offer, your friend simply uses your referral link to visit Away’s Get Rewarded page, where a unique code appears to apply at checkout. The discount is valid on suitcases and bags only, making it an ideal way to refresh your own travel setup while helping someone else discover the quality and design that make Away a go-to for savvy travelers.

Away proves that great design and thoughtful functionality don’t have to come at a steep price. The brand’s lineup of best-selling luggage under $300 includes sleek staples like The Carry-On ($275) and The Bigger Carry-On ($295)—lightweight, durable pieces that glide effortlessly through terminals and tuck neatly into overhead bins. You can explore more travel-ready finds in Away’s Under $300 collection.

For families, Away’s Family Travel collection makes group trips easier with space-maximizing suitcases, kids’ luggage, diaper bags, crossbody bags, and even pet carriers. Larger pieces like The Medium Flex and The Trunk offer extra capacity and deep compartments, perfect for storing everyone’s essentials in one place.

A great way to save on luggage that's new to you and help reduce waste? Away Reclaimed, the brand's hub for secondhand luggage. Many pieces go for up to $100 less than their original retail value, and each item is graded on a scale of ‘Good’ to ‘Great’ to ‘Excellent’, based on how many cosmetic flaws are present. Per Away, every item is in “travel-ready condition,” and the “surfaces and interiors are cleaned and refreshed.” As you can imagine, inventory comes and goes fairly quickly. If you have something specific in mind, know that you can select the “Notify Me” button on any item page to receive an email notification when the size and color you're looking for becomes available.

Away’s appeal goes beyond its minimalist design—it’s the thoughtful details that make the brand a trusted travel companion. Orders over $100 ship free, and if something isn’t quite right, you can return or exchange unused items within 100 days, either online or at one of Away’s 17 stores. Every suitcase is backed by a lifetime warranty, covering functional repairs so your luggage lasts trip after trip.

There’s purpose behind the polish, too: With sustainability in mind, Away incorporates more recycled materials into its luggage and ships everything in 100% recyclable packaging. And with Shop Pay, you can choose interest-free installments to make investing in quality gear a little easier.

If your Away promo code isn't working at checkout, don't panic—there are a few simple things you can do. First, double check that the code is spelled correctly with no extra spaces or typos. If that doesn't work, take a look at the exact details of the promo code to make sure it's still active and hasn't expired already. Keep in mind that some discount codes have a minimum spend requirement, so you'll want to be sure you've hit any necessary criteria for the deal. If everything looks right and your Away promo code still isn't working, clear your browser's cache and give the page a refresh. Shoppers can also contact Away's customer service for help.

#6201. Singapore Airlines Becomes The 1st Airline To Reveal A Full Boeing 777-9 Seat Map

As the Boeing 777X series of widebody twinjets edges ever closer to finally receiving its long-awaited certification, one of the main questions surrounding the aircraft is how airlines will configure it. With the popular stretched 777-9 model in particular being longer and wider than most other airliners today, there is ample space to install luxurious premium products. Singapore Airlines plans to do just this.

When the carrier revealed its new first and business class suites for the Boeing 777-9 at an event in Singapore last week, it also shared its planned seat map for the aircraft, becoming the first airline anywhere in the world to do so. This finally gave a concrete indication of the premium-heavy nature of how airlines might configure the 777X, with almost a third of the seats being non-economy ones.

Singapore Airlines plans to seat 300 passengers on its Boeing 777-9s. According to ch-aviation, the Star Alliance member has 31 of these new widebody twinjets on order, having bought 20 in June 2017 and another 11 in February 2021. The most luxurious seats on these aircraft will be the six first class suites: of these, four will be located at the windows while the other two are an exclusive center pair.

Behind the six first class suites are 54 business class flatbeds that are laid out in a 1-2-1 setup, with every seat offering direct aisle access. The rear of the second section has 36 premium economy recliners in a 2-4-2 layout, meaning that there are 96 non-economy seats (32%) overall. The rear section features 204 economy seats in a 3-4-3 layout that narrows to 2-4-2 in the last three rows. The airline says that:

"While each cabin has been designed individually, they are united by the same ambition to make the experience more comfortable, flexible, and rewarding for our customers."

With the arrival of the Boeing 777-9 at Singapore Airlines heralding a new era of long-haul travel for the Star Alliance member, the carrier is using the jet as a means of showcasing various luxurious new cabin products. As previously noted, the most notable of these is the center pair of suites in the first class cabin, offering a private and exclusive retreat for couples traveling together in the best seats in the house.

Regardless of whether first class passengers are seated in the center pair or one of the four outer solo suites, they can expect 89.5 inches of pitch (227 cm) and 23 inches (58 cm)of width, with the latter figure increasing to 30 (76 cm) when the armrests are lowered. When converted to a bed, the seat stretches to 80 inches (203 cm), making for a good night's sleep for even the tallest of passengers. Entertainment comes from a 32-inch (81 cm) 4K screen.

Singapore Airlines is also set to roll out a new business class product as part of this initiative in the second half of 2027, with Airbus A350s also included. These spacious flatbeds will offer 50 inches (127 cm) of pitch and 24 inches (61 cm) of width on the 777-9 when upright, with their bed length being 79 inches (201 cm). However, the silver and yellow color scheme has drawn criticism online for not being very Singapore Airlines-coded.

Singapore Airlines is making a surprising choice for its next-generation premium economy cabin. The reason involves a much-delayed aircraft.

As well as replacing older Airbus A380s, Singapore Airlines also plans to use its Boeing 777-9s to replace older examples of the 777-300ER. With this model being the 777-9's most natural predecessor, it is worth examining how Singapore Airlines configures these aircraft as a point of comparison. On the first class side, capacity is lower, with the carrier's seat map showing just one row of four spacious suites.

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

These are laid out in a 1-2-1 configuration, as are the 777-300ER's 48 business class flatbeds, which are split between the rear of the first cabin section and the whole of the second. Behind these are 28 premium economy recliners in a 2-4-2 layout, which occupy the front of the third section, followed by 184 economy seats in the rear of the third and the whole of the fourth section. A key reason for the lower capacity is the less dense 3-3-3 configuration in the economy class cabin.

#6200. JSX Adds Two Nonstop Routes From New City

JSX announced Tuesday that it will begin flying to New England for the first time in February 2027.

The carrier will operate from Jet Aviation’s terminal at Hanscom Field in Bedford, Massachusetts, northwest of Boston. Flights to Teterboro Airport in New Jersey will begin Feb. 8, with four flights on weekdays, two on Saturdays, and three on Sundays.

JSX markets the route as New York City service and requires passengers to sign up for its free Club JSX membership to book.

Service to Miami-Opa Locka Executive Airport will follow on Feb. 11, with one flight each day on Mondays and Thursdays through Sundays. JSX will use 30-seat aircraft on both routes.

“We’re excited JSX has chosen Hanscom to operate these flights to the New York and Florida markets,” Hanscom Field Director Chris Willenborg said in a statement.

JSX outlined its plans for Hanscom Field at an advisory commission meeting in September. At the time, the carrier was targeting a January launch and had also proposed flights to Naples, Florida. Naples was absent from Tuesday’s announcement.

#6199. Always-Sunny San Diego Keeps Getting Better—Here's How to Explore

San Diego's calendar of sunny days, endless string of beaches on which to enjoy them, and family-friendly attractions have long drawn visitors year-round to the city and surrounding county. Lately new, design-centric hotels and a growing slate of destination restaurants are joining the enduring pleasures to create an era of vibrancy for all travelers to enjoy.

A surfer emerges from the waters of La Jolla Cove

With walkable streets, vintage shops, and craft breweries, North Park and Hillcrest districts are also rich in restaurants and nightlife. In North Park, sample French bistro fare at the Smoking Goat or Iberian seafood at Mabel's Gone Fishing, then end at listening bar Part Time Lover. Hillcrest, the epicenter of the LGBTQ+ scene, is home to the Brass Rail, the city's first gay bar, and Urban Mo's Bar and Grill, a beloved hub.

Soaring sea cliffs and palm-lined boulevards are only part of La Jolla's appeal—visit arts and culture institutions like La Jolla Playhouse and the Museum of Contemporary Art, and try classic restaurants such as George's at the Cove or The Marine Room for lunch with a view.

Historic neighborhood Barrio Logan is the heart of the city's Mexican American culture. Grab a mocha at Por Vida and queue for tacos and tamales at Las Cuatro Milpas, a stalwart since 1933.

The vintage elegance of peninsula Coronado, long a vacation spot for the well-heeled, endures thanks to buzzy openings attracting visitors across the bridge for a stroll on palm-lined Orange Avenue.

Up the coast in North County, Encinitas is the quintessential Southern California beach town, a quirky little mecca for yoga, wellness, and, of course, surfing at beaches like Swami's and Moonlight.

Next door, find everything in Carlsbad from outlet shopping and golf to fine dining—don't miss chef Eric Bost's Michelin-starred bistro, Jeune et Jolie. He runs two other restaurants in the area: Lilo, with a coastal tasting menu, and lively Campfire, designed to look like a glamping site.

San Diego's biggest hotel news is coming out of Coronado. Few stays channel classic Americana quite like the Hotel del Coronado, which, over its 138-year history, has hosted everyone from Marilyn Monroe to Franklin D. Roosevelt. It underwent a massive revamp in 2025, but that's not the only change afoot here: Across the street the sleek Bower Coronado also began welcoming guests in summer 2025; it was joined by the maximalist, seashell-inspired Baby Grand this spring. Last May, Hilton's new Outset Collection unveiled The Margot Hotel, with 135 sprawling suites, in the Gaslamp Quarter, right by Petco Park, home of the Padres. January will see the debut of the nearby 231-room Le Méridien San Diego Pinnacle, a gleaming tower close to the trendy restaurants and nightlife of Little Italy. Up in Carlsbad, an erstwhile Sheraton resort was reborn in March as the botanical-themed Hotel Solea, Autograph Collection, a stone's throw from Legoland.

LA Bryson’s Nocturnal Nostalgia (2021), on display in Liberty Arts District

Everybody knows a visit to the world-class San Diego Zoo and a ballgame at Petco Park are must-dos, but there's much else to consider. With 17 museums dedicated to everything from science and architecture to world music and Comic Con spread throughout a 1,200-acre expanse, Balboa Park has enough going on to keep you busy for a whole visit. Cast a wider net and you'll find creativity surging all over the city. Set in the Spanish Colonial Revival–style former Naval Training Center, the Liberty Station Arts District was recognized this year as one of California's state-designated cultural districts, thanks to its dense concentration of galleries and performing arts venues. Up the coast in Oceanside—a thriving creative enclave that's home to the Oceanside Museum of Art and a downtown arts district splashed with dozens of murals—surfer Ryder England opened Dear Tomorrow, a community art house with residencies, a shop, and events including botanical dyeing and figure drawing. In the San Diego Black Art and Culture District in Encanto, celebrated street artist Maxx Moses established Graffiti Gardens, a vibrant community hub with plenty of alfresco space to showcase his murals. You'll find lots of murals in historic Barrio Logan too: In the 1970s artists and activists painted vast murals at the base of the San Diego–Coronado Bay Bridge; today Chicano Park is a National Historic Landmark. Nearby, in a 45,000-square-foot former bakery, James Brown and Isabel Dutra opened Bread and Salt, a sprawling center for experimental art and craftsmanship. Every second Saturday join the Barrio Art Crawl, which pops into galleries, breweries, and record shops throughout the neighborhood. But the city's biggest draw remains its natural beauty. Some of the best hiking trails are along the cliffs of Torrey Pines Natural Reserve, like the three-quarter-mile Beach Trail, which winds through clusters of pine trees and wildflowers on the way down to the sand. If you're inspired by the surf culture and want to hit the waves yourself, ease in at La Jolla Shores or Tourmaline Surfing Park, but if you're more seasoned, you can try your luck at Windansea Beach or Sunset Cliffs.

Handmade ravioli with sage from Dora Ristorante

The proximity to Tijuana—drive 20 minutes from downtown and you're at the border—means you can sample the full pantheon of regional Mexican flavors here, including at Nómada, in Carlsbad, chef Alex Carballo's ode to Sinaloan fire-based cooking, or Carne y Hueso, a new North Park restaurant from sisters Chantelle and Crystal Godinez, who champion indigenous ingredients from Puebla, Jalisco, and Oaxaca in dishes like bone marrow sopes with hand-pressed masa and huitlacoche tetela with mole rojo. There's also a bounty of impossibly fresh seafood plucked from the coast, like at By the Sea, which opened in August near the beach in Coronado in a second-floor dining room styled to resemble a Mediterranean villa. It's directly opposite another newcomer to Orange Avenue, the splashy alfresco Greek restaurant Night Hawk at the Baby Grand, complete with large Greek statues and seating in grottoes. À L'ouest, chef Brad Wise's boisterous brasserie, was a hit the second it touched down in North Park in February; upstairs, the speakeasy Georgette's makes the wait for a table much more fun. And eating out in La Jolla has never been more interesting, thanks to a host of new destination restaurants: Chef Travis Swikard's Fleurette serves French-Californian fare such as “Oeufs & Eggs” with San Diego uni; across the street from the La Jolla Playhouse, Dora Ristorante, named for chef Accursio Lota's Sicilian grandmother, dishes up perfect pretheater bites of house-made gnocchi with pork sausage sugo and Pecorino; and Lucien earned chef Elijah Arizmendi San Diego's only new Michelin star this year. Also on deck: the ambitious 5,000-square-foot Roseacre development with multiple concepts under one roof, led by chef Erik Anderson, previously of the Michelin-starred Coi in San Francisco. Over in Liberty Station, meanwhile, a former navy outpost in Point Loma is being reimagined with restaurants, galleries, shops, and gardens. In 2027 the long-awaited Admiral will open its doors here, while the eventual 2028 completion of the entire project will transform five vacant World War II–era buildings into a new arts and dining hub.

“I grew up surfing Pacific Beach, right next to Tourmaline Surfing Park. I surfed there once or twice a day, seven days a week. In La Jolla there's a place called Marine Street Beach, which is great for bodysurfing; you get barreled on every ride. Up in North County, Swami's Beach is more crowded—you'll see a lot of pros there.” —Travis Swikard, chef, Fleurette and Callie

“We have a lot of arts here: Balboa Park and the museums, La Jolla Playhouse producing pieces that end up on Broadway. The Symphony has gotten a lot of love, and at the Rady Shell at Jacobs Park, you can see everything from pop concerts to the most classical Rachmaninoff.” —Roxana Velásquez, Maruja Baldwin executive director and CEO, San Diego Museum of Art

“I was born and raised in San Diego, and I'm not leaving. Picking my favorite Mexican food is tricky. My go-to order at Roberto's is rolled tacos with guacamole and cheese, because that's what I grew up on. Mexico Viejo is one of the most solid taco-stand type of places—I get the bean-and-cheese and the rice-and-guacamole burrito.” —Tony Hawk, professional skateboarder

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

Travelers on United Airlines Flight 1252 from Washington to Chicago on Tuesday are in for a surprise.

They will be the first to depart from the spacious new E Gates at Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD), the first piece of the airport’s more than $20 billion redevelopment and the future center of United’s hub operation at the airport.

“It’s much more spacious,” Andrew Nocella, the chief commercial officer of United, said at a ribbon cutting on Monday. “The gate hold areas are large so there’s plenty of places to sit and there are all kinds of new, great restaurants to enjoy.”

In the news: United went big on credit cards in 2026. More changes are coming, MileagePlus boss says

Nocella added: “It’s the tip of the iceberg to the future development of Dulles.”

The redevelopment calls for the extension of the E Gates far to the west with room for up to 50 gates. The rest of IAD will also get a needed upgrade, including the modernization and expansion of Eero Saarinen's iconic terminal, an extension of the AeroTrain and a new international arrivals facility. The aim is to open all of this by the mid-2030s.

“This is the first step to retiring Concourse C-D [and] eliminating mobile lounges — someday," said Jack Potter, the CEO of IAD operator the Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority.

For now, though, the focus at Dulles is on the new E Gates. They're located directly above the AeroTrain station for Concourse C. That is possible because the station was built in 2010, a long walk to the south of the existing Concourse C with the plan to eventually build a concourse above it.

Travelers coming from the train enter the E Gates in a large, high-ceilinged atrium with the new United Club immediately to their right. At 40,000 square feet, the new lounge is the second largest in United's system after the one recently opened at Houston's George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH).

United's massive new Houston club: Inside the largest airline lounge in America

The look and feel of the lounge draws its aesthetic from the Washington, D.C., area. The entryway is inspired by the Washington Metro's vaulted subway stations; a cherry blossom mobile hangs in the central seating area; and a Blue Ridge Mountain-themed mural is painted on one of the walls.

"Lounges are very important to our customers," said Nocella. "You can see no design detail was left untouched" in the new E Gates lounge.

From the E Gates atrium, travelers make their way down the concourse itself. Gate areas are interspersed with concessions along the length. And, above, a sterile hallway takes arriving international travelers to the end of the concourse where they can board a mobile lounge to the international arrivals facility in the main terminal.

United will operate both international and domestic flights from the E Gates, Nocella said.

And, for design enthusiasts, the authority used Saarinen's original font for the gate numbers in the new concourse.

The E Gates will allow United to grow its hub at IAD. The airline plans to grow departures by about 20% next summer to around 300 daily flights, up from 250 earlier this year, Nocella said.

United will operate up to roughly 275 departures from IAD in November, schedule data from aviation analytics firm Cirium shows. In June 2027, the number jumps to as many as 290 a day though schedules remain in flux.

What the E Gates will not do is replace the six ground-level gates at the end of Concourse A — gates A1 to A6 — used by United Express regional jets. This was the original plan when the project was approved in the early 2020s.

Instead, United will use the new E Gates to "take the pressure off the C and D facility," Nocella said.

Potter, when asked when the airport authority will close the ground-level A Gates, said: "They’ll stay open until construction has proceeded sufficiently such that they can be relocated."

The authority aims to complete the build out of Concourse E, and the first phase of Concourse G further to the south, by 2030, Potter added.

United plans to expand its IAD hub to around 400 daily departures with all the new gates, Nocella said.

Asked when the airline would grow to 400 departures, he smiled and said they will unveil that at a "different announcement."
