#6172. Highest To Lowest: How To Get From JFK To Manhattan For Just $3

In the film Highest 2 Lowest (2025), starring Denzel Washington, legendary filmmaker Spike Lee portrays two distinct sides of New York City, depending on your altitude and bank account. Nowhere is that contrast more apparent than in the choices travelers face when commuting between Manhattan and John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK).

Whether you are a visiting traveler or an NYC resident, navigating to and from the city’s primary international hub is a perpetual balancing act between cost, comfort, and time. Previously, I detailed what is literally and figuratively the “highest” mode of airport transit: Blade’s helicopter transfers (starting at $195 and easily topping $300, though rides can cost you nothing out of pocket using Bilt Cash). Each Bilt Cash award expires 12 months after you earn it, on the last day of that month.

In this Reader Story, I’m taking you down, subterranean, to the lowest option available: the Metropolitan Transportation Authority’s (MTA) $3 bus-to-subway hack.

Duke Ellington was onto something: “Take the ‘A’ Train.” However, he didn’t specify which A train branch, nor did he mention that a quick bus transfer might be involved!

Even some locals may ask: “Wait, isn’t the AirTrain $8.75, plus a $3 subway fare?” That’s true if you exit the AirTrain at Jamaica or Howard Beach. However, there is a lesser-known and dramatically cheaper workaround: just $3 total from JFK to nearly anywhere in NYC with the MTA, provided you don’t mind adding a few extra minutes to your journey.

For the reverse trip, take any Lefferts Blvd-bound A train, ensuring the destination sign explicitly says “Lefferts Blvd” rather than Far Rockaway or Rockaway Park. Importantly, Far Rockaway A trains often display “JFK Airport” on their digital side displays because most travelers use the more expensive $8.75 Howard Beach transfer route, so do not board those if you want the $3-only route. Once on the correct train, get off at Liberty Ave / Lefferts Blvd, exit to the street, locate the bus stop, catch a JFK-bound Q10 or Q80 bus to the Lefferts AirTrain station, and take the free AirTrain directly to your terminal.

If you type “JFK Airport” into Google Maps or Apple Maps, the app will almost never display the $3-only hack. Navigation algorithms prioritize minimizing the number of transit transfers over saving money, automatically suppressing the bus transfer in favor of the standard $8.75 AirTrain connection at Jamaica or Howard Beach.

Even typing “Lefferts Blvd AirTrain Station” into navigation apps often causes confusion because the AirTrain station and the Ozone Park A-train terminal are located roughly 1.5 miles apart.

To force your map app to show the correct route, search for the street-level bus-to-subway transfer point at “Lefferts Blvd & Liberty Ave.” From JFK, this will display the Q10 Rush or Q80 bus taking you to the A train turnstiles; from Manhattan, it will guide you on the Lefferts-bound A train directly to your bus connection.

Other than extreme weather events, strikes, and major crises, all three legs of this route—the AirTrain, the Q10/Q80 bus, and the A Train—operate 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, though timing varies. During daytime and peak hours (6:00 AM – 10:00 PM), AirTrain cars run every 7–10 minutes, Q10 and Q80 buses depart roughly every 8–15 minutes, and A trains run frequently as express services through Brooklyn and Manhattan.

However, late-night transit frequency changes significantly in NYC, so keep that in mind for overnight or early-morning flights: AirTrain headways drop to 15–20 minute intervals, late-night Q10/Q80 bus departures stretch to every 20–30 minutes, and the A train may shift to local-only service (check MTA Service Status for possible re-routings).

Thanks to the flat-fare structure of the New York City Subway (as opposed to distance-based transit networks found in cities like London, Tokyo, or Washington, D.C.), that single $3 fare (and free transfer) unlocks access to nearly the entire city once you pass through the turnstiles at the Ozone Park–Lefferts Boulevard station.

Because there are no exit turnstiles or zone caps inside the subway network, you can ride from Queens through Brooklyn, up Manhattan, and deep into the Bronx, all on that same initial $3 tap—as long as you stay within the fare-paid zone. And, if you exit the subway system in Lower Manhattan, you can walk over to Whitehall Terminal and board the free Staten Island Ferry to reach the fifth and final borough. While attempting to tap onto a Staten Island bus or the Staten Island Railway (SIR) on the other side would consume a second $3 fare (and likely break the 2-hour transfer clock), at least JFK to Manhattan for $3 remains one of the greatest transit bargains in the world.

All told—AirTrain, bus, and subway—you can get between JFK and Manhattan in about 75 to 90 minutes. Depending on brutal rush-hour highway traffic, you might even tie or beat a $100+ rideshare. That said, I would recommend this route exclusively for those traveling light (backpacks and carry-ons), willing to spend the extra time, and comfortable navigating city transit. But for the right traveler, it is a relatively safe, clean, reliable, and wildly affordable hack.

To put the $3 bus-to-subway hack into perspective, it helps to see how it stacks up against the other primary options for traveling between Manhattan and JFK:

Of course, there are other, less conventional ways of getting to and from JFK:

Whether taking a $300+ helicopter ride or a $3 bus-to-subway hack, commuting between JFK and Manhattan truly captures the two contrasting sides of New York City that Spike Lee brings to life in Highest 2 Lowest.

For light packers on a budget, the Lefferts Boulevard Q10 transfer stands as the undefeated champion of pure value. Duke Ellington was right all along—if you want to get to Sugar Hill or anywhere else in the city without breaking the bank, simply take the “A” train!

With so many options available, what’s your preferred way of getting to or from JFK, and which are your preferred payment methods to maximize value?

Eight articles of impeachment against Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth have been proposed in the House by Representative Thomas Massie, a libertarian Republican from Kentucky who lost his seat when the president pushed for his ouster in a primary earlier this year. #6169. The Runway Grooves That Help Commercial Jets Stop During Heavy Rain

RonaldoSoffel | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

The United States helped to pioneer runway grooving in an attempt to improve aircraft traction and water drainage. NASA's Wallops research runway carried out almost 200 braking tests with a McDonnell Douglas F-4D Phantom II fighter and a four-engine Convair 990 airliner.

It was found that grooves substantially increase the braking capability of heavy jet-powered aircraft on wet, flooded, and slushy surfaces. Over the history of aviation, a variety of runway cuts were used, including square grooves, V-shaped grooves, and trapezoidal grooves. Eventually, the FAA settled on the straight-line grooves common at airports today.

However, grooves are not the only way to achieve sufficient traction, with their effectiveness waxing and waning depending on the climate and other factors. Overall, it appears the worldwide trend in the 2010s and 2020s is for grooved runways to become more common, although it is difficult to quantify.

Some roadways, certain footpaths, and some runways have small grooves cut across them to improve traction and water drainage. These are designed to give rainwater a way out from under an aircraft's tires and to improve its traction. The key issue they are designed to solve is hydroplaning. At high enough speeds on a wet runway, an aircraft's tire footprint can lift off the pavement and ride on a layer of water.

Typical FAA specifications for transverse grooves are approximately 1/4 inch (6.4 mm) in width and depth and 1.5 inches (38 mm) in spacing. A 1997 FAA Advisory Circular titled 'Measurement, Construction, and Maintenance of Skid-Resistant Airport Pavement Surfaces' noted that:

"With the introduction of turbojet aircraft, braking performance on pavement surfaces has become more critical. Under certain conditions, hydroplaning or unacceptable loss of traction can occur, resulting in poor braking performance and possible loss of directional control."

It adds that NASA, the FAA, the USAF, and various foreign governments conducted a series of research projects that concentrated on two main areas. One was high skid-resistant pavement, and the other was "application of proper maintenance techniques and procedures." It asserts that runway grooves are a proven and effective technique for providing skid resistance and preventing hydroplaning during wet weather.

The 1997 FAA paper discusses the grooving techniques. These include cutting or forming grooves in existing or new pavement. Grooves in new PCC pavement need to be formed while the concrete is still plastic, while grooves in HMA pavement need to be saw-cut. It said that all runways that served or were expected to serve turbojet aircraft were considered a high priority for grooving.

Existing runways without grooving also had to be modified as soon as practical. The paper noted that some existing pavements may have surfaces that are now suitable for sawing grooves. It recommended that studies should be done to determine whether they could be overlaid or rehabilitated to allow grooving.

The need for grooves on runways that do not serve turbojets was not automatic and depended on circumstances. As mentioned below, this does not apply to US Navy or Air Force runways used by commercial airlines.

FAA groove specifications for transverse grooves (per FAA)

1.5 inches (3.8 cm) apart, center to center

Today, grooving is very common around the world at major commercial airports, although it is not fully universal (even among major international airports). Grooving at general aviation airports is considerably less common. It is particularly common in commercial airports in the United States, partly due to the FAA taking a particularly strong position on the matter.

Oceanic airspace is a challenging place to be, far away from civilization and communication outposts. Before entering, pilots reduce speed, but why?

In Europe and other international airports, grooving may be less common than in the United States. ICAO's international standards are less prescriptive than the FAA's, although it recognizes grooving as a way to improve wet-runway braking. It stops short of making conventional grooving universally mandatory.

Europe's EASA sees grooving as one possible method to improve runway friction and surface texture. Canada's Transportation Safety Board states that grooving reduces the potential for both dynamic and viscous hydroplaning by providing a place (such as grooves) where water can escape from underneath tires.

However, it explicitly states that "runway grooving is not a requirement for new or existing runway pavement in Canada." The FAA paper above was published in 1997, but it wasn't until 2013 that Ottawa International Airport became the first airport in Canada to groove its runway. Despite being often wet, Canada is a strong example that has historically resisted mandated grooving.

Instead, it has been content to leave it as an option. China is an example of a country that prefers alternative treatments such as stone mastic asphalt and other textured pavement surfaces. France also uses specialized asphalt surfacing as an alternative. A 2010 Canadian safety investigation found that grooving is present at almost all major airports in the US, UK, continental Europe, Australia, and Japan.

Most small general aviation airports do not have grooved runways, and this is driven by several practical reasons. One is that light aircraft have a lower landing weight and speed than commercial airlines and so are less susceptible to hydroplaning. Another is that low traffic volume may not justify the costs of grooving.

Engineers often assess that these airports are built with pavement characteristics that already provide adequate friction and drainage without the need for grooves. Some airports achieve adequate wet-weather friction through alternative surface treatments. These include porous friction course.

Here, a porous asphalt overlay allows water drainage, concrete texturing, surface aggregate selection, and runway gradients. With concrete texturing, concrete can be finished with wire combing or tining, creating a textured surface. General aviation aircraft are actually quite vulnerable to runway skidding and hydroplaning, but grooving is not necessarily seen as the way to address this.

Much of the issue stems from light aircraft often lacking anti-skid braking systems, operating from shorter and less frequently maintained runways, and their relatively small tires. Without anti-skid braking, if a pilot applies too much braking on a slippery surface, the wheels can lock and skid. After a wheel locks, its braking effectiveness tends to deteriorate. Making matters worse, locked wheels make directional control more difficult and make the aircraft vulnerable to crosswinds.

A landing starts 120 miles from the airport at 35,000 feet. Here is what pilots do between cruise and touchdown to set it up.

One of the main disadvantages of grooves is maintenance. Rubber from the aircraft tires accumulates in the grooves, especially at the touchdown zones. This can reduce their effectiveness over time. Consequently, grooves can add yet more maintenance for the airport. There are some other disadvantages of grooving beyond construction costs and maintenance, although they are typically manageable.

For instance, it can damage the pavement, add foreign object debris by accumulating rubber, slightly increase tire noise, and other minor considerations. One of the biggest cases against them is when the climate is dry. Wet airports like those in the US Pacific Northwest and Northern Europe can benefit from grooving. However, this does not transfer to dry airports, such as those in Saudi Arabia, Egypt, or Arizona.

With that being said, these areas can experience flash flooding, making grooving momentarily useful. At the same time, desert and sandy environments can increase the contamination problem, with grooves accumulating sand. A residual benefit is that in colder climates where there is ice and snow, grooves can retain anti-icing and de-icing chemicals. They can help drain melted snow and ice.

Modern airliners can lose traction on wet surfaces, but in cases where accidents have happened, hydroplaning is often seen as one contributing factor. Modern jets come with anti-skid braking, ground spoilers, thrust reversers, and autobrakes. Since 2000, one of the most notable incidents came in 2019, when a Boeing 737 operating as Miami Air International flight 293 overran the wet and ungrooved runway at Jacksonville.

The aircraft overran the runway into the St. Johns River, although there were no serious injuries. This accident happened at a US Navy airfield, not Jacksonville International Airport, and so was not covered under the 1997 FAA regulations. The NTSB report states that:

"The NTSB determined that the probable cause of the 2019 runway overrun of the Boeing 737 in Jacksonville, Florida, was, in part, 'an extreme loss of braking friction due to heavy rain and the water depth on the ungrooved runway, which resulted in viscous hydroplaning.'"

Another hydroplaning incident involved United Express in Ottawa in 2010, when an Embraer aircraft overran the wet and ungrooved runway. As previously noted, Ottawa became Canada's first airport with a grooved runway in 2013. Other notable incidents on this front included American Airlines flight 331 at Kingston (2009) and Southwest Airlines flight 1919 in Chicago (2011).

Found an error? Send it info@simpleflying.com so it can be corrected.

Elsewhere, Virgin Australia suffered a similar occurrence on New Zealand's then-ungrooved Christchurch runway in 2015. The Australian Transport Safety Bureau found that Virgin Australia's company policy at the time treated damp runways as dry, leading to a miscalculation of landing performance requirements and high crew workload during a revised approach.

When it comes to earning credit card rewards, sometimes two cards really are better than one.

Maybe you have a card that earns bonus points on dining and groceries but falls short on other everyday purchases. Or perhaps you love your card's travel perks but wish it offered better earning rates outside of travel.

That's where pairing cards can come in handy. By choosing two cards with complementary benefits and earning categories, you can get more out of your spending without relying on a single card for everything.

Here are three American Express card combinations worth considering, depending on your spending habits and travel goals.

Frequent travelers who want a combination of premium travel benefits and strong everyday earning rates may get the most value from pairing the with the .

The Platinum is, at its core, a travel and lifestyle card that offers access to an extensive network of airport lounges worldwide through the Global Lounge Collection, along with a range of statement credits and other travel benefits.

The Gold fills an important gap in the Platinum's earning structure. It earns 4 points per dollar spent at restaurants worldwide and at U.S. supermarkets (on up to $50,000 and $25,000 in purchases per calendar year, respectively*).

*Then 1 point per dollar spent for the rest of the year

By using the Platinum for eligible flights and the Gold for dining and groceries, you can earn elevated rewards across several major spending categories while enjoying premium travel benefits. Since both cards earn Membership Rewards points, you can also combine your rewards into one balance to use toward travel through Amex's transfer partners (after linking your accounts online).

The trade-off of this card combination is cost. The Platinum has an $895 annual fee, while the Gold has a $325 annual fee, bringing the combined annual cost to $1,220. For that reason, I'd only recommend this pairing to travelers who can take advantage of the Platinum's benefits and who regularly spend in the Gold's bonus categories.

If you spend a lot on dining and groceries but want to earn more than 1 point per dollar spent on other eligible purchases, the and could make a great pair.

The Gold earns 4 points per dollar spent at restaurants worldwide (on up to $50,000 in purchases per calendar year*) and at U.S. supermarkets (on up to $25,000 in purchases per calendar year*). It also earns 3 points per dollar spent on flights booked directly with airlines or through amextravel.com or the Amex Travel App™.

Then, use the Blue Business Plus for eligible business purchases that would earn only 1 point per dollar on the Gold. It earns 2 points per dollar spent (on the first $50,000 in eligible purchases each calendar year*) compared with the Gold's standard earning rate of 1 point per dollar spent.

*Then 1 point per dollar spent for the rest of the year

Since both cards earn Membership Rewards points, you can build up a single rewards balance to use toward travel through Amex's airline and hotel transfer partners.

The Gold has a $325 annual fee, while the Blue Business Plus has no annual fee, so you won't pay extra to add a flat-rate earning card to the mix.

Just keep in mind that the Blue Business Plus is a business card, so you'll need to qualify to apply. This combination could be especially useful for freelancers and small-business owners with eligible business expenses that don't fall into the Gold's bonus categories.

If your business spends a lot on things like advertising, software or gas, the and could make a great pair.

The Business Gold earns 4 Membership Rewards points per dollar spent in the two eligible categories where your business spends the most each billing cycle (on up to $150,000 in combined purchases per calendar year*).

*Then 1 point per dollar spent for the rest of the year

What I like about the Business Gold is that you don't have to choose your bonus categories in advance. Amex automatically determines your top two eligible categories each billing cycle, which is helpful if your business expenses change from month to month.

For purchases outside those categories, the Blue Business Plus earns 2 points per dollar spent (on the first $50,000 in eligible purchases each calendar year*). That's double the Business Gold's standard earning rate of 1 point per dollar spent.

*Then 1 point per dollar spent for the rest of the year

For example, you might use the Business Gold for advertising and software expenses, then switch to the Blue Business Plus for other eligible business purchases. Since both cards earn Membership Rewards points, you can build up one balance to use with Amex's airline and hotel transfer partners.

The Business Gold has a $375 annual fee, while the Blue Business Plus has no annual fee. This combination makes the most sense if you spend enough in the Business Gold's bonus categories to justify the annual fee while using the Blue Business Plus to earn more on other purchases.

Before adding another Amex card to your wallet, take a look at where you're spending the most money and what you want to get out of your rewards. The goal is to find a card that fills a gap in your current lineup, rather than one that offers more of the same.

And remember, earning more points isn't worth it if you're spending more than you normally would or carrying a balance and paying interest.

Related: Best credit card strategies for couples

There's no one-size-fits-all approach to choosing the best credit card combination. The key is finding cards that complement each other rather than simply offer more of the same benefits.

Whether you're looking for premium travel perks, stronger everyday earning rates or a way to maximize rewards on business expenses, pairing the right Amex cards can help you earn more Membership Rewards points.

Just make sure the additional rewards and benefits are worth the combined annual fees and that you're choosing cards that make sense for your spending habits.

#6167. Which Airlines Are Dry (No Alcohol)? Can You Bring Your Own Alcohol?

For many people, alcohol is an aspect of traveling by air that they enjoy. I’m not just talking about first or business class travel, where a glass of champagne might be part of the fun. Airports are also one of the few places where you can have a drink at 5AM and not be judged (too hard).

Admittedly customs differ around the globe, based on culture, religion, etc. In this post, I thought it would be interesting to talk a bit about dry airlines, as there’s a bit of nuance to this.

Which airlines don’t serve alcohol onboard? Which airlines don’t serve alcohol but let you bring your own alcohol? And does all of this even matter?

Let’s start by taking a look at the airlines that are dry, meaning that they don’t serve you alcohol. Here are the airlines that come to mind:

Admittedly that list isn’t totally exhaustive, since there are a countless number of small airlines out there. However, I think this covers the biggest and most interesting airlines that don’t serve alcohol (though if I missed any major ones, please let me know).

There’s an interesting twist to this. While some airlines are dry, they’ll let you bring your own alcohol onboard, and then you can consume it (within reason). The following three international carriers come to mind:

Now, it’s important to note that this isn’t without strings attached:

When I flew Kuwait Airways several years back, I wrote about how we brought a bottle of wine onboard, and they gladly let us consume it. It’s not that I couldn’t be without alcohol, but I was curious to experience a BYOB concept on a plane, since that was novel for me.

There’s an added layer of complexity to all of this, as there are some airlines that aren’t generally dry, but are dry on certain routes. Several situations come to mind (let me know if I’m missing any):

As you can tell, in some of the above situations, the lack of alcohol presumably has little to do with religion or concerns over behavior, and more to do with controlling costs.

People have different takes as to how “bad” it is to fly on a dry airline. On the one end of the spectrum, there are people who will avoid dry airlines at all costs. On the other end of the spectrum, you have billions of people who don’t drink alcohol at all, so this is a non-issue.

Personally I’m probably somewhere in the middle:

Regarding that last point, I do have to give credit to airlines that are dry, but still put effort into their drink selection. Take Saudia, for example, which goes above and beyond in terms of its non-alcoholic drink selection in premium cabins, with everything from cappuccinos and espressos, to excellent mocktails, to non-alcoholic wine.

Airlines often reflect their local customs and religions, so it’s not surprising that many airlines don’t serve alcohol onboard. If you definitely want alcohol when you fly, avoid airlines like Saudia. If you would like a drink when you fly, the good news is that some dry airlines actually let you bring your own alcohol, within certain limitations.

While the above doesn’t cover 100% of situations, hopefully it’s a useful, basic rundown of some of the bigger airlines that are dry.

How strongly do you feel about dry airlines? Does this policy impact your airline choice?

#6165. The Don Jr. Wedding May Be the Emblem of a Corrupt Age

‘Hogs get slaughtered,’ as the old saying goes — people will tolerate graft only up to a point.

Donald Trump Jr. and his wife, Bettina Anderson, disembark from Air Force One at Dublin Airport in Dublin, Ireland, September 12, 2026.

On May 31, 1871, William Marcy Tweed threw a spectacularly lavish wedding for his daughter, Mary Amelia, in New York City. “Boss” Tweed was then at the height of his power as the political master of New York City, its ruling Democratic Party, and its Tammany Hall machine. Elected to the U.S. House at 29 in 1852, he sacrificed his career in Washington to vote for the Kansas–Nebraska Act, which was massively unpopular in the North. This was not a stance on principle: The vote was a test of party loyalty, and the Pierce administration paid off Tweed by appointing a friend to a job as postmaster. Returning home to New York, Tweed was running Tammany Hall by 1858.

The corruption he oversaw was immense. It at least doubled the cost of building anything that the city could touch. The Tweed Courthouse cost some $13-14 million to build, twice the cost of the Alaska Purchase during the same period. David McCullough argued in The Great Bridge that the Brooklyn Bridge would never have been completed had the Tweed Ring not fallen early in its construction. Tweed and his cronies were convicted of stealing tens of millions of dollars — some modern estimates place the real amount in the hundreds of millions — which would be worth billions today. Alfred Ely Beach, who published Scientific American, decided to build a pioneering subway line between 1868 and 1870, powered by an immense pneumatic tube, and to avoid paying off Tweed, he built it like a bank heist, removing the dirt at night and not telling the city what he was building until it was ready for passengers.

Dan McLaughlin is a senior writer at National Review Online and a fellow at National Review Institute.

#6164. Military Member Calls Alaska Airlines Employee “Anti-Military” Over Denied Free Upgrade

A military member and social media influencer has taken to Instagram to complain about a recent interaction with an Alaska Airlines employee, where he asked for a free upgrade, and was denied. He’s accusing an employee at the airline of being anti-military. Is that a fair complaint, or is this being blown out of proportion?

A military member posted a 2min35sec video online, outlining his experience with an Alaska Airlines representative at Portland International Airport (PDX), which he claims was his first time encountering an “anti-military” employee at the airline. To summarize his version of events:

You can see the video for yourself below. As you’d expect, this guy’s followers are mostly military related, so the 1,300+ comments on the post are almost entirely in agreement with the person who posted the video.

First let me say that I of course respect and appreciate the service of those who are in the military (even if I fundamentally disagree with the extent to which we get into conflicts that accomplish nothing — that’s the fault of our elected leaders, and not the fault of those who put their lives on the line).

Of course if the Alaska Airlines employee in question was rude, that’s not acceptable, and people expect polite service. Now, I’m a little skeptical of how much of a direct transcript this was, rather than how this guy chose to interpret it. That includes things like him suggesting that the Alaska employee accused him of lying. If that were the case, that’s unacceptable, but again, it’s not clear if that was actually said, or just how he was made to feel.

All that being said, this guy sort of strikes me as being rather entitled. Airlines are extremely generous with active duty military members, as they should be. The airline has a page that outlines military and veteran benefits, and upgrades isn’t among those perks. The airline offers all kinds of other things, ranging from special fares, to lounge access, to priority boarding. But it seems a little greedy to then be like “oh, they do all these things, but they should do more” (since he chooses to reference this page).

But here’s my bigger issue with this guy’s approach. I don’t think there’s anything wrong with asking for an upgrade, but be ready to be shot down. However, I feel like his approach is more one of entitlement than “it can’t hurt to ask.” Why do I say that?

The very example he gives is that for all these times he flies Alaska, either they say “sure, we’ll upgrade you,” or they say “sorry, it’s full, we can’t upgrade you.” In other words, he assumes he’s entitled to the upgrade as long as there are open seats, which just isn’t the policy. If he’s going to be rejected for something he’s not entitled to, he wants to be lied to, rather than told “sorry, that’s not our policy.”

And again, he emphasizes how he has no level of entitlement, but also then argues by pointing out that he has been upgraded for free in the past. It all sounds to me a little like being caught with a liquid that’s too large at the TSA checkpoint, and then trying to argue with them, and say “well last time they let me through.” Well, that’s fine, but that’s not the policy.

So my take here is that airline employees should of course always be professional. I think it’s perfectly fine to say “I’m sorry, that’s not our policy,” which is something this guy seems to take issue with. If the employee did actually accuse him of lying about being upgraded in the past, that’s of course not acceptable. But I’m also not convinced that actually happened.

A military member has accused an Alaska Airlines employee of being anti-military, after being denied a free upgrade to a seat with more legroom. He argues that there’s no harm in asking, but also seems to think that the only acceptable rejection is a claim that the cabin is full.

While Alaska offers lots of perks to military members (as they should), upgrades isn’t among them. Asking once is one thing, but I do find it a bit entitled to essentially believe that you’re entitled to the seats as long as they’re empty, and then to argue if you’re not upgraded.

What do you make of this “anti-military” Alaska employee?

#6163. Atmos Global Concierge: Alaska Airlines’ New Invitation-Only Elite Status

Alaska Airlines is increasingly becoming like the “big three” US carriers when it comes to its route network, as the airline expands globally, following its takeover of Hawaiian Airlines. Now the airline is doing another thing you’ll find at competitors, which is introducing an invitation-only elite status. Let’s take a look at what we know so far about Atmos Global Concierge, which is the name of this new status.

Some Atmos Rewards members on Reddit are reporting receiving an invitation for the carrier’s new status tier that has no published qualification requirements, and it’s above the Titanium tier. Those who have been awarded the status can keep it through December 31, 2027.

So, what are the perks of Atmos Global Concierge status?

We’ll have to of course wait some time to get firsthand reports of the experience, but as you’d expect, this is a lot more about better “soft” treatment, plus having top priority for everything. There’s nothing particularly remarkable about this status otherwise, but that’s not surprising, since that’s typically not the focus on invitation-only elite status.

It’s anyone’s guess what exactly it takes to get an invitation, as it’s a bit of a mystery, much like with American Concierge Key, Delta 360, and United Global Services. It’s possible that criteria differ based on where you mostly fly out of. It does seem like frequent international travel in business class is something that increases odds of eligibility.

Based on the reports so far, it almost seems like this status is being dangled as a “carrot” for those who have maybe taken a few long haul business class trips, in hopes of keeping them flying on Alaska and Hawaiian.

There’s a reason that airlines offer invitation-only elite status, and it’s kind of brilliant. The idea is to keep people on the “hamster wheel,” and keep them booking high yield tickets on an airline over competitors.

Airlines of course have elite tiers with published requirements, and once you qualify for your planned tier for a year, you might consider branching out and booking another airline. But when there’s invitation-only elite status, you don’t know what you actually need to earn it, so you’re more likely to keep flying with the airline. And if you’re spending other people’s money, you’re also more likely to make sure that ticket is expensive as it should be.

At the end of the day, these kinds of status tiers aren’t really about the exact details of the perks. On some level, they’re intended to stroke the egos of travelers, and that works. People get excited when they get to board a flight first, etc., and this whole concept plays into that.

Alaska Airlines has introduced a new invitation-only elite status, named Atmos Global Concierge. The idea is that this is targeted primarily at those flying a lot internationally, and it offers perks like concierge assistance, upgrade priority, some partner elite perks, and more.

With the way Alaska has grown, it’s not surprising to see the airline also copying the “big three” with a status tier like this.

What do you make of Atmos Global Concierge?

#6162. British Airways Unveils 7 New International Routes: See Full List Now

British Airways has disclosed five new or returning routes. Not only are they from London Heathrow and London City, but also from Edinburgh and Glasgow. BA mainline and BA CityFlyer will operate them.

Other routes have already been revealed for 2027. BA will relaunch flights from Heathrow to Melbourne, this time via Kuala Lumpur rather than Singapore, while beginning service from London Gatwick to Kilimanjaro and Zanzibar.

On April 15, BA will take off from Heathrow to Bergen. Not only does Bergen have the second most populous metro population in Norway, but it is also a significant tourist destination for the highly beautiful fjords and cruises. BA will fly five times weekly, mainly on the Airbus A319. The lack of consistency in the following schedule is, of course, primarily due to LHR's renowned slot shortage.

This is not a new route for BA. OAG shows that the oneworld member previously flew from Heathrow to Bergen between 2012 and 2017, with up to two daily flights. BA had inherited the short route from bmi, which had served it from early 2011. BA will be one of only two operators from London to the Scandinavian city next year, joining Norwegian to Gatwick.

Then there's the Greek tourist destination of Skiathos, which is reasonably well-known for the very low final approach over a road. It is the St. Maarten of Europe. Covering 1,245 nautical miles (2,306 km), BA will operate three times weekly using the A320neo from May 20. It'll replace London City-Skiathos, which BA CityFlyer has served since 2017.

Significantly, it'll be the first time that the UK's busiest airport has had flights to Skiathos. While subject to change and reflecting the extent of higher-end premium leisure travel, Heathrow will now have nonstop flights to 12 destinations in Greece. Only Gatwick and Stansted will have a more extensive network (16 destinations).

All the following additions involve BA CityFlyer, whose fleet consists entirely of the 106-seat Embraer E190 due to its London City operations. On May 1, the regional jet unit will take off from London City to Perugia, with a weekly operation.

It'll replace Heathrow-Perugia flights, which have operated since 2022. This will be the first time the Italian destination has been served from LCY. The 'downtown' London airport will now have flights to four cities in Italy.

On May 15, BA CityFlyer will introduce a weekly service from Edinburgh to Split and Glasgow to Nice. Using aircraft that would otherwise be grounded for half the weekend due to London City's closure, the BA unit is used to flying from airports across the UK on weekends, especially during the summer. However, it appears that summer activity from Stansted has been axed next year.

One of the airlines has cut more routes than the other two carriers combined. Find out which here!

Reflecting what is known as of November 11, BA will introduce the following routes in 2027. Flights from Heathrow to Melbourne will resume after a 20-year absence. Significantly, BA will follow the launch of fellow oneworld member Finnair, which debuted in Melbourne at the end of October 2026.

One of the most notable developments is BA's return to Tanzania. The airline last flew there in 2013, when it served Dar es Salaam, which is the largest city but not the capital. Things will be very different in 2027, when BA will fly to tourist-driven Kilimanjaro and Zanzibar. The operating Triple Seven will fly Gatwick-Kilimanjaro-Zanzibar-Gatwick. You can read more about the new offering here.

Who’s ready for first class on United Airlines’s smallest regional jet?

The first Mitsubishi CRJ-450, a premium variant of the CRJ-200, is “on track” to begin carrying passengers by the end of the year. That's according to Andrew Nocella, United's chief commercial officer, who discussed the arrival of the CRJ-450 on the sidelines of the  brand-new E Concourse at Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD) on Monday.

The plane will debut at the airline’s Chicago O’Hare International Airport (ORD) hub, he added.

First look: United unveils gorgeous new Washington Dulles concourse, massive lounge

“It’ll be very exciting and it’s really critical that we connect big cities to little cities, and that’s what the CRJ-450 allows us to do,” said Nocella.

Nocella did not say where the CRJ-450 could fly from ORD but it is widely expected to serve some of the smallest cities in United's network, for example Akron-Canton, Ohio, or Fort Wayne, Indiana.

United unveiled the CRJ-450 in March in an effort to expand its premium offerings to smaller markets. Instead of the usual 50 economy seats on the CRJ-200, the 450 has seven first-class, 16 extra-legroom economy and 18 economy seats — for a total of 41 — a luggage closet for carry ons and high-speed Starlink inflight WiFi.

United's new CRJ-450: Could this be the fanciest regional jet in America?

The CRJ-450 is essentially a premium overhaul to the standard CRJ-200 that has been a workhorse of regional flying for much of this centutry. Passengers have routinely disliked the CRJ-200 for being small and cramped, an experience United hopes to improve with the less-dense CRJ-450 variant.

The plane is similar to the CRJ-550, a 50-seat premium variant of the CRJ-700 that typcially seats around 70 passengers. United debuted the CRJ-550 in 2019.

The CRJ-450 is the smallest plane in United’s premium airplane menu. Larger offerings include the Airbus A321neo “Coastliner” for premium domestic routes, the A321XLR for long-haul routes and up to the Boeing 787-9s with the “elevated” interior that features the new Polaris Studio in business class.

“We have realized that the demand for premium was much higher than we ever knew,” United CEO Scott Kirby, said in March. “It’s like we’re finally creating supply to meet the demand for premium.”

United regional affiliate SkyWest Airlines will operate the first 40 CRJ-450s under the United Express brand. The first two CRJ-200s are undergoing the necessary modifications and certification at one of the Utah-based regional carrier’s maintenance facilities, SkyWest President Wade Steel said at the end of October.

“The first airplanes just take longer naturally just because you’re working through the first-time issues,” he explained. Subsequent CRJ-200 conversions will take 2 to 3 weeks.

Steel, and SkyWest CEO Chip Childs, emphasized that the first CRJ-450s would enter service with United by the end of the year despite at the time having only about eight weeks left in 2026.

Both executives were bullish on the opportunity for the CRJ-450. Steel estimated demand for around 100 aircraft in the coming years as major airlines seek to increase premium offerings across their fleets.

“Putting first class seats on a CRJ-200 in a very good LOPA [Layout of Passenger Accommodation] with an outstanding interior is a very valuable aircraft,” said Steel

Delta Air Lines, for example, joined United in offering the CRJ-550 on regional routes in 2024. SkyWest flies the CRJ-550 for Delta.

American Airlines is the only major U.S. carrier not offering the CRJ-550. However, the airline can fly more larger regional jets, particularly the Embraer E175, than either Delta or United under a more lenient contract with its pilots.

#6159. Alaska Airlines Launches Global Concierge—Its Answer To United Global Services And American ConciergeKey

Alaska Airlines has started inviting customers into Atmos Global Concierge, its new unpublished invitation-only top tier status along the lines of United Global Services, American Airlines ConciergeKey and Delta 360. The first reports point to an effort to win expensive international business class tickets, with benefits that include a next-flight guarantee during travel disruptions, dedicated assistance and Avis Chairman’s Club. Some of the early reaction has been that the benefits look underwhelming. I disagree. I used to have Avis Chairman’s Club, and it was special. And American’s next-flight guarantee came through for me when I needed it, having this benefit at Alaska could be really clutch. Invitations started surfacing November 9. One recipient shared this language: As one of our most valued status holders, you’ve been selected for two exceptional privileges: a complimentary upgrade to Atmos Titanium status and an inaugural membership in Atmos Global Concierge, our most elevated level of service. The invitation emphasizes travel across Europe, Asia and Oceania, backed by a dedicated team. Global Concierge membership begins immediately and runs through December 31, 2027. You’re invited to ATMOS GLOBAL CONCIERGE by u/iZoooom in AlaskaAirlines Alaska is giving these customers Titanium status and Global Concierge membership. What Atmos Global Concierge Members Get An invited member posted the following benefits in the discussion. Direct access to a concierge team. Proactive itinerary monitoring. A next-flight guarantee. Arrival assistance at destinations in Asia, Europe and Oceania. A car transfer at London Heathrow for tight connections. Upgrade priority on global flights. CLEAR+ membership. Avis Chairman’s Club. Another recipient reports already communicating with the team through WhatsApp. The original poster also mentioned luggage tags and being able to nominate their child for Gold status. Benefits disclosed so far lean heavily toward international service. We haven’t seen a promise of a separate boarding group, new lounge access or expanded award availability. That makes this closer, structurally, to a service overlay like Delta 360 than proof of a fully developed fifth elite tier. Who’s Getting Invited? There’s no published spending threshold. Reports suggest that expensive international business class travel matters more than a large status-point balance. The member who posted the invitation hadn’t yet reached Titanium. They expected to get there in another two weeks. They buy last-minute business class tickets to Europe and Asia, flying Alaska as well as British Airways and Japan Airlines, and hold the Atmos Summit card. They’d been trying Alaska’s Seattle–London service after years of flying British Airways. Another invitee reported more than 150,000 status points, almost all from international business class, with frequent travel to or through Heathrow and a shift toward Alaska for most flights. A Seattle-based member with more than 170,000 status points received an invitation, with roughly half the points coming from flying and promotions and half from the Summit card. Another recipient reported 261,507 status points and had already contacted the concierge team through WhatsApp. Meanwhile, a member with more than 400,000 status points, all from coach travel, reported no invitation. Neither did a Seattle-based member with 205,000 status points who said nearly all their flying was paid international business class booked two to three weeks before departure, mostly on partners but increasingly on Alaska. This fits with Alaska’s investment in premium cabins and a new Seattle business class lounge. Avis Chairman’s Club May Be The Sleeper Benefit It’s easy to skim past rental car status in an airline benefits list. We’re used to getting rental car elite cards bundled with credit cards and other memberships. Avis Chairman’s Club is nice. I used to have it. When I wrote about the program in 2007, I enjoyed upgrading a midsize reservation to the best eligible car on the lot, guaranteed availability, car delivery within 25 miles, and a valet ride back to the terminal. A manager would generally meet you at the car and help with your luggage. By 2009 I was also writing about an unpublished benefit I enjoyed: paying market price for gas. I could return the car without filling it myself and avoid the usual punitive rental car refueling price. The terminal ride was great also. You could return the car and be driven to your airline, without unloading everything to board a rental car shuttle. The Next-Flight Guarantee Could Matter Even More For an airline building a long haul network, recovery when something goes wrong matters a great deal. A missed departure can cost a full day. A dedicated phone number helps, but what matters is whether the person answering can get you onto a flight that another agent can’t book. I don’t yet have Alaska’s guarantee terms. But confirming a seat on a sold-out flight means getting where you’re going when other travelers wouldn’t. I’ve experienced what American Airlines’ ConciergeKey next-flight guarantee can do. My Austin–Miami flight was cancelled while I was on the jet bridge. Storms were disrupting Miami, and every alternative was sold out. I called the ConciergeKey desk and they confirmed me on the next nonstop to Miami, even though it was full. Alaska Airlines has grown up, with premium international service and now a service tier for its top elite customers to match. It’s worth reflecting on why this benefit is so valuable. Heathrow may have the best connections in the world but it has the worst connections between terminals. In 2026 there is no dedicated, all-terminal, airside connecting train. Shameful.

” and a valet ride back to the terminal.”

Throwing Concierge in there is most definitely a shot across the bow at their oneworld partner… wonder if they got permission first, or just went with it.

UA GLOBAL services AA CONCIERGEkey AS GLOBAL CONCIERGE

@1990 I’d suspect the opposite. It’s so strikingly familiar to Concierge Key that it seems like they’re actually trying to purposefully associate themselves with a different program but one that either airline elites will use..

Truly wild speculation on my part, but it does make one wonder if they could push for a joint mileage program as part of the rumored domestic JV. It would make a lot of sense if they did since there is some leakage and play between the two mileage programs for those that enjoy the game.

For the people underwhelmed by this, what do 360 and GS offer that this doesn’t? I’m legitimately asking, I’ll never get an invite like this

The real question is whether they can deliver. They have so many bungled processes, and staff that can’t even do a PDB half the time. I get that they’re trying to court high value flyers, but can they actually execute?

Interestingly no invite on my end. 173K status points mostly on international business, much of which is with partners, but also Alaska. I fly out of SFO though, which may have to do with it.

@ L3 — LHR terminal transfer isn’t so bad once you learn how it works. Just allow plenty of time and it’s not that bad.

I wonder if this will mostly be for west coast flyers, as they are most likely to fly international premium classes on AS?

So in the next flight is completely full I guess this means one of the poors, even with a guaranteed seat, gets bumped to make room for this elite traveler. And if the elite had a business class seat, some schmuck there gets bumped down to coach, with a coach passenger being knocked off the flight to make room.

Does Alaska have enough of a global network for this elite status to really make sense? Probably not for anyone who is not located in the Washington/Oregon area.

Many of the new flights don’t seem to have onward connecting opportunities. Does ICN? FCO? CDG? It’s really only in LHR and NRT. I don’t know to what extent AS has good connections and through fares. LHR really isn’t an efficient connecting hub. I prefer MUC, FRA, AMS – but AS doesn’t have partners.

I haven’t tried Alaska’s international service in part because they launched without Internet connectivity and the initial reviews were poor. Even today the Hawaiian crews get mixed reviews. I wonder if there has been enough time and enough trial for Alaska to be able to accurately identify who should qualify for the Global Concierge level. Maybe it will be primarily determined by their sales department seeking out corporate customers and giving it to top executives and travel executives. We shall see.

Alaska has historically been terrible at reaccommodating passengers during IRROPS. They don’t have adequate staff handling IRROPS and that staff isn’t supposed to rebook you onto other airlines if that’s the way to complete your journey. They usually limit themselves to their own metal and when they only serve a destination once a day, that can be a long wait. I guess that the Global Concierge level customers will be insulated from the poor IRROPs experience, especially if they relax the restrictions on rebooking onto OALs. Otherwise, the next available flight guarantee is of limited use if Alaska only flies once a day.

#6158. Frontier Airlines’ Unique First Class Now On Sale (No Food, Drinks, Or Recline)

Frontier Airlines has just put first class tickets on sale, with the product launching systemwide for flights as of March 2027. This is a major development for the Denver-based airline, as the historically ultra low cost carrier tries to move upmarket, and respond to consumer preferences. This is only one of several initiatives we’re seeing, along with the introduction of Starlink Wi-Fi, plus charging ports at select seats. Let’s cover all the details.

Frontier Airlines has just put first class tickets on sale for flights as of March 5, 2027. For context, Frontier plans to reconfigure its entire fleet to add eight first class seats at the front of the cabin, with two rows of seats in a 2-2 configuration. Specifically, the airline has selected the Geven Comoda seating platform, with seats having up to 37″ of pitch.

Frontier has already started reconfiguring planes with first class cabins, and the idea is that by early March 2027, the entire fleet will have these seats, which is the point at which they’ll be sold as a separate product. So while the seats will already be in service, and some customers will luck out, that’s the formal launch plan.

Obviously this is a fast timeline for retrofitting cabins, but keep in mind most of the cabin will remain unchanged, so it shouldn’t take much time to reconfigure each aircraft. So, what should we expect in terms of the first class product? Here’s how the airline describes it:

First Class seats offer our most spacious seating experience, providing exceptional comfort and additional personal space at the front of the aircraft. These seats are pre-reclined and do not convert into lie-flat beds.

Complimentary food and beverages are not included with the First Class experience. However, a variety of food and beverage options are available for purchase by all passengers.

Frontier’s first class seats will be “pre-reclined” (meaning they won’t recline), and won’t actually offer complimentary snacks and drinks, so it’ll be just like economy in that regard. On the plus side, the seats are expected to feature USB-C charging ports, which will be the first time that the airline offers in-seat power. The carrier is also going from offering no Wi-Fi, to offering Starlink Wi-Fi as of mid-2027, so that’s pretty exciting.

The airline will also be introducing a dedicated extra legroom section in rows three through eight, with seats having up to 34″ of pitch. Not only that, but these seats will also have USB-C charging ports (while the remainder of economy seats won’t offer in-seat power).

With Frontier Airlines first class tickets now on sale, what is pricing like? The airline is increasingly leaning into the concept of bundles, so we’ll see the Basic Fare, Economy Bundle, Premium Bundle, and First Bundle.

The First Bundle includes a carry-on bag and personal item, two checked bags weighing up to 50 pounds each, priority boarding, and no change or cancel fees.

Pulling up a random one-way flight from Denver (DEN) to Los Angeles (LAX), I see the Basic Fare starting at $119, the Economy Bundle starting at $142, the Premium Bundle starting at $172, and the First Bundle starting at $244.

Those are some incredibly attractive prices, especially if you intend to check bags. However, the airline emphasizes how it has promotional pricing at launch, so only time will tell how that pricing evolves.

There’s no single right or wrong way to offer a premium product. However, I feel like Frontier might be taking the wrong strategy here. What Frontier is offering is essentially more along the lines of the initial Spirit “Big Front Seat” — you get more space, and nothing else.

This just strikes me as a missed opportunity, because I feel like psychologically, willingness to pay is going to be substantially higher if you just include free alcoholic drinks and at least some sort of food. It’s not like I was expecting them to install ovens and have hot meals (JetBlue’s new first class will only have cold food).

But I feel like if the airline just invested $10 in drinks & snacks they could charge more, and would also expand the potential customer base. Whether logical or not, there are some number of passengers who would be more likely to even consider a product if it actually had a dedicated soft product, rather than just being a more spacious seat. At least that’s my take.

Obviously at the current pricing, this is an incredibly attractive proposition for customers. However, I also feel like the airline probably wants to be able to charge higher fares in the long run.

Frontier Airlines has started to reconfigure planes with first class seats, with tickets now being on sale for flights as of March 5, 2027 (at which point the entire fleet should be reconfigured). While Frontier first class will have first class-style seats (minus the recline), there won’t be any differentiation in terms of the soft product, as food and drinks will still be available for purchase.

I would’ve liked the airline to actually roll out a differentiated soft product, but it sounds like that’s not happening. Then again, between Starlink Wi-Fi and in-seat power, this will be a much more attractive proposition than flying with Frontier in the past.

What do you make of Frontier’s first class concept?

Now, if they would only add bags and a schedule that doesn't change every 2 weeks!

Flew F9 RT TPA LAS and NEVER EVER again. And yes, they could have tossed in at least one comp beverage and snack. Yes, missed opportunity for those good folks that would chose F9. I have fond memories of the original FL and THAT was a great airline.

Honestly, this is exactly the kind of “First Class” Americans deserve. 😂 The same crowd that endlessly whines about European Business Class because “OMG, it’s the same seat as Economy!” — conveniently ignoring the guaranteed empty middle seat, lounge access (yes, even on domestic flights), and generally far superior food and service — now gets a First Class product with a non-reclining seat and not even a complimentary drink. #6157. Lufthansa’s First Airbus A350-1000 Has Arrived: 299.5 Seats, Four Cabins, Munich Routes

In 2023, Lufthansa Group placed an order for the Airbus A350-1000 — the order was initially for 10 frames, before being increased to 15 frames the following year. The Lufthansa Group is undergoing a massive long haul fleet modernization at the moment, with both Airbus and Boeing planes on the way.

Along those lines, the first Lufthansa A350-1000 has just joined the carrier’s fleet (in a dazzling livery no less), so let’s cover all the details, including the routes the plane will fly, how the plane is configured, etc.

Between late 2026 and 2030, Lufthansa is taking delivery of 15 Airbus A350-1000s. This is only one of several aircraft types the airline is acquiring, as it’s also taking delivery of Airbus A350-900s, Boeing 787-9s, and (eventually) Boeing 777-9s.

The first A350-1000 has just been delivered today, with three more planes expected to be delivered in the coming weeks, before the end of the year. This first plane even features the special 100th anniversary livery, as Lufthansa has seven of these flying, with one representing each fleet type.

The first plane has the registration code D-AIFA, and is named “Deutschland” (since Lufthansa names all of its planes). This is a special plane for another reason, as it’s also the 700th aircraft that Airbus has delivered to Lufthansa Group. How gorgeous is this plane?!?

Here’s how Heiko Reitz, Lufthansa’s Hub Manager for Munich, describes this:

“We are proud that the Airbus A350-1000—Airbus’s most modern long-haul aircraft—is coming to Munich. The introduction of the new A350-1000 is part of the largest fleet modernization in the history of the Lufthansa Group and a key driver on the path to more sustainability. Our new flagship features 40 percent more Business and Premium Economy seats. To put it simply: The A350-1000 strengthens our premium hub in Munich.”

On a slight tangent, over the summer I saw the 100th anniversary Boeing 747-8 in Frankfurt (FRA), and I must say, I think it might be the most breathtaking plane in commercial service. Is it just me?

We’ve known that the Airbus A350-1000s will get the new Allegris cabins, including the new Allegris first class and Allegris business class. So, what can we expect in terms of the configuration? The A350-1000 features 300 seats, spread across four cabins, as follows:

As a point of comparison, the A350-900 (the non-stretched version of the plane) features 267 seats, as follows:

So the stretched version has 11 more business class seats, 11 more premium economy seats, and 11 more economy seats (11 more seats across three cabins, what a funny coincidence). The airline is still maintaining only one row of first class, which is kind of “bleh.”

You can find the Lufthansa A350-1000 seat map here.

Lufthansa Airbus A350-1000s will all be stationed in Munich (MUC), which is where Lufthansa bases all of its A350s. The first of these planes is entering long haul commercial service as of early December 2026.

Specifically, as of December 3, 2026, the A350-1000 will fly between Munich and Tokyo Haneda (HND), with the next two destinations being Shanghai (PVG) and Singapore (SIN), and those services expected to launch within weeks, though the schedule hasn’t yet been updated to reflect that.

Note that initially the flights won’t be operated by the A350-1000 daily, so there will be alternating service with the A350-900. It’s interesting that the initial route isn’t to North America, where a single plane could do a same day turn, and continuously stay in service. but I guess there’s enough commonality between the A350-900 and A350-1000, so it’s not a big deal.

As far as US destinations go, it’s expected that Chicago (ORD) and Newark (EWR) will be the first two cities to see the new plane, though there’s no exact timeline for that yet.

In 2023, Lufthansa placed an order for the Airbus A350-1000, and the first of these planes has just been delivered, and will enter service in early December 2026. The plane features 300 seats across four cabins, though still only expect one row of first class seats. The Munich-based plane will initially fly to Tokyo, Shanghai, and Singapore. I must say, Lufthansa knocked it out of the park with its centennial livery, and I can’t wait to see this plane flying.

What do you make of Lufthansa’s Airbus A350-1000 deliveries?

299.5 is exactly how many seats this aircraft has.

It remains to be seen whether Lufthansa or Air India presses its first A350-1000 into service first. At present, Ethiopian is the only A350-1000 operator in the Star Alliance, so these will become the second and third — though in what order is unknown. AI is all set to take delivery of VT-JRP some time in November 2026, so it will be a tight race as to whether D-AIFA or VT-JRP enters service first. Funny that came with a 100th anniversary special colours, when the year is just a month and a bit more than half remaining. I hope that this is a sign that these liveries will be here to stay after the end of this year though.

"On a slight tangent, over the summer I saw the 100th anniversary Boeing 747-8 in Frankfurt (FRA), and I must say, I think it might be the most breathtaking plane in commercial service. Is it just me?" - is not just you, the 747-8 in that livery looks AMAZING!

#6156. New Bilt Deals With Hyatt, Marriott And Sports Team Reveal Bigger Bet On Rewards Across Your Whole Neighborhood

Bilt wants the building you live in, the hotel program you belong to, and the team you root for to get you recognized and rewarded at businesses around you. Its new Neighborhood OS and membership platform bring together merchants, housing communities, Hyatt, Marriott and professional sports teams in a much bigger play than earning points on rent. The ambition is to become the company that helps businesses find their next customer, gives that customer a reason to do business, and makes the experience good enough that they come back. I’ve been writing about Bilt’s distribution advantage since 2021. They figured out how to reach customers everyone else wanted but failed to reach – through their homes. They’ve since built what I consider the most valuable points currency and the best rewards for my everyday credit card spending. Now they’re opening up the technology and merchant network behind those rewards for other companies to use. There are two pieces to the announcement: Tools for merchants. Neighborhood OS connects the reservation, payment, point of sale and loyalty systems a business already uses. The goal is to help it recognize customers, deliver benefits, bring in new business and encourage repeat visits. Loyalty programs for other organizations. Bilt is making its membership platform available under other companies’ brands. A sports team, hotel company or residential community can build a new membership program, or extend its existing one, with benefits at businesses around it. The partners include the Phoenix Suns, Houston Rockets, Houston Texans and Sacramento Kings; Marriott and Hyatt; and real estate companies including Related and Presidio Bay. Broader integrations and new membership experiences will roll out in phases beginning in 2027. Bilt CEO Ankur Jain describes a $6.6 trillion opportunity in annual U.S. retail and food services spending that takes place in person. That’s the size of the market they’re aiming at. Small goals! “Your neighborhood is your most important amenity.” — Ankur Jain, introducing Bilt Neighborhood OS What originally interested me in Bilt was the way they acquired customers. An airline already has people who want its miles sitting on its planes. A new, independent rewards program has to find consumers, persuade them to join, and give them a reason to stick around. That’s tough, but Bilt had a truly original angle in reaching people through their homes, rewarding them for paying rent. Bilt helped solve billing and resident relationship problems for landlords, and found a way to become focal for customers. As I wrote earlier this year, move-in is an especially valuable moment: someone is choosing a new coffee shop, gym, dry cleaner and place to order dinner. Their habits are up for grabs. The company says it has signed one in four U.S. apartment buildings and expects to process more than $100 billion in housing payments this year. Their customers are far broader than the small minority of Bilt members with one of their credit cards. They’re equally happy for you to participate with whatever cards you already carry. We’ve seen attempts to create a common rewards program across different merchants before. American Express launched Plenti in 2015 with companies including AT&T, ExxonMobil, Macy’s and Rite Aid. It shut down in July 2018. Bilt’s chairman Ken Chenault was running American Express when Plenti launched. Plenti had enormous merchants with plenty of customers, but struggled to create was a compelling new relationship that made those customers change where they spent. The tech wasn’t very good, they didn’t broaden out merchants, and the value proposition was more modest. Coalition programs have a much longer history abroad. Canada’s Air Miles built a huge membership, although its financial troubles led to BMO acquiring it in 2023. Britain’s Nectar has 24 million active users. The U.S. still hasn’t produced a modern coalition on the scale Plenti promised. Bilt, though, offers a better way to reach customers and a more leveraged rewards system. A small discount is worth its face value. Points that can become a great hotel stay or an international business class award can be worth a lot more to the member than they cost to deliver. And Bilt’s partnerships work together to provide better experiences (e.g. a discount, together with a free Lyft ride to the restaurant, and a comped dessert). And their scale gives local merchants a much more compelling rewards program than they could have on their own. A customer might never visit one restaurant often enough to care about its standalone program. But their rewards can pool with others in the community to create something customers value. And they can reach the customers of those other local businesses, too. That restaurant can identify someone as a customer to solicit and a potentially valuable client to treat especially well. So for merchants: Find customers who can become regulars. A restaurant with empty tables on Tuesday can reach people in nearby buildings who are deciding where to eat. Spend the reward budget where it helps. An offer can be aimed at a first visit, a quiet evening or someone who hasn’t returned recently without giving away half the bill to everyone on a Saturday night when the restaurant is already full. Connect the visit to the relationship. Reservations, purchases and loyalty information can help the business recognize a customer, remember preferences and follow up. A good owner does this for the regulars they know, but the software can help scale it for more people. Offer something customers value more than it costs. A complimentary appetizer, a preferred table when available, or access to an otherwise empty fitness class can make a customer feel appreciated without requiring an equivalent cash discount. There’s a second distribution advantage here. Bilt is working with Verifone, Fiserv, Adyen and OpenTable. Those companies already have relationships with merchants and systems inside their businesses. Connecting to that installed base makes expansion much easier than persuading every restaurant to replace its payment terminal and reservation software. Bilt’s tech is better than what others have tried in the past. Here’s Bilt’s illustration of the merchant experience: The artificial intelligence component isn’t just buzz marketing. They can handle requests and coordinate actions across systems that otherwise require staff to do the work manually. Being able to identify the audience, make an offer, apply it correctly and help the merchant understand what happened is more useful. And Bilt says 91% of actions are completed without manual intervention. I’m not sure if that’s really good, or if a 9% failure rate is unacceptably high at scale. But it’ll clearly improve quickly. Bilt’s merchant sales page lists a $495 monthly Neighborhood OS subscription and an optional $195 monthly Neighborhood Marketplace subscription, or $690 for both. It lists a $1,500 onboarding fee waived through December 31, 2026. Bilt says members generated more than $12 billion in rewarded commerce at local merchants over the last year. A hotel company has a relationship with a guest while they’re traveling, but the guest spends money at restaurants and shops outside the hotel. A sports team has fans all year, including days when there’s no game. Those are valuable relationships with plenty of spending happening outside the company’s own business. Sports fans. The Phoenix Suns and Phoenix Mercury plan to launch in spring 2027 inside their existing app including concession offers, the ability to purchase seat upgrades when inventory opens, and neighborhood benefits connected to team wins. A fan concierge could help with a ride after the game or a restaurant offer nearby. Hotel loyalty. Hyatt and Bilt say they’re expanding incentives and exclusive offers at Hyatt properties, and exploring ways to reward World of Hyatt members through neighborhood experiences. Marriott is also named as a partner. Delivery and dining. Grubhub’s partnership is designed to connect delivery and restaurant visits. A restaurant could encourage someone who orders at home to come in for dinner, or give a diner a reason to order delivery later, through connected campaigns. Bilt announced a $300 million acquisition of LAVA last week, bringing relationships with 56 professional sports franchises and more than 300 technology adapters. That buys both access to fan communities and connections to the systems those teams use. Bilt calls its consumer pass Neighborhood Pass and has an identity system that lets businesses recognize eligible customers across systems without exchanging raw customer data. Getting the benefit applied correctly is a big part of the value. Nobody wants to explain a promotion to a waiter who’s never heard of it. In contrast, one senior executive who sought my counsel on whether to work with Plenti a decade ago concluded it was a non-starter that customers were going to have to submit individual receipts to the program for credit. I already get value from Bilt that goes well beyond a points balance. I’ve redeemed Bilt Cash this year for two BLADE flights, Blacklane and hotel discounts, and use benefits with Lyft, Grubhub and Walgreens. The opportunity here is to make useful benefits available across many more of the places people already spend time. Bilt already earns merchant commissions for sending spending to partners. Subscription fees add another revenue stream. Aggregating many small businesses gives it something valuable to offer a national hotel company, bank or sports sponsor. Bringing those companies’ customers and budgets to local merchants makes joining more attractive. They raised $250 million at a $10.75 billion valuation in July 2025. That provides resources to build and buy the technology, sign partners and support expansion. I think they have a real shot, but what they are doing is really hard. But each piece they successfully build makes subsequent pieces more valuable. A restaurant makes the network more useful to residents nearby. Those residents make it more attractive to the next merchant. A competitor has to assemble both sides in the same places. Two sided markets are hard! Bilt, which launched publicly just five years ago, has built this incredibly quickly. Co-founder of frequent flyer community InsideFlyer.com, emcee of the Freddie Awards, and named one of the "World's Top Travel Experts" by Conde' Nast Traveler (2010-Present) Gary has been a guest on most major news media, profiled in several top print publications, and published broadly on the topic of consumer loyalty. More About Gary »

This is the biggest bunch of meaningless PR fluff I’ve ever read.

They want to be a middleman and they’ve done payment processing for some big landlords. Exciting. Unfortunately, their 2026 was a complete disaster – dumped by a real bank, picked up by PE who wanted pie in the sky but instead got 3 versions of a credit card in 8 months that never achieved any market penetration. On the heels of that failure they’re pulling the rug out from the only part of the credit card that offered a bit more value to consumers than they could get from reliable banks.

All that means is that the marketing dollars they put into their growth plan did not result in more growth, so the marketing dollars had to be cut off because the hockey stick growth that would have supported the charade never materialized.

Now, of course, they have PE investors that would like to make some money off of this failure. So what do they do? They have some digital infrastructure that is underutilized and that they’d like to more broadly deploy. So back to basics… meaningless puffery and branding! They’re trying to refocus on the “meh” stuff that they originally did, because when pie in the sky fails, that’s what you do. Notably absent from this announcement though are any real, meaningful partnerships for “the Neighborhood OS”. Such branding and hubris.

Anyway, good news everyone, our neighborhoods are about to be brought together like never before by Bilt’s amazing AI capabilities… you know, the ones that couldn’t even answer questions about its own program accurately? In fairness, Bilt executives couldn’t answer questions about its own program accurately, so seems harsh to blame the AI.

Enjoy the grandfathering while it lasts, folks.

Wuttt. This was supposed to be a big jetBlue announcement day. So much for that… Oof. So, they’re now pulling an Allbirds, Boom Supersonic “but, but, actually, we’re now an AI company”? Very 2024/2025 of them. I think they missed the gravy train on that one.

If Bilt and Hyatt really want to make a difference, allow their hotel bookings through Bilt to qualify for EQN like Amex FHR program does.

That will make me want to stay at Hyatts using Bilt.

This is the biggest bunch of meaningless PR fluff I’ve ever read.

Re Sports teams sponsorships, hopefully they only view it as an advertising for new customers /sponsorship sort of thing. I have no interest in redeeming my points for watching overpriced US franchises.

@Too many – I think Bilt has been talking about that exactly

Remember, all of this is only worth $620, less than most other cards. Frequent Miler says so, and thye are so omniscient they don’t even need facts to prove it.

At the end of the day, loyalty programs operate within the razor-thin margins of retail. Why would these businesses fund rewards for another ecosystem instead of their own?

No amount of corporate spin can hide the obvious: Bilt bought market share with a credit card point system they certainly lost money on. Pretending it’s business genius to attract cardholders when you literally paid for them to be your customer is a choice.

“And Bilt’s partnerships work together to provide better experiences (e.g., a discount, together with a free Lyft ride to the restaurant, and a comped dessert).”

I love this fairy tale of “integrated rewards” where one credit seamlessly leads to another in a virtuous cycle. That is completely disconnected from how consumers actually behave. Nobody plans a night out three months in advance around stringing together a free Lyft, a free appetizer, and an ice cream.

People burn rewards when they get them or hoard them for flight. Marketers love drawing neat, circular diagrams of loyalty ecosystems, but real usage is jagged.

And sports? Live entertainment and sports are notorious for offering terrible value. At this point, it’s literally cheaper to take my girlfriend to Italy than it is to buy a decent seat at MSG against a competitor.

Hotel Loyalty? Once everyone is special, no one is.

And Grubhub? It’s the bottom of the barrel among delivery platforms. Every single party in the food delivery economy is miserable: consumers get gouged by markups and fees, drivers make pennies, and restaurants watch their margins get stripped away.

Want a real loyalty program? Become a regular at your local neighborhood spot. Get to know the owner, the bartenders, and the staff. You’ll get far more genuine hospitality, comped drinks, and a sense of community by supporting a local business than you ever will churning points.

@L3 — Bahaha… I love that you cannot let that go… L3 again… never change!

Not sure how they’ll get this to work considering every time I try to use Bilt Checkout at the handful of places listed in the app I get a confused stare

Agree, elite night credit on Bilt hotel bookings is what would move people, otherwise it’s just another booking channel. Until then the Hyatt direct rate plus your status perks is the bar to beat. FWIW you can also check Arbitrica or similar free tools, which search the same Hyatt from dozens of countries to find kind of the lowest price in the world, since rates and inventory vary by country. If Bilt can’t match that and give nights, booking direct still wins
