The world's largest hotel groups reported a Middle East recovery in the third quarter from the collapse that followed the outbreak of the U.S.-Iran war, but most now guide to renewed weakness in the fourth quarter — the region's peak season. Accor, with about 11% of global room revenue in the region, saw Middle East RevPAR fall 3% in Q3 and assumes a roughly 12% decline in Q4, with CFO Martine Gerow saying the company has taken a tougher view on Saudi Arabia as Houthi attacks intensify on Riyadh. Marriott's Middle East RevPAR fell 12% in Q3, an improvement from a drop of more than 40% in Q2, and the company expects a steeper fourth-quarter decline against tough comparisons. Hilton's Middle East and Africa RevPAR fell 5.6% and the company now expects a low double-digit decline for the region for the full year, with CEO Chris Nassetta saying owned hotels there will cut more than $20 million from earnings this year. IHG was broadly flat across the wider region but down 12% across the six Gulf countries, and Hyatt held RevPAR down only about 3% as domestic travel offset a 40% drop in international inbound. Development pipelines, meanwhile, are holding: IHG said it is aware of no project cancellations, and Wyndham recently signed five new contracts across Saudi Arabia and the UAE.

#6142. ATMA: Aman’s New Brand, Debuting With A 1,049-Foot Miami Tower

Aman is known for being one of the world’s top luxury hotel groups. Currently Aman Group consists of Aman (the original hotel group) and Janu (intended to be more of a “lifestyle” version of Aman). Aman is now launching a third brand, and it’s yet another departure from the origins of Aman.

Aman Group has announced the launch of ATMA, described as a “new ultra-luxury brand pioneering performance living.” ATMA means “the spirit” or “the true self” in Sanskrit, and the intent is for the brand to combine wellness, sport, nutrition-led dining, design, and experiential entertainment.

ATMA will “focus on advanced wellness programming and world-class sport facilities, which have been developed exclusively by ATMA Global Partner Novak Djokovic.”

The first location will be ATMA Miami, and it will include a hotel, branded residence, and a private members club. Specifically, the property will be in the Brickell neighborhood and will have a private marina, with an anticipated opening in 2031.

ATMA Miami is expected to be a standalone 1,049-foot tower, which is as tall as buildings can get in Miami. In terms of height, it’ll be match the new 100-story Waldorf Astoria Miami that’s currently under construction, which will be the tallest building in Florida, once complete.

Details about ATMA Miami are still fairly limited, but we know there will be 480 residential units, in addition to the hotel. Residential units will be between one and six bedrooms, and will be “supported by Aman Group’s service standards.”

There will also be a 120,000 square foot spa and wellness area, set to be the largest of its kind in Miami. Developed in partnership with Djokovic, it will offer performance and recovery experiences alongside indoor padel, tennis and squash courts, a fitness center, group and private training studios, mobility and conditioning labs, a medical wellness center, and dedicated recovery spaces.

So far we’ve only learned about the Miami location, but the claim is that the brand will span urban and remote destinations.

Look, I’ve made my opinions about the Aman brand pretty clear, so I don’t want to sound like some old dude just ranting about the “good old days.” When Aman was founded by hospitality legend Adrian Zecha, it was truly among the most innovative and passion driven hospitality projects we’ve ever seen.

In 2014, Zecha sold the brand to Vladislav Doronin, and since then, the entire philosophy has changed. It’s hard to fault someone for purchasing a brand and trying to cash in and maximize profitability — I mean, that’s kind of how the business world is supposed to work, right?

But of course that doesn’t mean we have to be happy about the evolution. It started with Aman ditching its approach of largely opening hotels in the middle of nowhere, where that was part of the charm. Instead, we saw Aman focus on city hotels. Then Aman became all about opening members clubs. Then we saw the launch of the Janu brand, essentially a higher room count version of Aman, with a more lively spirit.

And now we’re seeing Aman getting into building full-on skyscrapers. Well, or at least partnering on them in terms of branding. Of course some Aman properties already have a residences component, so that’s nothing new, as such. However, the scale of this project couldn’t be more opposite of what Aman initially was. We’re talking about a 100-story building that will have nearly 500 residences, and who knows how many hotel rooms (it hasn’t yet been announced).

Of course in Miami, one of the biggest trends is branded residences, with brands just selling out their name. But if Aman were to just slap its name on a residential project, you’d think it would be something smaller scale than this. This is among the highest unit count developments we’ve ever seen in Miami, at least for a project spanning just one building.

Aman Group has just announced its third brand, and it will be named ATMA. It’s described as a “new ultra-luxury brand pioneering performance living.” The first location will open in Miami in 2031, and it’ll be a roughly 100-story building with 480 residences, a hotel, and a members club.

Aman as a brand has become unrecognizable compared to what it was 15 years ago. But that’s fair enough, and it’s also what happens when you sell a company to someone looking to maximize their ROI. You can hardly fault someone for that, as much as I don’t personally like it.

Airbnb has courted business travelers for a decade, but corporate bookings mostly happened off to the side, through referral deals and workarounds. Letting Perk tap its API puts live Airbnb listings inside a corporate booking tool for what Perk says is the first time. Rival travel management companies are undoubtedly on the way.

Perk, a business travel and spend management platform, will announce Tuesday it’s the first travel management company to integrate Airbnb’s API for business travel.

Employees of Perk clients can now search Airbnb listings with live pricing and availability, book them within company travel policy, and send them for approval alongside flights, cars and rail, without leaving Perk.

Bilt is changing how its credit cards earn rewards, and cardholders who want to keep earning 4% Bilt Cash on everyday spending need to make a choice. New applicants must apply, be approved and accept their offer by December 31. I’ve already opted to keep the benefit—it’s a big reason my Bilt Palladium gets most of my spending.

Frequent Miler‘s latest ‘Ask Us Anything’ was a strong endorsement of Bilt. Their three Bilt Palladium Card (See rates and fees) cardholders plan to renew, and even the group’s Bilt skeptic plans to apply. They all want to keep earning 4% Bilt Cash.

If you don’t have a Bilt card, I’d get one now. You need to apply, get approved and accept the card offer by December 31, 2026 to preserve the choice of earning 4% Bilt Cash. Existing cardmembers also need to actively choose to keep it before their first card anniversary in 2027. Doing nothing means moving into the new rewards structure.

Nick Reyes calls renewing Palladium “pretty much a no-brainer.” It’s his “daily driver,” the card he uses most often. He’s happy earning two or three Bilt Points per dollar because they’re “very valuable,” with “plenty of great transfer partners” and continued good transfer bonuses. With a points accelerator active, he’ll often use it even for spending that another card would bonus. He’s approaching Platinum status (thanks to his card spend), but says the card’s earning makes sense even before transfer bonuses and status benefits.

Tim Steinke says he expects all three Palladium holders—Greg Davis-Kean, Nick and himself—to renew and retain the current rewards structure. Stephen plans to get the card before the old earning option closes, despite having no intended use for Bilt housing payments. He calls the points “absolutely fantastic.”

That’s also how I use the Bilt Palladium Card: it gets the majority of my spending. I pay my mortgage through Bilt, but the card would be valuable to me even without that.

I’ve written that Palladium looks complicated, but it’s the best everyday rewards card.

I consider these the most valuable points. You can redeem them at 1.25 cents apiece through Bilt’s travel portal, but I usually want to transfer them. The transfer partner lineup gives me access to:

Most transfers are 1:1. Accor is 3:2, I Prefer is 1:2, and Amtrak is 2:1. Bilt also runs large Rent Day transfer bonuses, often with better offers for higher elite tiers. I’ve used bonuses for transfers to Japan Airlines, British Airways, Virgin Atlantic and Air France KLM. Earning points quickly and then transferring with a bonus is why I want so much of my spending here.

Bilt is changing the earning choice in 2027. Today, cardmembers can choose:

Most cardmembers already choose the second option. Palladium is still a great card that way. But for most people putting significant spending on the card, especially when they’re generating more Bilt Cash than their housing payments would consume, I think the 4% option is better. Once you’ve reached the highest housing multiplier, spending more doesn’t increase that multiplier. With Flexible Bilt Cash, more spending keeps producing more Bilt Cash to use.

There are exceptions. I’ve explained how the housing option can produce an effective 4 points per dollar on everyday spending. At the 25% spending threshold, $1,000 of everyday spending and $4,000 of eligible housing payments earn 2,000 points from the purchases and 2,000 from housing. That’s 4,000 points against $1,000 of everyday spending. The relationship between your spending and housing payments determines which choice works best.

For me, the accelerators alone are a reason to preserve Bilt Cash earning. Spend $200 in Bilt Cash to activate one and you earn an extra point per dollar on the next $5,000 in eligible spending. Palladium’s 2X becomes 3X. That $5,000 also generates another $200 Bilt Cash, which can fund the next accelerator. Each eligible cardholder can activate five per calendar year.

My wife and I have both maxed out our accelerators this year: 3 points per dollar on $50,000 of combined spending. We’ve earned points on housing payments as well.

She has an authorized user card on my Palladium account. It costs $95 annually and comes with her own Priority Pass membership. She doesn’t receive a second set of my annual hotel and Bilt Cash credits, but she can earn rewards in her own Bilt account (or I can switch it to mine).

I’ve laid out how my wife and I use this. I directed the points and Bilt Cash from her spending into her account instead of mine. She earns her own status, funds her own accelerators, and can take advantage of transfer bonuses separately. When an offer bonuses transfers of up to 100,000 Bilt Points per member, two accounts give us room to bonus 200,000 points, with each person’s bonus determined by their own status.

An authorized user’s spending doesn’t automatically get the primary cardholder’s active accelerator. They need to activate their own, using their own Bilt Cash. Bilt also gives the primary cardholder separate card numbers and controls over authorized user spending, including transaction and monthly limits. You can add an authorized user starting at age 13. But for my wife and me, the separate rewards accounts are the reason this has been so useful.

And I’ve gotten far more out of Bilt Cash than just faster points earning. I’ve redeemed it for:

These are benefits I’ve actually used. For my everyday spending, Palladium earns the points I want faster than any other card, and the benefits have been incredible.

The new structure still allows Palladium and Obsidian cardmembers to use accelerators. Palladium’s $400 annual hotel credit and $200 annual Bilt Cash become a $600 annual Bilt Cash deposit at the card anniversary. That can fund three accelerators. Members can also earn Bilt Cash from other activity, including $50 for each 25,000 qualifying points. But they won’t replenish it at 4% of everyday spending.

Keeping the existing structure also preserves my separate $200 hotel credits, which I can stack with Bilt Cash hotel redemptions. The Bilt Cash hotel redemption allowance moves from monthly to twice yearly starting January 1 even for those keeping 4% earning, but I can still get the two $300 discounts this way.

Plus, Bilt Cash now expires at the end of the month 12 months after it’s earned. Cash earned in February 2026 lasts through February 28, 2027. The old rule would have wiped out everything over $100 at year-end. Having more time to use what I earn makes the 4% option better for me.

If you don’t have a card, I’d apply now and complete approval and acceptance before December 31. My choice is Bilt Palladium. The ability to preserve 4% Bilt Cash also applies to the Bilt Obsidian Card (See rates and fees) and no annual fee Bilt Blue Card (See rates and fees).

And if you already have a card, don’t assume your current selection of Flexible Bilt Cash protects you from the change. You need to proactively choose to keep it. I’ve already done this:

The new rewards model is selected by default. Swipe right.

You have until your first card anniversary in 2027 to make that election. Preserve it now and you can still move to the new structure later. Once that switch takes effect, you can’t move back. That’s why getting a Bilt Palladium Card makes so much sense – keeping the earning option. They’ll pry the 4% Bilt Cash earning option from my cold, dead hands, as they say.

#6139. Will Credit Card Interest Rates Be Capped At 10%? Democrats Want To Work With Trump

With the recent midterm elections, the balance of power in Washington is very quickly changing. Given the extent to which things shifted left, Democrats certainly want to be able to show that they can accomplish something in the next two years, to make life better for average Americans.

Along those lines, we’re once again seeing a proposal floated regarding capping credit card interest rates. There’s a lot more support for this than in the past, given the majority that Democrats have, plus the fact that President Trump has also been in support of this concept (or at least claimed to be). Will it actually pass, though?

Senate Democrats are renewing a proposal to cap credit card interest rates at 10%, with Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts specifically bringing this up in a “Face The Nation” interview. Warren is likely to chair the Senate Banking Committee, and could use her position to help advance the proposal.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) says she wants to work with President Trump to cap credit card interest rates at 10% and Democrats “have the bills ready to go” to work with the president. “We got a whole bunch more that the American people have told us that they want on price… pic.twitter.com/0r17PwXPQT

Now, before anyone gets political, keep in mind that this is a concept that Trump actually proposed earlier this year. He claimed that Americans were being ripped off by credit card companies, and that as of January 20, 2026, credit card interest rates should be capped at 10%. However, this just came in the form of a social media post, rather than any actual legislation:

Please be informed that we will no longer let the American Public be “ripped off” by Credit Card Companies that are charging Interest Rates of 20 to 30%, and even more, which festered unimpeded during the Sleepy Joe Biden Administration. AFFORDABILITY! Effective January 20, 2026, I, as President of the United States, am calling for a one year cap on Credit Card Interest Rates of 10%. Coincidentally, the January 20th date will coincide with the one year anniversary of the historic and very successful Trump Administration. Thank you for your attention to this matter. MAKE AMERICA GREAT AGAIN! PRESIDENT DONALD J. TRUMP

Donald J. Trump Truth Social Post 08:10 PM EST 01.09.26 pic.twitter.com/47SQ03yMeo

Unsurprisingly, there was no enforcement mechanism, and this never happened, especially since he got pushback from other Republicans. If he really believed in that proposal, then it sounds like this will be his chance to actually turn it into some sort of a law, with support from Democrats. We’ll have to mark this as “developing” for now.

Just for some context, credit card issuers make money in three primary ways — through interchange fees, through interest charges, and through annual fees. When it comes to interest rates, credit card companies are known for having very high rates, an average of over 20%. These are the charges that apply if you don’t pay your full balance before the payment due date. You don’t pay interest charges if you simply charge your purchase to a credit card, and then pay your balance in full.

On the surface, capping credit card interest rates of course sounds great — some of the rates are really high, and many people view banks as greedy, and think they can afford to give up some of their margins. Obviously for those who are currently financing charges, a cap on interest rates would be positive.

The thing is, a policy change like this wouldn’t come without some other changes. There’s no denying that if interest rates were capped at 10%, lots of consumers with not-great credit would be locked out of getting credit cards, and might even have their accounts closed, because card issuers would find it too risky to loan them money at that rate.

After all, there’s a huge risk to people not making payments, and the economics of that work differently with 10% interest rates rather than 25% interest rates. I would imagine that tens of millions of Americans would have their accounts closed, that we’d see fewer no annual fee cards, etc.

Beyond that, if we did see a long term cap on credit card interest rates, it would likely change the credit card landscape in terms of how rewarding cards are, with everything ranging from welcome bonuses, to rewards on spending, to perks.

Right or wrong, credit card economics are heavily reliant on a cross-subsidized system. That’s the whole reason some of us are able to get such outsized value. Credit card rewards structures nowadays largely more or less rebate back interchange fees to consumers, as it’s easy to earn 2% cash back with cards, or even to earn huge multipliers on spending.

The reality is that the revenue that subsidizes a lot of rewards is the interest charges, since that’s the highest margin revenue stream from many card issuers. So we’re partly earning huge welcome bonuses and 5x points on some transactions because someone else is paying close to 30% interest.

I’m not saying that’s a good system, but I’m just being realistic about how it works. If interest rates are forced to be slashed by more than half in the long run, it will have major implications for rewards. Maybe that’s objectively not a bad thing, but it will happen.

For that matter, it would even have a major impact on airlines — they’re so reliant on credit card revenue nowadays to turn profits, and this would greatly hurt their margins in that area as well.

With Democrats soon controlling both the House and Senate, there’s a renewed push to cap credit card interest rates at 10%. This is a proposal that Trump made earlier this year, but it didn’t get support from Republicans.

While I totally appreciate that credit card interest rates are often incredibly high, it’s not without reason, given the rate of default on some cards. Approval standards for cards would change, many consumers would have their cards shut down, etc. It would also likely change the economics of the credit card industry, which could even impact airlines.

However, I’m not some lobbyist or apologist for the credit card industry. If the change happens, many people will benefit, and I’m sure the industry will adapt. However, unarguably many people will go from paying 25% interest on their credit card, to potentially paying even higher rates for payday loans, doing business with loan sharks, etc.

What do you make of this proposal to cap credit card interest rates?

There are many ways to deal with this, but capping rates at 10% won't happen; it would destroy the entire business model. Lots and I mean lots of people would see their cards cancelled or their credit limits lowered, resulting in many people having to repay funds and look elsewhere for credit. Ripple effect on the economy, etc. In Quebec, they raised the legal minimum payment you have to make on credit cards from next to nothing to 5%. The Bank of Canada had a detailed report on credit cards in Canada, and the summary was that access to credit was diminished, and delinquency rates went up slightly, but people carried less debt on average. Nothing earth-shattering, but I guess it's a positive change if people have less debt. I think people should be better educated that credit cards should not be used as a loan. You should never spend money you don't have except for a mortgage. I know that's not easy when you are young.

following short term rates & set monthly by fed, prime + 10% seems a solid compromise. currently prime is 7% so 17% cc interest rate cap. a haircut on our rewards ecosystem seems likely if a law emerges. deal with it!

Within the public debt markets, there are credit rating agencies that assign AAA, AA+, AA, AA-, A+, etc. Each rating has a historic average default rate and an interest rate premium consistent with that default rate. It would seem consistent and reasonable to tie an individual's interest rate to that person's credit score.

Honestly, I think the incoming Congress might very well pass a 10% interest rate limit. The question would then be will Trump veto it? If that happens, even though Democrats made huge gains in the recent elections, it likely will not be law as they won't have anything approaching a veto-proof majority in either house. @Ben, I agree with your analysis. Current credit card interest rates are legalized usury but if restricted, we can kiss a lot of related loyalty program perks good-bye. I am starting to see another trend that will affect credit card usage: pushback from merchants, who are tacking on fees for using credit cards. If this trend continues, it will cost you more to get those points and miles. Some merchants who tack on credit card usage fees don't do that for debit cards. Apparently, the fees they pay banks for debit card usage are lower than for credit cards. However, in the US, there is a legal liability limit of $50 per fraudulent credit card transaction. That limit does NOT apply to fraudulent debit card transactions, making debit card usage relatively dangerous in this day and age, as it exposes your entire bank balance to fraud. Debit card transactions should probably also be protected against fraud but if that happened, banks would likely just raise merchant fees to match credit card fees or maybe even higher fee levels as the loss potential is higher.

Maybe there will be a carve out for cards with benefits (travel, hotel, airline, etc) to a different higher cap

#6138. Trump’s Amnesty Talk

President Donald Trump looks on as White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller speaks about birthright citizenship in the Oval Office at the White House in Washington, D.C., August 6, 2026.

Vice President JD Vance warned in his famous post-midterm X post that Republicans would begin advocating for amnesty in the aftermath of the election. He was right, although he didn’t mention that the president of the United States would be one of them.

In a 60 Minutes interview over the weekend, Trump said he’d like to find a deal with Democrats to regularize the legal status of good, hardworking illegal immigrants. Whenever Trump has talked in these terms in the past, or mused about increasing levels of legal immigration, his restrictionist aides have — rightly — pulled him back.

This will probably happen again, given that the president has just made the ur-immigration hawk Stephen Miller his chief of staff. Even if Trump persists, it’s hard to see how there’d be any deal in the offing with Democrats who think they won, in part, on the excesses of the president’s immigration enforcement and have a chance for a trifecta in 2028 that could roll back his immigration agenda entirely. Are they really going to make concessions on enforcement or legal immigration numbers?

There’s no doubt that the administration’s immigration regime hurt among Hispanics voters and the general electorate as well, although not nearly as much as corruption, prices, and the Iran war. With a vast illegal immigrant population in the United States and limited enforcement resources, the administration has understandably looked to self-deportation as a force multiplier. If there are high-profile apprehensions and deportations, illegal immigrants see that and decide to go home on their own. This dynamic has clearly contributed to a notable diminishment in the foreign-born population in Trump’s second term.

The political problem is that everyone else sees those apprehensions and detentions and may not like them, especially if they are needlessly combative for the sake of cable-news coverage and internet clicks. This was the approach of former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem, whose subtraction from the administration was a net addition. Border czar Tom Homan took over the immigration portfolio and has tried to avoid headlines, but enforcement has still been overwhelming based on apprehensions in public places.

What’s been missing is an emphasis on what our friends at the Center for Immigration Studies call bureaucratic or briefcase enforcement, the nuts-and-bolts work to track down, warn, and punish as necessary employers who hire illegal workers. Ideally, we’d have a national E-Verify system to instantaneously flag such workers. Still, there’s much that can be done with currently existing tools, and Homan himself favors deploying them.

If we squeeze illegal workers out of the labor market, it creates an incentive for them to leave, since so many came here looking for a job. At the same time, such largely invisible enforcement doesn’t generate occasions for demonstrations and turmoil in the streets.

Yet the president is an obstacle to adopting this tactic. He has sympathy for employers desperate for immigrant labor — since he was one himself — and influential business constituencies will balk at intense workplace enforcement. So, we have the president wildly swinging from supporting splashy actions targeting specific cities to talking about throwing in the towel.

At some point, when the illegal population is down substantially and there’s an enforcement system in place that can’t be ignored or gamed, there will be a case for amnesty for specific categories of illegal immigrants. We aren’t there yet, and we shouldn’t be thinking of giving up after one election loss. Vance implied that it was GOP quislings who would immediately turn to amnesty after the midterm drubbing, but, alas, the call is coming from inside the house.

#6137. ‘Is This Hilton?’ An Ad Blitz Answers: Yes, We Have Lifestyle Hotels

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: Hilton ads on electronic bill Moynihan train hall at new york city penn station Hilton

Hilton spent years buying and licensing non-traditional hotel brands. Its new ad campaign is the bill coming due: It has to teach travelers about the new places to stay.

Hilton’s fastest-growing hotel categories are the ones travelers least associate with Hilton: luxury and lifestyle. Its “New Ways to Stay” marketing campaign is an attempt to close that gap.

“Our luxury and lifestyle portfolios continue to grow the most quickly across categories, with trailing 12-month net unit growth rates of 11% and 20%, respectively,” CEO Chris Nassetta said on an earnings call last month. ("Lifestyle" brands  are design-forward hotels with distinctive decor and amenities.)

Since 2024, Hilton bought Graduate Hotels and NoMad, partnered with outdoor lodging operator AutoCamp, and signed a loyalty licensing deal with Small Luxury Hotels of the World that put hundreds of independent hotels into its channels.

Customer awareness about the new properties was limited, and Hilton's research found that many travelers didn’t know they could earn loyalty points by booking them through its site and app.

Hilton's luxury and lifestyle portfolios are growing faster than any other category — trailing 12-month net unit growth of 11% and 20%, respectively, CEO Chris Nassetta said on an earnings call last month — but the company's research found many travelers didn't know they could earn loyalty points by booking those properties through Hilton's site and app. The "Is This Hilton?" campaign, launched September 14 around the Emmys, is the fix. Hilton spent $2.5 million on national linear TV across 579 airings, about two-thirds of its linear TV spending across all brands in that period, according to iSpot.tv estimates, and paired it with real-time social posting, a creator roster that runs from niche influencers to Formula 1 driver Lando Norris, Paris Hilton, and a Times Square pop-up. Much of the new inventory isn't Hilton-run: by Skift's count, Hilton neither owns nor operates roughly 585 of the luxury and lifestyle properties it has added in recent years, most through the Small Luxury Hotels loyalty licensing deal, alongside Graduate Hotels, NoMad, AutoCamp, Yotel, and an Explora Journeys cruise partnership. SVP of global marketing Daniel Reynolds said the real test is whether Hilton's brand tracker shows a shift in perception among target audiences, "and that can take a long time."

#6136. American First Class Will Get Mini-Meals On Shorter Flights (700-899 Miles)

American Airlines will reportedly be making a very nice change to first class service on some short haul flights that didn’t previously qualify for a meal service, and it’s something I’m sure passengers will be happy to see.

As things currently stand, American serves meals in first class on flights of at least 900 miles during meal times (900 miles roughly correlates to a little over two hours of flying, on average).

In the US, this is basically the industry standard, as Delta and United have the same cutoff of 900 miles for serving meals. On flights shorter than that, airlines only offer drinks and a snack basket in first class.

It looks like American will soon be leading the industry when it comes to service in first class on shorter flights, as it brings back a program it used to offer.

JonNYC reports that American will soon be bringing back the “light bites” concept on flights of 700 to 899 miles (700 miles correlates to a little over 90 minutes of flying, on average). The exact timeline for this remains to be seen, but it sounds like this will debut on flights between New York and Chicago, which isn’t surprising.

AA:"Light bites”/mini-meals coming back to short haul domestic first class flights 700-899 milesStarting on NYC/ORD.

It must be a decade at this point since American offered this concept. The idea was to serve mixed nuts on these flights in a ramekin, and then to offer some sort of fresh item that’s plated, and comes with cutlery, a napkin, etc. For example, I remember options including a small fruit & cheese plate, a hummus & veggie plate, etc.

It wasn’t really a full meal replacement, but it was better than the snack basket, and definitely showed some effort than just packaged snacks. It remains to be seen what exactly this iteration of the concept looks like, so I’ll report back when we learn more.

It goes without saying that expectations of premium cabin travelers differ massively around the globe. In the Middle East, it’s common to have a 30-minute business class flight with a lie flat bed, cappuccinos, champagne, and a substantial, tasty snack.

In Europe, you’re typically stuck with a pretty underwhelming hard product on short haul flights (just economy with a blocked middle), but regardless of the length of the flight, you’re almost always served something fresh, even if the flight time is well under an hour.

In the United States, we have the benefit of actually having a dedicated first class cabin with larger seats, but the soft product just isn’t great. You can be on a flight of nearly two hours and just be served packaged snacks.

We do have to give credit to Alaska for this, as it’s the only US carrier to serve some sort of fresh food on flights of under 900 miles. On most Alaska flights you’ll get a snack on shorter services, so kudos to the airline for that.

American Airlines is expected to once again serve fresh food in first class on flights of 700-899 miles. The exact timeline remains to be seen, but this marks a resumption of the mini-meals we saw the airline serve in first class many years back.

Among the “big three” US carriers, American will be the only one to serve fresh food in first class on flights of under 900 miles, so kudos to the airline for that. I’m curious to learn more details.

What do you make of American serving mini-meals on shorter first class flights?

Apple TV costs either $14.99 per month or $119 for the annual plan, so either way, you're saving a lot of money with this perk. Be sure to activate it soon, since you only have until the end of 2026.

With the , you'll earn Ultimate Rewards points at the following rates:

*Excludes Target, Walmart and wholesale clubs

TPG credit cards writer Stephanie Stevens calls out the vacation homes category as a big plus for her. She's booked over 60 Airbnbs, so there's plenty of opportunity for her to earn lots of bonus points with this category.

I live in Portland, Oregon, a city with a strong mass transit system (by U.S. standards). That means I often swipe my Sapphire Preferred for transit tickets, so I'm glad that this card's general travel rewards category is broadly defined.

My main criticism of the Sapphire Preferred's earning categories is that its grocery category is restricted to online orders only. Walmart, Target and wholesale stores are also excluded from this category, which is a major downside for me as a frequent Walmart shopper. Still, this is a relatively minor critique given that the card's overall earning structure is very strong for a $95 annual fee.

You can redeem Ultimate Rewards points for a variety of options, including statement credits, gift cards, Amazon.com purchases and travel booked through Chase Travel.

The includes access to Chase's Points Boost feature, which means you can redeem your points for up to 1.75 cents per point (depending on the redemption). While Points Boost can offer solid value in the right circumstances, I generally prefer transferring my points to Chase's airline and hotel partners, where I can often get significantly more value.

Speaking of transferring points, Chase offers 14 transfer partners, including World of Hyatt, United MileagePlus, Air Canada Aeroplan and Air France-KLM Flying Blue.

Personally, I transfer most of my Ultimate Rewards points to World of Hyatt. Last year, I transferred 87,500 Ultimate Rewards points to Hyatt to book 10 nights at different hotels across Germany, easily saving me hundreds of dollars. (Note that the number of points you'd need to replicate this strategy would be higher by default with the updated 4:3 transfer ratio.)

Despite the unfavorable transfer ratio, Hyatt is still a compelling transfer partner thanks to its fixed award chart pricing. And with a deep roster of airline and hotel partners, Chase still offers plenty of opportunities for valuable redemptions with other partners.

For example, TPG's managing editor for credit cards, Giselle Gomez, transferred 22,000 Ultimate Rewards points to Air France-KLM Flying Blue for a one-way flight between Miami International Airport (MIA) and Charles de Gaulle Airport (CDG). Thanks to a 20% transfer bonus, she was able to save 3,000 points. This ticket would've cost $1,504 without points, so after accounting for $139 in taxes and fees, she received a phenomenal over 6 cents per point in value.

This card provides the most value to people who travel regularly and redeem their rewards for travel. #6133. Prices Prop Up Travel as Demand Cools

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: A pedestrian walking alongside the Tiber River in Rome. Pexels / Bruna Santos

Travel interest is slipping, but revenue is holding because prices are doing the work. That cushion only lasts as long as travelers keep paying more, which makes falling search activity worth watching closely heading into 2027.

Across global markets, fewer travelers are searching for trips and fewer say they plan to travel, but the slowdown hasn’t reached the bottom line yet. Higher airfares and accommodation rates are holding up revenue as traveler interest cools.

The Skift Travel Health Index stood at 99 in September, down 1% year-on-year. The destinations index, which measures travel interest through online search activity, fell by 12% to 88, as inbound flight and hotel searches weakened across most tracked markets.

Skift Travel Health Index · September 2026

Travel demand signals softened in September 2026 while pricing kept revenue intact. The Skift Travel Health Index stood at 99, down 1% year-on-year, and the destinations index, which tracks travel interest through online search activity, fell 12% to 88 as inbound flight and hotel searches weakened across most tracked markets. Inbound flight search growth was negative in the majority of the 21 destinations tracked, with the United Arab Emirates down 37%, Hong Kong down 18%, Australia down 16%, and Mexico down 15%, while China (+11%), India (+7%), and Italy (+5%) gained. Intent data points the same way: the European Travel Commission found the share of global travelers planning a long-haul trip fell from 55% in autumn 2025 to 50% in autumn 2026, and interest in visiting Europe slipped from 38% to 34%. The share of travelers who had already booked flights stayed broadly unchanged, so the cooling is concentrated at the top of the funnel. Higher airfares and accommodation rates are holding up revenue as traveler interest cools.

We’re currently seeing an excellent Amex Business Gold Card welcome offer, which is the biggest bonus we’ve ever seen on the card, making it the ideal time to apply. If you’re eligible for this card and the highest possible bonus, it’s absolutely worth taking advantage of, in my opinion.

Link: Learn more about the American Express® Business Gold Card

The Amex Business Gold Card currently has a massive welcome offer that’s as high as 200,000 Membership Rewards points after spending $15,000 on eligible purchases within the first three months. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer. Find out your offer.

Amex uses a variety of factors when it comes to deciding what offer people are eligible for, including history of opening and closing cards with Amex, spending history with Amex, how many welcome offers people have earned, etc. So, how does this Amex Business Gold Card bonus actually work?

You should find the highest possible offer through the above link. However, if you don’t, it can always be worth checking refer-a-friend links, opting in to targeted emails from Amex, or even using the CardMatch tool to see what you’re eligible for there. OpenAI didn't acquire Odessia for its revenue. It bought a team that built a working AI travel agent in months, plus a founder who ran a lodging company, which included hotels and short-term rentals, for a decade. It's a sign ChatGPT wants to do more in travel than send users to Booking.com and Expedia.

OpenAI has acquired Odessia, the AI travel agent startup that Sonder co-founder Francis Davidson launched just five months ago. Davidson announced the deal Tuesday and said he will join OpenAI “to focus on the future of travel.” Terms weren’t disclosed.

“We’ll have more to share on the shape of the future soon,” Davidson wrote. He didn’t say whether Odessia will keep operating as a standalone company.

Davidson unveiled Odessia in June with a team of eight in San Francisco and about $6 million in seed funding led by Sequoia Capital. It plans and books flights, hotels and itineraries through a single conversation, and it opened to the public on Oct. 14 as a free concierge that users reach by text.

OpenAI has acquired Odessia, the AI travel agent startup founded by Sonder co-founder Francis Davidson, less than a year after its launch. Davidson announced the deal Tuesday and said he will join OpenAI "to focus on the future of travel." Terms weren't disclosed, and Davidson did not say whether Odessia will keep operating as a standalone company. Until now, OpenAI's travel strategy has leaned on partners: Booking.com and Expedia were among the first apps inside ChatGPT when OpenAI opened its app platform in October 2025, and OpenAI has been building travel advertising and booking into ChatGPT so users can buy without going to a merchant's site. Odessia brings what those partnerships don't — a team that has built a booking agent end to end, IATA accreditation, hotel content, and a founder who knows the economics of lodging from both the consumer and operator's side. Odessia launched in June with a team of eight in San Francisco and about $6 million in seed funding led by Sequoia Capital, and opened to the public on October 14 as a free concierge reached by text.

Alaska Airlines is rolling out a new invite-only status level called Atmos Global Concierge. Like the other major U.S. airlines that have such a tier, Alaska is not publicly disclosing what it takes to earn an invitation — though you can be sure it will require a lot of spending.

News of Alaska's new invite-only tier began spreading across aviation blogs Tuesday, and the company confirmed the move to TPG.

"Atmos Global Concierge is a new, invitation-only program," said Alaska in a statement, " ...  that, in addition to all the award-winning benefits of Atmos Rewards membership, provides personalized travel support when you need it the most."

For now, this is a beta program rollout, so it's likely to change over time.

In addition to published top tiers, like American Airlines' AAdvantage Executive Platinum, Delta's Diamond Medallion and United Airlines' Premier 1K, all three major U.S. carriers offer an even higher level of status generally saved for the elites who spend the most with the airline (and some travel providers and C-level executives and celebrities).

American Airlines has ConciergeKey, Delta Air Lines has 360, and United Airlines has Global Services. And now Alaska has Atmos Global Concierge.

None of these airlines publicly disclose the exact qualification requirements for their invitation-only programs, which makes pontificating about what it takes to qualify something of an unofficial pastime for loyalty die-hards.

Among the theories: Invites are tied not only to flight spending, but also to credit card spending and even to your home airport. For example, an American Airlines frequent flyer based at the carrier's Dallas Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) hub might have a harder time securing an invitation than a similarly high-spending traveler based in a more competitive market.

Alaska isn't revealing the full list of benefits that come with its new status, but it did share some details with TPG.

"Members are supported by a dedicated Concierge team throughout their journey, including proactive trip monitoring and travel assistance, along with exclusive benefits and curated experiences," Alaska said.

That means help with travel disruptions, such as a next-flight guarantee and dedicated, specialized assistance.

Reports suggest other benefits include the ability to gift Gold status, a free Clear+ membership and Avis Chairman's Club status. Those invited are also reportedly being given Atmos Titanium status, even if they haven't already qualified organically this year.

If Alaska follows the lead of its larger competitors, additional perks could include VIP airport transfers, higher upgrade priority and expanded lounge access. However, Alaska has not confirmed those benefits.

As for what it might take to get invited to this special club, it will likely require spending tens of thousands of dollars on tickets. Some reports suggest the invitations appear to be targeted at potential customers for Alaska's new international routes with lie-flat business class. On the flip side, some Titanium-level Alaska flyers haven't been invited even after earning as many as 250,000 Alaska Atmos status points and buying international business-class tickets.

"Through this beta program, we’re creating new ways to recognize some of our most loyal members as our global network grows," Alaska told TPG.

While this won't mean much for most of us, it's still exciting to see a new layer of potential perks for some of Alaska's most loyal flyers. Alaska has been one of the most innovative U.S. airlines when it comes to loyalty, so it's an interesting development to see the carrier recognize its highest-value customers with an invite-only tier that matches what the other big global U.S. airlines have done.

Alaska is also now the only major U.S. airline that lets you earn elite status from actual flight miles (though you can choose to earn status by spending). A new top-tier status level is another way the airline is differentiating itself.

#6127. California City Approves Protections for Polyamorous Arrangements

Nobody could have seen this coming, except all the conservatives who said it would happen.

Then-mayor of West Hollywood Chelsea Lee Byers attends the Stonewall Democratic Club’s 50th-anniversary celebration in West Hollywood, Calif., November 15, 2025.

Wilbert Roberts/Getty Images for Connor Treacy

The West Hollywood City Council unanimously approved an ordinance that allows multi-partner relationships (like a so-called throuple) to formally register as a domestic relationship and receive certain legal protections at the local level, such as visitation rights in jail and rental privileges. A “multi-partner relationship,” per the ordinance, requires that the individuals involved share “the common necessities of life,” are over age 18, are competent enough to enter a contract, are all participating consensually, are “responsible for one another’s welfare,” and are not related by blood or a member of an already declared partnership. There is no expressed limit to the number of individuals who may be involved in a recognized multi-partner relationship, and people living outside the city can register their relationship.

The idea of protections for polyamory was brought to Councilmember Chelsea Lee Byers last year by Christina Fialho, an attorney who founded the “Rewrite the BiLine” organization that “reshape[s] cultural norms and drive[s] policy change” through media narratives to “advance health equity, economic opportunity, and civil rights for bi+ people and non-nuclear families.” Fialho told the Los Angeles Times that “this law is just the beginning. . . . I think it makes it possible for people to dream about a future they once thought was out of reach.” According to public records, the city council deemed it “necessary” to recognize “diverse relationship structures,” such as those involving more than two adults, because they are “becoming increasingly common.” The city frames the ordinance as an anti-discrimination measure with symbolic value:

#6126. Aman Confirms Its Secret Third Brand Is Atma, Opening in Miami in 2031

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: Photo-illustration of what Atma Miami, and its Baywalk View, might look like when the project opens in 2031. Aman Group

Aman has confirmed what the paper trail suggested to Skift in January. The open question is delivery: Janu, the group's second brand, has one hotel open after more than six years since its launch.

Aman Group said Tuesday it's launching Atma, a third hotel brand built around sports, wellness, and "performance living." The first property, a hotel with branded residences and a private members club, is set to be completed in Miami in 2031.

Tennis champion Novak Djokovic is a "global partner" who will help lead the brand's focus on longevity, nutrition, and wellness programming, Aman said.

The Tuesday announcement confirms Skift's reporting in January that the ultra-luxury operator planned to open a brand under the Atma name and that the Miami project would be its first location.

Aman Group is launching a third brand, Atma, built around sports, wellness, and what it calls "performance living," with the first property — a hotel with branded residences and a private members club — set for completion in Miami in 2031. Tennis champion Novak Djokovic is a "global partner" who will help lead programming on longevity, nutrition, and wellness, Aman said. The Miami project sits in a planned 1,049-foot tower on the Brickell waterfront, with a 120,000-square-foot spa and wellness center including indoor tennis, squash, and padel courts, a thermal spa, and a medical wellness center. Residences run from one-bedroom units to six-bedroom penthouses, and owners get priority nomination to the invitation-only Atma Club. Developers are OKO Group, owned by Aman Chairman and CEO Vlad Doronin, and Oak Row Equities. Aman didn't disclose a room count, financial terms, or how it will fund the growth. The announcement confirms Skift's January reporting on the brand name and the Miami location. It also lands against a slow rollout record: second brand Janu debuted in 2020 and only Janu Tokyo has opened, while Janu Dubai has moved from a 2027 opening to 2029 on the brand's website.
